World.title: City Hall in rush to expand drainage system ahead of El Nino
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja during an inspection tour of the ongoing drainage system expansion. [GPS]

Nairobi County has embarked on drainage expansion works aimed at mitigating floodwaters ahead of El Nino rains.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, while calling on city residents to remain alert and proactive, said City Hall has intensified preparations and accelerated identification of hotspots.

The governor on Friday said his administration is taking early and coordinated action to minimise the impact of heavy rains, urging residents to stay calm, pay attention to official information and follow guidance from the multi-agency team established to coordinate the city’s preparedness and emergency response.

“We are working proactively to address the challenges of flooding before El Nino hits the ground. We urge our people not to panic but to be alert and get information from our multi-agency team,” said Sakaja.

The Governor spoke during an inspection tour of several flood-prone areas in Nairobi, including the Mombasa Road-Bunyala Junction corridor and Globe Roundabout, which experienced significant flooding during previous heavy rains.

Sakaja said drainage works are already underway in the affected areas, with teams working to open up and deepen drainage channels, clear obstructions, and improve storm-water flow to prevent a repeat of the flooding witnessed previously.

His remarks come as weatherman warned of increased rainfall in the coming months, with Nairobi among the urban areas requiring heightened preparedness because of its exposure to flooding and the impact of heavy rainfall on roads, settlements and other critical infrastructure.

Sakaja said the county has so far brought together the disaster management teams, Kenya Red Cross, Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA) and Kenya National Highways Authority (KeNHA) under a coordinated programme worth Sh2.4 billion to strengthen Nairobi’s flood resilience.

Of the amount, Sh2 billion has been set aside for drainage and flood-mitigation works targeting 19 roads in flood-prone areas.

The projects are at an advanced stage, with tenders awarded and contractors expected to commence implementation after completion of the necessary processes.

Sakaja reiterated that the programme will complement ongoing county interventions under the Nairobi Regeneration Programme, which includes the rehabilitation and upgrading of critical infrastructure across the city.

“The Sh2 billion will support a comprehensive drainage overhaul that complements the ongoing Nairobi Regeneration Programme. Our goal is to permanently address the flooding challenges that have affected the city for many years,” Sakaja said.

He said the focus is not only on responding to floods after they occur, but on addressing the infrastructure weaknesses that have historically made Nairobi vulnerable to flooding.

To strengthen preparedness, the county has established five specialised sub-committees under the multi-agency framework.

The committees include Infrastructure and Drainage; Emergency Response and Evacuation; Shelter and Relief; Security and Traffic and Communication.

While the Infrastructure and Drainage committee will coordinate the clearing and improvement of drainage systems, rivers and other critical infrastructure, the Emergency Response and Evacuation committee will oversee rapid response, rescue and evacuation operations whenever emergencies occur.

The Shelter and Relief committee will prepare safe shelters and coordinate the provision of food, water, medical assistance and other essential support to affected residents.

The Security and Traffic committee will coordinate security, traffic management and emergency access, while the Communication committee will strengthen early-warning systems, public alerts and timely dissemination of information.

Sakaja said the county is also mobilising personnel, equipment and other resources to clear blocked drains, remove silt and waste and strengthen emergency response systems in areas identified as vulnerable.

He urged residents and their associations, businesses and other stakeholders to play an active role in flood preparedness by keeping drainage areas clear and paying attention to official warnings.

The county chief said residents in high-risk areas will be provided with timely information on emerging weather conditions and the actions they should take when heavy rains occur.

“We don’t want people to panic. We want people to be proactive, to listen to information and to work with us. The multi-agency team is in place, and we are preparing before the rains intensify,” Sakaja said.

According to him, the multi-agency approach will also help eliminate jurisdictional gaps by bringing together national and county agencies to operate as one coordinated team.

He said the combination of drainage upgrades, emergency preparedness, early-warning systems and coordinated response would strengthen Nairobi’s resilience and reduce disruption caused by heavy rains.

The multi-agency team is expected to meet next week to review progress, coordinate ongoing works and further push the city’s El Niño preparedness agenda.

World.title: Public officers eyeing elective posts to resign by February 10 - IEBC
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon addressing the press at a past press conference. [File, Standard]

Public officers seeking to contest elective positions in the 2027 General Election have until February 10, 2027, to resign from office, the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has announced.

IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said the deadline falls exactly six months before the August 10, 2027, General Election, which the Commission has confirmed will be held on a Tuesday.

“Any public officer who intends to contest in this election must resign from public office by Wednesday, 10th February 2027, which is exactly six months before the election,” Ethekon said.

The IEBC said adherence to the timelines will be non-negotiable, noting that they are legally binding and essential to ensuring an orderly electoral process.

Under the timetable, political parties must submit their membership lists and details of candidates participating in party primaries by March 16, 2027.

Party primaries and any related disputes must be concluded by May 8, while independent candidates are also required to meet their legal obligations by the same date.

Presidential aspirants will have until May 24 to submit lists of supporting voters drawn from a majority of Kenya’s counties.

Candidate registration will begin on May 29, with specific deadlines applying to the various elective positions.

The official campaign period will commence after candidates are registered, but not earlier than May 29, 2027.

Ethekon warned political parties, candidates and their supporters against breaching the prescribed campaign period, saying any electioneering outside the legal window will be unlawful.

The restrictions cover campaign posters, billboards, political caravans and other forms of campaigning.

Campaigning will close on August 7, 2027, 48 hours before Kenyans head to the polls.

“The law prescribes when election campaigns may commence,” Ethekon said, urging political parties, candidates and their supporters to strictly comply with electoral laws and regulations.

The deadline is among key milestones unveiled by the electoral commission as political parties, aspirants and other stakeholders begin preparations for the next General Election.

World.title: Schools will open on August 24 as scheduled, Ogamba says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Students heading home during recent demonstrations. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Ministry of Education said the official academic calendar remains unchanged.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, August 19, Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba insists that learners will return to school on Monday, August 24, 2026.

The CS has dismissed reports circulating on social media claiming that the reopening of schools for the third term has been postponed, warning parents, teachers, learners and education stakeholders against relying on unauthorised online notices.

“We wish to clarify that the academic calendar for Basic Education institutions and Teacher Training Colleges remains unchanged,” the CS said.

The clarification comes two days before the scheduled reopening of schools, amid reports circulating on social media platforms suggesting that the government had pushed back the start of Term III.

"Our attention has been drawn to misleading information circulating on various social media platforms, purporting that the academic calendar for basic education institutions and Teachers Training Colleges has been changed," he stated.

The Ministry termed the reports “FALSE” and urged members of the public to completely disregard them.

Ogamba said the Ministry had directed Regional Directors of Education, County Directors of Education and Sub-County Directors of Education to ensure strict compliance with the approved academic calendar contained in a circular dated October 9, 2025.

According to the Ministry, pre-primary, primary, junior, senior and secondary schools will begin Term III on Monday, August 24. The term will run for nine weeks and end on October 23, 2026.

The reopening marks the final academic term of the school year, with schools expected to implement the approved programmes as they prepare learners for the end-of-year national assessments and examinations.

Diploma Teachers Training Colleges will also resume academic operations on August 24, with their third term scheduled to conclude on November 6, 2026.

The Ministry further confirmed that the national assessment and examination calendar has not been altered for KPSEA, KILEA, KJSEA, KPLEA and KCSE are scheduled to begin from October 26, 2026, as earlier announced.

The Ministry also reminded schools that extracurricular activities and visits to secondary schools will remain banned during Term III.

The latest clarification is part of efforts by the government to prevent confusion among parents, learners and teachers as schools prepare to reopen.

Ogamba urged education stakeholders to obtain information through official Ministry communication channels, rather than social media posts whose authenticity cannot be established.

“Parents, teachers and learners and members of the public are advised to strictly rely on the Ministry's official communication channels and field officers for accurate information," he said.

World.title: Ruto denies Sh104bn SHA technology contract
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto has dismissed claims that the government entered into a controversial Sh104 billion contract with Safaricom and Apeiro Limited for the Social Health Authority (SHA) technology system.

Speaking on Tuesday evening at the Presidential Townhall held during the National Health Summit at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) in Nairobi, Ruto defended the government's investment in digital health, saying the technology was designed to improve transparency and accountability in the management of SHA services.

“There is no Sh104 billion contract. What we have done is design a digital system to make sure that everything is visible. Every treatment must be traceable, and every payment must be accounted for,” Ruto said.

He explained that the government had not purchased the technology outright but had engaged investors who own the equipment, with the State paying for the services provided.

His remarks were echoed by Digital Health Agency Chief Executive Anthony Lenaiyara, who rejected claims that SHA had committed Sh104 billion to technology upgrades.

“It is not correct or true that SHA has undertaken any upgrade or invested Sh104 billion in technology upgrades. What we did is build a digital superhighway comprising 43 systems to support Universal Health Coverage,” Lenaiyara said.

Lenaiyara said the technology infrastructure had been rolled out without requiring health facilities to purchase the devices, adding that the system had transformed the processing and accountability of SHA claims.

He contrasted the new system with the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) model, where claims were processed using physical files that moved between different offices for verification and approval.

Ruto also addressed other government programmes, saying the State had mobilised resources to construct 23,000 additional classrooms to ease pressure caused by shortages of learning spaces.

World.title: 'That was not healthcare, it was theft'- Ruto on old health system
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during the official opening of the Kenya Health Summit at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC), Nairobi, August 18,2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has accused the defunct National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) system of enabling theft from sick Kenyans, citing claims for procedures that never happened.

Speaking on Tuesday, August 18, at the opening of the Kenya Health Summit at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) in Nairobi, Ruto described the old system as opaque and vulnerable to abuse.

"We heard of claims for procedures that never happened, fictitious patients and inflated bills. That was not healthcare, it was theft, and theft from sick Kenyans," said Ruto.

He called digital health systems the backbone holding the reforms together and said they would close loopholes that let people profit from the system's weaknesses.

Ruto ranked Universal Health Coverage (UHC) alongside the Affordable Housing Programme as one of the government's most consequential social transformation efforts, crediting collaboration between national and county governments for changes in how healthcare is financed, delivered and accounted for.

The two-day summit, themed "Reforms Delivered, Health as a Right," has drawn more than 5,000 delegates to audit progress under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) and set priorities for the remainder of Ruto's term, according to Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale.

Ruto said 32.3 million Kenyans are now registered with the Social Health Authority (SHA), which replaced NHIF in October 2024.

Eight million have received treatment, more than 1.2 million mothers have been supported to deliver safely and more than 500,000 surgical procedures have been supported, he added.

He put Kenyans' previous annual out-of-pocket health spending at Sh150 billion ($1.16 billion), saying families had borrowed, sold assets or organised harambees to cover medical costs before the reforms.

"Millions paid out of pocket, borrowed, sold assets, organised harambees or stayed away from hospital because they could not afford care," said Ruto.

Since October 2024, SHA has received more than Sh209 billion ($1.62 billion) and paid more than Sh178 billion ($1.38 billion) to contracted facilities across all 47 counties, Ruto added.

He credited 107,800 Community Health Promoters, deployed under a shared financing arrangement between national and county governments, with reaching more than nine million households and referring over 750,000 people for further treatment.

On supply chains, Ruto said the Kenya Medical Supplies Authority's (KEMSA) fill rate had risen from about 40 per cent to 91 per cent, helped by a Sh1.5 billion ($11.6 million) recapitalisation and a Sh10 billion ($77.4 million) credit line.

The reforms rest on four laws Ruto signed on 19 October 2023: the Primary Health Care Act, the Social Health Insurance Act, the Digital Health Act and the Facilities Improvement Financing Act.

Ruto acknowledged gaps remained in registration, benefit clarity, claims processing and digital systems.

"The ultimate measure of reform is not the laws we pass or the numbers we register, but the experience of the patient in terms of dependable, affordable and dignified care," said Ruto.

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki, Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, Duale and Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja attended the opening session, alongside county governors, principal secretaries, members of Parliament and development partners.

The summit runs through Wednesday.

World.title: Gachagua: Opposition does not need Uhuru's money to send Ruto home
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua during a church service at PCEA Rev. Samuel Marima Memorial Church in Gatundu South, Kiambu on August 16, 2026. [Kimaku Chege, Standard]

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims that former President Uhuru Kenyatta is financing opposition activities against President William Ruto.

Addressing the allegations that Kenyatta was financing opposition campaigns, Gachagua insisted that the movement did not require money from the former President.

Gachagua says the movement seeking political change is driven by Kenyans and does not depend on financial sponsorship.

“Nasikia kwamba Uhuru is sponsoring us to campaign against you. Uhuru is not sponsoring us, we don't need any sponsorship, this is a mass movement for change which does not need funding,” he said.

He was speaking on Sunday, August 16, 2026, during a church service at PCEA Rev. Samuel Marima Memorial Church in Gatundu South, Kiambu County.

Gachagua further said the opposition had sufficient public support to challenge the Kenya Kwanza administration ahead of the 2027 General Election, insisting that Kenyans themselves were the driving force behind calls for a change of government.

He added that the public itself would determine the political fate of the Ruto administration.

“We don't need money but Kenyans will send you home,” Gachagua said.

The comments come against the backdrop of renewed debate over political alliances and the role of former leaders in Kenya's 2027 succession politics. Kenyatta, who served as President from 2013 to 2022, has largely remained outside the day-to-day administration of government since handing over power to Ruto.

Gachagua also defended Kenyatta against what he described as attempts to drag the former President into the current political contest.

“Uhuru Kenyatta asiguzwe na mtu yeyote. Alindwe na atetewe na apatiwe amani. Uhuru alifanya kazi yake na akastaafu,” Gachagua said.

The former Deputy President said Kenyatta should not be treated as a political candidate or blamed for the activities of opposition politicians.

“Nimemwambia Ruto unauliza Uhuru nini na sio candidate in the next election. I am your main opponent,” Gachagua said.

His remarks came amid an increasingly heated political contest over the direction of the country ahead of the 2027 elections.

Ruto and his administration have faced criticism from opposition figures over the economy, cost of living and the government's record since taking office.

Gachagua's comments also followed his broader criticism of the government's economic record.

Earlier in the church address, he challenged Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi's argument that increased consumption of soft drinks could indicate improved household incomes.

Gachagua argued that ordinary Kenyans were experiencing economic difficulties despite government claims of improved economic indicators. He said declining church offerings would provide a more meaningful indication of household financial wellbeing.

“If you want to know if the economy is doing well, ask the pastor about the offering; it will tell you how the economy is moving,” he said.

He further urged Kenyans to prepare for political change in 2027, arguing that the country required new leadership.

“Let us get in line. We look for new leadership that will fix our country and return it to where Uhuru Kenyatta left us,” Gachagua said

World.title: Gachagua: We will protect ourselves against goons
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua addresses residents of Naivasha where he lashed out at President William and told him to keep of former President Uhuru Kenyatta. [Antony Gitonga, Standard]

Former Deputy President and DCP party leader Rigathi Gachagua has vowed to fight back against goons allegedly disrupting his political rallies, saying his supporters will defend themselves if the police fail to protect them.

Speaking during the opening of DCP offices in Nakuru, Gachagua said they had received intelligence that the National Police Service (NPS) had been instructed to keep off areas where his rallies were being held.

Gachagua spoke a day after goons attacked his convoy at Kaptembwo in Nakuru West Sub-County, forcing him to abandon a DCP campaign rally and flee the scene alongside other leaders.

Six vehicles belonging to leaders, including Ol-Kalou MP Samuel Waweru, were vandalised during the incident as DCP leaders and supporters scrambled for safety.

Gachagua accused President William Ruto of allegedly planning the chaos through a Nakuru MP who, he claimed, had paid goons to disrupt his rallies.

“President William Ruto planned the chaos using a Nakuru MP who paid goons to attack us. This was despite his assurance that our campaign rallies would be protected,” Gachagua said.

He claimed he had received credible intelligence that police officers had been advised to keep away from Kaptembwo during the attack.

Gachagua further alleged that although the MP was associated with the Jubilee Party, he was being used by President Ruto to cause chaos.

“I have also spoken to Jubilee Party leaders to put their house in order. If it is proven that the MP is being used by the President, then he should be removed. That will inform how we relate to the Jubilee Party,” he said.

The former Deputy President said goons had allegedly been deployed to cause chaos at various stopovers, but some police officers who were unhappy with the Kenya Kwanza administration had provided his team with intelligence.

“We stood down our guard, hoping for protection from the government, but we are now on high alert and we will protect ourselves,” Gachagua said.

He also accused senior police officers in Nakuru of allegedly working with goons to disrupt his rallies.

According to Gachagua, junior police officers were unhappy with being allegedly forced to work with goons to cause chaos, steal property and kill Kenyans.

“These police officers have reduced salaries, they are not funded, they lack fuel and they are suffering,” he said.

World.title: Trump’s threats anger Omanis, leave observers puzzled
World.content:
Oman, a historic partner for the United States and proven mediator to Iran, was once again threatened by President Donald Trump over its negotiations with the Islamic Republic, leaving many in the region confused.

Trump’s warning on Monday reiterated a threat he issued in May to “blow up” Oman over its ongoing negotiations with Iran, again concerning the Strait of Hormuz, despite Trump himself agreeing in a signed document that Muscat would “conduct dialogue” with Tehran to define the future administration and maritime services in the strait.

Washington’s former ambassador to Oman, Marc J. Sievers was left “puzzled” on what caused the threats to the Gulf Arab country.

“Perhaps Trump didn’t mean to be taken literally but more the matter of getting the Omani attention, which I’m sure he did,” Sievers told CNN. “It’s hard to think of Admiral Cooper planning bombing raids on Oman,” a reference to US Central Command Chief Adm. Brad Cooper.

Muscat has branded itself as a neutral operator during the war, maintaining relations with Iran even as the latter fired large salvos of missiles and drones at neighboring Arab countries, and sometimes on Oman Throughout the war, it continued dialogue with Iran over ships transiting the vital Strait of Hormuz – which runs through Omani territory – and is currently negotiating with Tehran on managing the waterway despite global concern over Iran’s ambitions to seize the chokepoint.

During the war, Oman allowed vessels to use its sea routes to evade the waterways precariously designated by the Revolutionary Guards.

The former US top diplomat in Oman said Trump’s previous threats “upset” Oman, but Muscat “ought to see risk” in the repeated warnings.

“This is the second time that President Trump has issued (a) threat. … There is obviously something behind it that you would think the Omanis would want to pay attention to,” Sievers said.

It’s unclear how much progress Oman and Iran have made in their talks, or whether Washington has been involved in the ongoing negotiations – an absence that could factor into Trump’s anger toward the Gulf nation.

“(Trump’s) frustration broadly stems from the fact that Muscat pursues an independent policy toward Iran that does not always align with US preferences. Ironically, however, this is precisely what enables Muscat to play the mediating role that Washington often relies upon to facilitate contact with Tehran,” Hasan Alhasan, senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told CNN.

Qatar, another Gulf Arab country that has successfully mediated agreements with Iran, had coordinated its negotiations closely with the US.

“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News’ Trey Yingst.

A drone view shows vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, in June. Stringer/Reuters

Muted reaction

In Oman and across the wider region, governments remained quiet and issued no condemnation or rebuke of Trump’s threats. CNN reached out to the Omani Foreign Ministry for comment but has received no response.

Yet Omani social media commentators were critical of Trump’s threats. One commentator, Zakaria Al-Muharrmi, spoke about Oman’s past diplomatic assistance to the US.

“America’s wise leaders know that Oman is the one that freed many detained American citizens in Tehran, and that it is the one that convinced the Houthis to stop shelling American warships, and that it is the key to the solution in the Strait of Hormuz crisis,” Al-Muharrmi wrote on X.

The Omani commentator added that Trump’s “rude language” could lead to Oman freezing its efforts to save Republicans from “rising fuel bills” and an “anticipated loss in the midterm elections”

Another Omani commentator, Abdullah Adawi, said that Trump chose “escalation and threats” against a US ally because it “stuck to its position and its independent decision.”

Abdulkhaleq Abdullah, a political scientist from neighboring United Arab Emirates, said Trump’s threats are “completely rejected” and must be condemned by Gulf Arab countries in the “strongest terms.”

The Al Mirani Fort and traditional houses are surrounded by mountains, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Muscat, Oman, March 12, 2026. REUTERS/Benoit Tessier Benoit Tessier/Reuters

‘Misdirected and short-sighted’

An agreement intended to lead to peace talks between the US and Iran expired Monday, leaving both nations deadlocked in a stalemate over management of the Strait of Hormuz, the future of frozen Iranian funds and Tehran’s nuclear program.

Both countries committed in the Memorandum of Understanding in June to achieve a “final deal in maximum 60 days” but the ceasefire was soon mired by infringements.

Iran had rejected how ships were choosing to transit through the strait and began targeting vessels, and the US launched intensive strikes against Iranian targets in response. The Islamic Republic also fired missiles and drones onto neighboring countries hosting US bases.

Oman and Iran are now engaged in negotiations to resolve how ships cross the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian officials. If the issue of movement in the maritime chokepoint is resolved with agreement from Washington and its allies across the region, it may remove a major hurdle towards unlocking further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions.

“Trump’s anger at Oman is both misdirected and short-sighted,” Alhasan, the IISS analyst, said. “It is misdirected because Omani mediation has been sought by successive US administrations including the current one to facilitate talks with Tehran. … It is short sighted because Oman will likely be key to any future US-Iran peace deal and transit regime in the strait that emerges from it,” he said.

“The US, whose strategic credibility in the region is already in shambles, cannot afford to lose a partner as critical as Oman is to the future of one of the world’s most significant and hotly contested maritime choke points.”

World.title: Israeli military admits for first time to firing on car carrying 5-year-old Hind Rajab as it opens criminal probe
World.content:
The Israeli military acknowledged for the first time on Wednesday that it opened fire on the vehicle carrying 5-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza and said it had opened a criminal investigation into the killing.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) had previously denied involvement in the January 2024 killing, saying months later that a preliminary investigation found its forces were “not present near the vehicle or within firing range” of the vehicle.

The case is one of two-high profile incidents into which the military has opened criminal investigations. But the military said that it would not probe three other attacks from the early months of the war that killed aid workers.

Palestinian Ambassador to the UN Riyad Mansour slammed Israel’s past investigations as “not independent and not credible,” telling CNN’s Jim Sciutto that he doesn’t believe this investigation will be any different. A credible investigation, he said, would result in the arrest of those responsible for Rajab’s killing.

Rajab was one of seven family members traveling in a vehicle in northern Gaza on when they came under Israeli fire. Rajab survived the initial fire and pleaded on the phone for hours with Palestinian paramedics to come rescue her. Afterwards, an ambulance dispatched to save her also came under fire.

Twelve days later, Rajab’s body was found in a car riddled with bullets.

“The findings of the examination indicate that IDF troops fired at a vehicle that was approaching them,” the IDF said in a statement.

“Following review of the findings an due to apparent failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division.”

The Hind Rajab Foundation said in a statement that investigations by Israeli forces “overwhelmingly end without meaningful examination, prosecution, or punishment. In the small number of cases in which soldiers have been convicted of crimes, the punishments imposed have often been exceptionally lenient or administrative in nature.”

Recordings of Rajab’s call with paramedics gained international attention, driving calls for accountability for her killing and that of thousands of other children in Gaza. A film about the incident, “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” was nominated for an Oscar in 2026.

A destroyed car where the body of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who begged Gaza rescuers to send help after being trapped by Israeli military fire, was found along with her family. REUTERS/Stringer Reuters

The investigation into Hind Rajab’s death is part of the IDF’s first comprehensive report on alleged war crimes since the start of the war in Gaza in October 2023.

The IDF General Staff’s Fact Finding and Assessment Mechanism concluded investigating 150 incidents, which were transferred to the military’s top lawyer to decide on opening criminal investigations. Of the 150 inquiries, five decisions were published on Wednesday, while the others await a decision from the military advocate-general.

The IDF also announced it has launched a criminal investigation into the March 2025 killing of 15 paramedics and first responders who were traveling in ambulances and other emergency response vehicles.

The IDF initially claimed the vehicles were driving suspiciously without headlights or emergency signals, which was later directly contradicted by video of the convoy of vehicles traveling with flashing lights. The group were buried in a mass grave along with their emergency vehicles.

The Israeli military subsequently acknowledged “professional failures” in the incident and insisted there had been “no ethical gaps.” But in its statement on Wednesday, the IDF said “the firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct.”

Outrage over other killings

In three other incidents, the military determined there was no reasonable suspicion of criminal conduct to justify opening a criminal investigation: the April 2024 killing of the seven World Central Kitchen (WCK) humanitarian aid workers in Deir El-Balah, a February 2024 strike on a Doctors Without Borders / Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) shelter in Khan Younis that killed two employees, and a November 2023 strike on an MSF convoy which killed two additional employees.

In the attack that killed the WCK employees, the IDF said it found “serious failures” in the process that mistakenly led the military to believe the humanitarian convoy was taken over by a group of Hamas fighters. But the military advocate-general did not find “reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said.

In a statement, WCK blasted the decision not to open a criminal investigation, calling it “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.”

“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.

Australia too, expressed outrage at the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings for those behind the attack that killed WCK employees, including Australian national Zomi Frankcom.

“Zomi represented the best of Australia. Her courage deserves to be celebrated. Her family deserves justice,” Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement on Thursday. “This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect.”

Wong said she would call in the Israeli ambassador to Australia, and has told Australia’s envoy to Israel to convey Canberra’s views to the Israeli government directly. The Australian foreign minister said her government would “not step pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues.”

The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF’s illegal conduct,” WCK said.

World.title: Melania Trump prioritizes policy over public presence this term
World.content:
Melania Trump grew up attending Formula 1 races with her father in her native Slovenia.

On Thursday, America’s first lady will merge that longtime personal interest in cars and racing with a new one: foster youth.

She’s teaming up with IndyCar and Fox Corporation to launch new scholarship opportunities for young adults transitioning out of foster care, to be unveiled at a White House Rose Garden announcement alongside President Donald Trump ahead of this weekend’s Grand Prix in Washington, DC.

The event — which her external senior adviser previewed as “a plopdown on culture like you’ve never seen before” — marks a rare public appearance for Melania Trump, who has kept a much lower profile during her husband’s second term and hasn’t been seen in public since the FIFA World Cup on July 19. But it’s also reflection of how she’s charting her own course as first lady — eschewing some of the more traditional, public roles of the job while engaging behind the scenes in substantive policy work — specifically on her foster care initiative, “Fostering the Future.”

In recent weeks, for example, Trump skipped events where any of her predecessors’ absence might have been noticed: the funeral of the president’s close friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham, the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner and a recent dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base for US service members killed in the Iran war.

She’s spent most of that time at the president’s Bedminster, New Jersey, golf club and away from the White House, which is an active construction zone amid her husband’s various pet projects. And earlier this year, aside from a surprise statement seeking to distance herself from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, many of Trump’s public appearances were dedicated to promoting her multimillion-dollar deal with Amazon on her eponymous documentary.

But away from the glare of the cameras, sources told CNN, the first lady and her team are intensely engaged in a more focused policy operation than during her husband’s first term, when her multi-pronged “Be Best” initiative failed to gain significant traction or results.

It’s not clear what first spurred the first lady’s interest in foster care. She’s been engaged in other efforts around children — to promote the responsible use of AI, for example, and working to reunite kids separated from their families during Russia’s war against Ukraine. But her office declined to provide information about her specific motivation on this issue. (Approximately 400,000 American youth live in foster care, according to the US Department of Education, with one in five experiencing homelessness when transitioning out of the system, per the National Youth in Transition Database.) Trump’s advocacy began shortly after her husband’s first term, when she launched a series of scholarships in 2021.

First lady Melania Trump sits next to President Donald Trump as he holds a signed executive order regarding foster care, in the East Room of the White House on November 13, 2025. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Since returning to the White House, she’s pushed for an executive order signed by the president last November, which officials say has kickstarted action at the state level to track child welfare data and to end the so-called orphan tax; debuted IRA-style savings accounts for children in foster care; and secured a $25 million investment in her husband’s 2026 budget for housing and support for youth transitioning out of the system. She’s appealed on Capitol Hill for children aging out of the foster care system, and her team is working closely with Congress to overhaul programs supporting housing, education and training programs for foster youth and former foster youth, although the legislation remains stalled.

Her office, one senior administration told CNN, is “thinking much more about legacy,” including by bringing in “folks with bona fide policy chops to help implement that.”

While Trump has assembled a much smaller staff of seven — compared to more than a dozen on her team during the first term — foster youth advocates have taken note of the hiring of Sarah Gesiriech, a former USAID official who advised former first lady Laura Bush and Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, as her director of policy. Trump’s office frequently engages across agencies, often with specific asks, the senior official said.

“They’re really driving agencies to take actions that will be beneficial to foster youth. Ultimately, the agencies have to take those actions, but the first lady’s office is sitting in the cockpit,” the official said.

Experts in child welfare who spoke to CNN generally applauded the first lady’s advocacy, though some privately questioned whether other policies driven by her husband’s administration have undermined the work she is doing.

“It’s good that there is a national conversation about these young people,” said Chantal Hinds, a lawyer and senior policy manager at Children’s Defense Fund of New York who specializes in historically marginalized and underserved children and families.

“However, I think that the big elephant in the room is what’s happening on the side of the administration and how those things will also impact and likely hinder the true effectiveness of some of these changes that are happening for young people,” she said.

Hinds cited cutbacks to safety net programs, like food stamps and changes to the Medicaid system, as examples of how the Trump administration “is putting families in more precarious situations,” which, she suggested could increase “the number of young people that enter the system to begin with.” Hinds also pointed to the Trump administration taking aim at transgender rights, noting that roughly 30% of foster youth identify as LGBTQ.

Her message to the first lady? Keep up the advocacy but push back on some of what her husband’s administration is doing.

First lady Melania Trump stands between President Donald Trump and their son Barron Trump during the UFC Freedom 250 event on the South Lawn of the White House on June 14. Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC/Getty Images

The office of the first lady did not respond to CNN’s inquiry as to whether Melania Trump, who has long held an independent streak, had offered any of that pushback privately.

But Trump’s attention on foster youth has already “accelerated action,” the senior official said, leading to more acceptance in some political corners of what’s typically been a bipartisan issue. That’s been the case for something called “kin licensure,” a policy advocates have long pushed for that enables relatives and family members to register to become licensed foster parents.

“We’ve had some red states say, ‘Hey, thanks so much. We were hitting some brick walls with our legislature. Now that we’ve been able to say this is related to the Trump Fostering the Future initiative, it got us over some of those initial hurdles,’” the official said.

World.title: World’s top humanoid robot maker surges in blockbuster market debut in China
World.content:
Shares of the world’s largest humanoid robot maker by sales Unitree jumped more than 600% in its trading debut in Shanghai on Wednesday, in a testament to its status as the poster child of China’s robotic advancement.

Having captured global attention with its dancing and kung-fu fighting androids, Unitree raised 6.1 billion yuan ($905 million) in its initial public offering that was oversubscribed more than 8,000 times, a record for the city’s tech-focused STAR market, which is seen as China’s version of the Nasdaq.

On Monday, the Hangzhou-based company unveiled a new humanoid robot dubbed “Superman,” which it said can jump as high as two metres and run at a speed of 12.66 metres per second.

Unitree shot to national prominence last year after its robots took to China’s biggest stage, the annual Lunar New Year gala, with sleek dancing choreography. Since then, the company has emerged as a key strategic firm in the country’s ambition to dominate future technology, with its founder Wang Xingxing seated in the front row at President Xi Jinping’s rare symposium with top tech businesses last year.

As China’s economic growth slows and its workforce shrinks, Beijing has bet billions of dollars on humanoid robots as the next disruptive product, seeing them as the “new high ground of technological competition and a fresh frontier for future industries,” according to a 2023 policy document.

Getting ahead in the burgeoning industry could also boost China’s standing in the intensifying competition with the US on artificial intelligence and advanced technology.

The market debut makes Unitree the first humanoid robot maker to be listed in mainland China. Other Chinese android firms, including UBTECH and Dobot, have been trading in Hong Kong, while Agibot, another frontrunner in the sector, is pursuing an IPO in the city.

“Unitree IPO is regarded as a key milestone for the humanoid industry and can serve as a benchmark for other IPOs in the pipeline,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at market analysis firm Counterpoint Research.

China already dominates humanoid robot sales globally. Last year, Chinese firms accounted for the vast majority of global android deliveries, far outpacing American competitors like Tesla, Figure AI and Boston Dynamics.

However, the technology remains under both hardware and software constraints, with bipedal robots still years away from full-scale deployment, whether on factory floors or at home, experts say.

For now, research and educational institution use accounted for the majority of Unitree’s sales, while industrial deployments remained less than 10% in the first three quarters of 2025, its earlier filing showed.

“Unitree has demonstrated strong technology and commercial traction, but moving from demonstrations and early deployments to widespread industrial adoption will take time,” said Kangyuxiao Li, equity analyst at Morningstar, a financial services firm.

Proceeds from the IPO, according to its prospectus, will be used for the research and development of embodied AI models and robot hardware, as well as factory expansion.

Going gaga over Unitree

Unitree may not be a household name yet. But if you have scrolled past videos of human-like robots performing backflips or dancing to Lady Gaga’s Abracadabra on America’s Got Talent, you have likely seen the company’s products.

Founded in China’s eastern tech hub of Hangzhou in 2016, Unitree is backed by several well-known Chinese companies, ranging from food delivery giant Meituan, tech mammoth Tencent, Alibaba and AI startup DeepSeek.

Besides humanoid robots, the firm also makes quadruped robots, known as robot dogs, which accounted for about 42% of its revenue last year.

In just two years, its revenue skyrocketed more than 10 times to nearly 1.7 billion yuan ($252 million) in 2025, its prospectus showed.

Unitree is also one of the few companies in the field which has achieved profitability, delivering a net profit of 278 million yuan ($41 million) last year.

Last year, it delivered more than 5,500 humanoid robots across the world, making it the world’s largest seller of androids.

Despite being a frontrunner in the industry, Qi of Counterpoint Research cautioned that Unitree’s edge appears to rely mostly on hardware and motion control capability, and that they need to beef up their research and development investment in embodied AI models, which serve as the machines’ brains.

In an apparent bid to address such a weakness, a partnership between Unitree and US tech giant Nvidia was announced in June for research and development.

Geopolitical restrictions

The future of Unitree, however, hinges beyond its product competitiveness.

In June, Unitree was added to the US government’s blacklist of Chinese military-linked companies and barred from doing business with the Pentagon.

And last month, Washington banned new humanoid and quadruped robot imports from foreign manufacturers, calling them a national security risks – in a move aimed at China.

While the restrictions do not cover existing models approved to be sold in the US, it could hurt future sales for companies like Unitree, particularly as over 40% of its revenue is generated overseas.

Unitree has said in its prospectus that it “may be unable to sustain rapid growth in overseas sales and could even see its performance decline” if the US continues to impose restrictions.

Beyond borders, Ming Lee, head of Greater China autos and industrials research at BofA Global Research, said Unitree also has to show it can successfully deploy its robots across various industry applications, and build up its embodied AI system.

World.title: The North Coast’s “Forbidden City”
World.content:
For 500 years (1420–1924), China’s “Forbidden City” served as the exclusive realm of 24 emperors—off-limits to the public, shielded by high walls, massive gates, stern guards, and a deep, wide moat.

Today, that once-impenetrable palace sits in the heart of Beijing as one of the world’s most famous tourist landmarks, welcoming millions of visitors from every corner of the globe.

I was reminded of the Forbidden City during my visit to New Alamein this summer.

Granted, New Alamein is physically wide open to the public; it boasts ultra-wide avenues, soaring skyscrapers, beautifully diverse residential neighborhoods, and modern commercial hubs.

Yet, it feels strangely exclusive—far beyond the financial reach of most average visitors, with an empty, ghost-town atmosphere where actual residents are nowhere to be seen.

The city appears engineered strictly for car owners, yet you quickly realize that every single convenience comes with a price tag. While almost every building features covered parking garages, they remain locked for one reason or another.

Open-air parking is available, but at an official fee ranging from LE 100 to LE 200—collected exclusively via Visa card by young workers hired by the city authority.

New Alamein was designed to serve as Egypt’s modern northern waterfront, however you mostly glimpse the sea from a distance.

Reaching the shore from your parked car requires at least a 15-minute walk.

Actual beach access comes with its own entry fees, starting at LE 600 per person and soaring to LE 3,000 at certain venues if you happen to be alone just looking to take in the view.

The city features a massive mall housing dozens of shops, restaurants, and cafes, alongside an overpriced covered parking garage.

Nearby lies a new waterfront market complex known by its English name, the “North Market.”

Finding it is a challenge regardless of the language you speak; the city is so new that most staff—despite wearing formal uniforms and distinctive white caps—are unfamiliar with its own landmarks.

One of the most peculiar sights in New Alamein is a dense cluster of nearly twenty well-known coffee chains lined up side-by-side along the corner of a massive plaza. Their sole redeeming feature? Free parking.

Founded eight years ago in 2018 with investments ranging between LE 240 and LE 350 billion, New Alamein is still struggling to take off.

Compared to private-sector developments built during the same period—which now host hundreds of thousands of residents and pulse with activity—the city remains surprisingly quiet.

This stark contrast raises serious questions about why such a promising project continues to stall despite unlimited government backing.

World.title: Over 100 dead in Central African Republic mine collapse
World.content:
An underground collapse triggered by severe landslides has leveled an informal gold mine in the border community of Zamboye, leaving over 100 miners dead. The site of the disaster—situated in the western reaches of the Central African Republic near the Cameroonian border, about 50 kilometers from Baboua—suffered a catastrophic structural failure when several subterranean tunnels caved in simultaneously. The collapse released a massive torrent of unstable, sandy earth that quickly buried the laborers working below. Casualties and demographics

Emergency workers and local Red Cross volunteers have retrieved upwards of 100 bodies from the debris.

The victims consist of both Central African nationals and workers from neighboring Cameroon.

Regional officials from eastern Cameroon are coordinating cross-border identification efforts.

Rescue concerns

Recovery crews are currently using heavy excavators and machinery to clear the heavy soil layer. However, community leaders have expressed deep concern that using heavy equipment might crush any pockets of space where survivors could potentially be clinging to life.





Outlook

Local authorities have launched an inquiry to trace the exact cause of the structural failure. Given that the precise count of workers inside the shaft during the cave-in remains unconfirmed, officials caution that the death toll will likely climb as recovery operations continue.

World.title: Liberia: Golden Touch Pushes Back Against MPR/APM Investigation, Says Dukuly’s Role Was Lawful
World.content:
Golden Touch said that description was inaccurate and insisted that Dukuly’s involvement with the company was neither improper nor unlawful. “There is nothing improper, unlawful, or fraudulent about Mr. Dukuly’s involvement with Golden Touch,” the company said.

MONROVIA — Golden Touch Health Care LLC has mounted a strong defense of its operations and the involvement of Sekou Dukuly, rejecting what it describes as inaccurate implications contained in an investigation published by MPR News and APM Reports.

The healthcare company issued its response Friday, four days after the August 17 publication, maintaining that it has operated with a commitment to providing stable and long-term care to Minnesotans with significant medical and behavioral health needs.

Golden Touch said the report prompted the company to clarify its position, particularly concerning claims surrounding Dukuly and his relationship with the healthcare organization.

At the center of the company’s response is its rejection of the characterization that Dukuly was “moonlighting” in Minnesota while simultaneously living and working in public service in Liberia.

Golden Touch said that description was inaccurate and insisted that Dukuly’s involvement with the company was neither improper nor unlawful.

“There is nothing improper, unlawful, or fraudulent about Mr. Dukuly’s involvement with Golden Touch,” the company said.

The company did not disclose additional details about Dukuly’s specific responsibilities in its statement but maintained that his involvement with Golden Touch should not be interpreted as evidence of wrongdoing.

Golden Touch also defended the structure of its Minnesota operations, emphasizing that it works to comply with applicable assisted living laws and regulations.

According to the company, licensed assisted living directors are present in Minnesota to oversee the care and supervision provided to residents at its facilities.

The company said those arrangements are intended to ensure that residents receive the necessary care and oversight required under Minnesota regulations.

Golden Touch further highlighted its history in the healthcare sector, saying it has provided services since 2017 to residents with complex medical and behavioral health needs.

The company said its work has helped some residents progress toward greater independence, while its directors, caregivers and nurses have remained responsible for providing services throughout the year.

“Our directors, caregivers, and nurses show up 365 days a year,” Golden Touch said, adding that it stands behind their professionalism and compassion.

Alongside its defense of its operations, Golden Touch expressed sympathy to families who lost loved ones while receiving care from the company.

The statement said the company recognizes the significance of those losses and extended condolences to affected families before addressing the issues raised by the MPR/APM investigation.

Golden Touch’s response also took issue with what it described as political implications arising from the report.

The company suggested that some individuals could attempt to use the report for political purposes, but it maintained that such considerations would not change its focus on healthcare delivery.

“It is unfortunate that some may seek political gain based on the inaccurate implications made in the MPR/APM report,” the company stated.

Rather than engage in what it considers political distractions, Golden Touch said it intends to continue concentrating on its healthcare responsibilities and the people who depend on its services.

The company’s statement places particular emphasis on its commitment to Minnesota residents, arguing that its primary responsibility remains providing quality care to people with medical and behavioral health needs.

The dispute highlights the broader importance of oversight, management and compliance within residential healthcare facilities, particularly those serving residents requiring specialized support.

Golden Touch said its continued operations are guided by Minnesota’s assisted living requirements and that licensed professionals oversee care at its facilities.

Golden Touch said it will remain focused on its stated mission rather than the controversy surrounding the report. “Golden Touch will remain focused on what it has always done: providing quality care to Minnesotans in need,” the company said.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-VP Howard Taylor Remains Hospitalized in Police Custody as Bong Residents Rally Behind Her
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County — In the streets, communities and political circles of Bong County, the detention Wednesday of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has opened a new chapter in a political story that stretches from the civil war years to the highest office in Liberia.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected] & Webster Clayeh

For a county that once gave Howard-Taylor two consecutive mandates to represent it in the Liberian Senate, later rallied behind the political ticket that carried her to the vice presidency and watched her influence produce other elected officials, her current predicament has been met with emotions ranging from disbelief and sadness to defiance, caution and demands for evidence.

Howard-Taylor, a native of Sanoyea District, is facing serious criminal allegations following her detention at Roberts International Airport on Wednesday as she attempted to travel outside Liberia.

Her arrest has placed one of Bong County’s most recognizable political daughters at the center of an investigation the government says is aimed at dismantling an alleged transnational narcotics trafficking network.

But the reaction from Bong County shows that the case is unlikely to be viewed simply as another criminal proceeding. For many residents, Howard-Taylor’s political history has created a deep emotional connection between the former Vice President and the county she represented for 18 years.

Her supporters argue that the allegations must be proven in court. Others are questioning the circumstances surrounding her detention and demanding that the government explain the evidence linking her to the alleged drug network.

Still others say the investigation should be allowed to proceed without political interference, while insisting that Howard-Taylor, like every other accused person, deserves due process.

Howard-Taylor’s political roots are firmly planted in Sanoyea District, where her journey into national politics began to take shape. In 2005, she won election as senator of Bong County by an overwhelming margin, establishing herself as one of the county’s most powerful political figures.

Her victory was not a short-lived political moment. In 2014, she successfully returned to the Senate, winning another nine-year term and reinforcing her position as a dominant force in Bong County politics.

Her two victories meant that for 18 years she was not merely a national political figure with connections to Bong County. She was one of the principal political representatives of the county in Monrovia.

That history has become central to the current reaction. Residents who once saw Howard-Taylor travel between Gbarnga, Sanoyea and Monrovia as a senator and later as Vice President are now watching as she faces detention and criminal charges. Now, she is an accused person in a major narcotics investigation.

The Taylor Legacy and Bong County

Howard-Taylor’s political story cannot be completely separated from the political history of Charles Taylor. Her former husband, Charles Taylor, used Gbarnga as a major base during Liberia’s civil war before eventually becoming President of Liberia. The Taylor movement’s presence in Bong County left a lasting political imprint.

Gbarnga became closely identified with Charles Taylor’s political and military rise, and the Taylor name subsequently carried substantial political weight in the county.

When Howard-Taylor entered politics, that historical connection formed part of the political environment surrounding her. But over time, Howard-Taylor developed a political identity of her own.

Her two Senate victories demonstrated her ability to maintain an electoral constituency in Bong County, while her later selection as George Weah’s running mate in 2017 elevated her from county-level political prominence to national executive power. Her political journey therefore became intertwined with both the history of Bong County and the evolution of Liberia’s opposition politics.

2017 Changed Everything

The 2017 presidential election became one of the defining moments of Howard-Taylor’s political career. George Weah selected her as his running mate on the ticket of the Coalition for Democratic Change, a political alliance that included Howard-Taylor’s National Patriotic Party and the Liberia People Democratic Change. The partnership proved decisive.

In Bong County, the CDC secured victory in both rounds of the 2017 presidential election. For supporters of Howard-Taylor, the result was evidence that her political influence had survived beyond her Senate years.

The former senator had helped position herself at the center of a political movement that eventually captured Liberia’s presidency. Her influence was also reflected in the political careers of other lawmakers.

Edward Karfiah won election as representative of District Five in 2011, while Josiah Marvin Cole later won election as representative of Jorquelleh District Three. Those victories contributed to the perception that Howard-Taylor’s political network extended well beyond her own campaigns.

For years, her supporters viewed her as one of the county’s most effective political mobilizers. Her detention therefore has consequences that extend beyond one individual.

A Sudden Turn at the Airport

The latest chapter began at Roberts International Airport. Howard-Taylor was stopped from leaving Liberia and subsequently taken to the headquarters of the Liberia National Police. The action immediately generated questions among supporters and political observers.

The government, however, says the action was connected to an ongoing investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. Following investigative procedures and a review of evidence presented by the Joint National Security Investigative Team, Howard-Taylor was formally charged.

The Justice Ministry said the charges include offenses under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act of 2023, Liberia’s Penal Law and the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law.

Seven Serious Allegations

Under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act, Howard-Taylor is accused of unlicensed importation of a controlled drug or substance, unlicensed sale, trading, administration, dispensation, delivery, distribution, dispatch in transit and transportation of a controlled drug or substance, and illicit trafficking of a controlled drug or substance.

Under Chapter 10 of Liberia’s Penal Law, she faces allegations involving criminal solicitation, criminal facilitation and criminal conspiracy.

She also faces a money-laundering allegation under the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law. The government has also announced charges in absentia against three alleged members or organizers of the network: Croatian nationals Nikolai Ivancic and Mihovil Vrlovac and Ukrainian national Tara Zaderieko.

Bong County Asks for More Than Headlines

For residents like Marvelene Lepukoi, the seriousness of the allegations makes evidence even more important. Lepukoi has called

on the government to demonstrate independent evidence connecting Howard-Taylor to the alleged narcotics operation. “If Sheikh Basirou is truly the government’s star witness, then the public deserves to know exactly what independent evidence corroborates his claims,” she said.

Her position is that the case should be determined through the courts rather than public accusations. “If there is credible evidence against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, present it before the court and allow it to be properly authenticated, challenged, and tested under the law,” she said.

Lepukoi’s remarks reflect a central concern among some residents: whether the public debate surrounding the case is moving faster than the evidence that will eventually be presented in court. She insists that communication with another person, without more, does not establish participation in an alleged narcotics organization.

He said: “Bring the evidence, establish the connection, and prove the allegations beyond reasonable doubt.”

Emmanuel Weah of Gbarnga said the opposition should not allow Howard-Taylor’s detention to distract from the larger questions surrounding the country’s narcotics investigation. He argued that Liberians still need answers concerning the drug case and that the government must not use prominent political figures to divert attention from unresolved questions.

“The government must not be allowed to shift public attention away from the central questions by turning political figures into scapegoats,” Weah said. His comments reveal a suspicion among some residents that the case could become politically charged because of Howard-Taylor’s history and continuing influence.

But Archie Gboe, a Bong County native residing in Monrovia, approached the issue from a democratic perspective. “What a sad day for Liberia’s democracy,” Gboe said.

He described the repeated emergence of what he considers political witch-hunts as damaging to Liberia’s democratic culture. Although he acknowledged that nobody should be above the law, Gboe questioned the manner in which the former Vice President was stopped at the airport. For him, the government could have used established investigative procedures to request her cooperation rather than allowing the detention to occur in such circumstances.

Ebenezer Gotolo offered another perspective. Rather than immediately defending or condemning Howard-Taylor, he urged Liberians to recognize that being questioned or charged does not amount to being convicted.

“If a former Vice President is invited by the police in connection with an ongoing drug investigation, the matter should be approached through the rule of law and due process—not immediately turned into a political battle,” Gotolo said.

He emphasized that the fight against drugs should not belong to either the government or opposition. “An invitation for questioning is not the same as a declaration of guilt,” he said. Gotolo urged investigators to conduct their work professionally while protecting the rights of everyone involved.

His position may represent the middle ground emerging from the county: support the investigation, but do not abandon due process. Among the strongest reactions has come from Howard-Taylor’s home district.

David Gorlormator, a native of Sanoyea District, questioned the circumstances of the former Vice President’s detention. He asked why Howard-Taylor was allegedly not formally invited before being stopped at Roberts International Airport.

He also questioned the government’s broader handling of the drug investigation and whether all individuals alleged to have connections to the case are being treated equally. For Gorlormator and others, the government must demonstrate that its investigation is not influenced by political considerations.

Dr. George Toto, a native of Totota now living in the United States, responded to the allegations from a deeply personal perspective. Toto said he feels ashamed as a son of Bong County hearing allegations of such magnitude involving a daughter of the county.

For a county that has celebrated Howard-Taylor’s political accomplishments for years, the allegations have created a difficult moment. Residents are now being forced to reconcile the image of the powerful political figure they know with the allegations being brought against her by the state.

Victor Tokpah, a Gbarnga resident and Bong County native, said the government’s announcement has raised questions that should be answered through the legal process. Tokpah said he was neither defending Howard-Taylor nor suggesting that she should be exempt from the law.

He asked what specific drug, quantity, transaction, agreement or alleged proceeds form the basis of the charges. He also questioned whether the case involving Howard-Taylor is directly connected to the approximately US$317 million cocaine investigation or whether that connection is being assumed because the developments emerged around the same period.

Howard-Taylor hospitalized

On Thursday, Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor was rushed to GIMS Hospital in Sophie, Monrovia, after experiencing a medical emergency while in police custody.

Taylor was transported to the medical facility Thursday evening under heavy police escort after health practitioners reportedly observed a significant rise in her blood pressure.

The medical emergency occurred as authorities were preparing to transfer the former vice president to the Monrovia City Court, where she was expected to face proceedings stemming from allegations of drug trafficking and money laundering.

Medical personnel were called to the Liberia National Police Headquarters after concerns were raised about Taylor’s condition.

At the Gomez Institute of Medical Science hospital in Sophie Community, scores of individuals especially from the CDC along with her legal team visited the former Vice President.

Former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwel Saah Kemayah went to the hospital a visit former Vice President Taylor. While Kemayah was allowed entry, three lawmakers were denied.

Frank Saah Foko, Marvin Cole, and Eugine Kollie were prevented from entering the fence of the hospital. “I don’t know the reason for which they are denying me other people went and the police have them assets. But it is ok, at the appropriate time we will have asset,” Montserrado County District 9 Representative Foko said.

He added: “We are to make sure that transparency takes place, that is all we are asking for. We are also asking the citizens of Bong County to be on their alert, to remain peaceful, democratic. The strongest person is the law. We are going to invade the laws; it is our hope that all uphold the dignity of the law.”

While at the Hospital, her legal team issued a statement that it has requested additional time to gather information it says it needed to support the ongoing investigation involving the former vice president.

In the brief statement issued Thursday, August 20, Taylor’s lawyers said she remains at Police Headquarters while they seek additional time to prepare and gather information in connection with the investigation.

“Let it be known that the Former Vice President remains at the Police Headquarters as her counsels have requested additional time to gather information in support of the ongoing investigation,” the legal team said.

World.title: Liberia: First Group of 20 Third-Country Deportees Arrive In Liberia, Secretly Whisked From RIA as Five Reportedly Refuse Disembarked Plane
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia’s controversial deportation arrangement with the United States took effect Thursday with the arrival of the first 20 third-country deportees at Roberts International Airport, but the transfer was overshadowed by a dramatic standoff after five of the deportees reportedly refused to leave the aircraft and were restrained by U.S. federal agents.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The five men were among the 20 deportees flown to Liberia under an agreement between the Liberian government and the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump that could see as many as 1,200 third-country nationals sent to Liberia over the next 12 months.

According to The New York Times, the five men resisted efforts by American federal agents to remove them from the aircraft after it landed at Roberts International Airport.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes and eventually forced them off the plane. However, the five were subsequently returned to the aircraft.

The men were reportedly later flown onward to Equatorial Guinea, although the circumstances surrounding their reported transfer remain unclear.

The Liberian government has not publicly explained what happened to the five men, whether they were formally admitted into Liberia, or why they were reportedly flown to another African country.

Neither Liberian nor U.S. authorities had, as of publication, provided a detailed public account of the incident.

The episode has intensified questions about the implementation of the deportation agreement, including the legal status of the deportees, their consent or otherwise to being transferred to Liberia, and what happens when individuals refuse to disembark.

Five Refuse to Deplane

The confrontation reportedly began after the aircraft carrying the 20 deportees landed at RIA.

According to The New York Times, five men refused to leave the plane when U.S. federal agents attempted to remove them.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes before forcing them off the aircraft. The five were later returned to the plane, according to the report.

Their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea has raised additional questions about whether Liberia was ultimately their intended destination and whether other countries are involved in the implementation of the U.S. third-country deportation arrangement.

The Liberian government has yet to provide an official explanation.

Deportees Secretly Moved from RIA

The drama surrounding the five deportees unfolded against a backdrop of secrecy surrounding the arrival of the 20-person group.

Airport and state security personnel restricted journalists from accessing the arrival area and prevented local and international media organizations.

including AFP and DW, from observing the deportees’ processing.

According to a FrontPage Africa reporter at the scene, security officers ordered doors closed and were deployed at entry points, restricting movement in and out of the area.

Journalists later discovered that the deportees had already been moved from the airport without media access to their departure.

The group was reportedly transported from the airport in a bus operated by the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission through a back exit, rather than through the main arrival hall.

No interviews were permitted, and journalists were unable to obtain photographs or video footage of the deportees.

The manner in which the group was moved out of RIA has fueled criticism over the government’s handling of the arrangement and its commitment to transparency.

LRRRC Tight-Lipped

Officials of the LRRRC, the government agency responsible for receiving the deportees, declined to provide details about the group at the airport.

Staff referred questions to the commission’s headquarters in Montserrado County but did not provide information about the identities, nationalities or immediate plans for the 20 deportees.

The government had previously stated that the deportees would include nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries, with most expected to come from Latin American countries, including Venezuela, Cuba and Colombia.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah has said the deportees would be received “as guests” and would have the option to apply for asylum in Liberia.

Secretive Arrival Sparks Youth Anger

The secrecy surrounding the arrival has also triggered frustration among some Liberian youths, who argue that the government should prioritize addressing domestic unemployment and poverty before accepting deportees from other countries.

Youth advocate Levi Levala told FrontPage Africa that Liberia is already struggling with unemployment and inadequate social services.

“We, the youth in this country, have nothing right now. No job. No support. And now these people are being brought here? They say America will sponsor them, but Liberia is already suffering. This is not the partnership we need,” Levala said.

“My message to America is: take them back. Liberia is not a dump site,” he added.

Levala and other residents of Unification Town argued that Liberia’s economic challenges make the country ill-equipped to accommodate large numbers of third-country deportees.

How the Deal Came About

The Liberian government announced earlier this week that it had agreed to accept up to 1,200 people deported from the United States who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

The government has described the arrangement as “entirely humanitarian” and not a “quid pro quo,” while acknowledging that Liberia will receive U.S. support to manage the program.

The Ministry of Justice has not disclosed when the next group of deportees will arrive, although the government expects the full group of up to 1,200 to be accommodated over a 12-month period.

Rights Groups Demand Answers

The agreement has generated growing concern among human-rights advocates in Liberia and elsewhere in Africa, particularly over the prospect of countries accepting deportees who have no meaningful connection to them.

Liberian human-rights lawyer and activist Adama Dempster said the government must answer fundamental questions about the arrangement.

“The issue of deportations is raising many concerns that can’t be left unanswered,” Dempster said.

“What conditions will they be held in?” he asked, while questioning other aspects of the agreement.

The identities and backgrounds of the 20 deportees have not been publicly disclosed, making it unclear whether any have criminal records in the United States.

The lack of information has intensified calls for the Liberian government to publish the agreement and explain the legal framework governing the deportees’ arrival, stay and possible departure from Liberia.

A New Test for Liberia

Thursday’s events have placed the Boakai administration under renewed scrutiny over an agreement officials have defended as being in Liberia’s national interest.

But the refusal of five deportees to leave the aircraft — followed by their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea — has raised fresh questions about the humanitarian, legal and diplomatic dimensions of the arrangement.

It also remains unclear whether Liberia is simply the destination for the deportees or whether the agreement forms part of a broader U.S. arrangement involving multiple African countries.

As Liberia prepares for potentially hundreds more arrivals, pressure is mounting on the government to disclose the terms of the agreement, explain the treatment of the first 20 deportees and provide a full account of what happened to the five men who refused to disembark at Roberts International Airport.
