World.title: President Nicușor Dan to lead Romania’s delegation to UN General Assembly
World.content:
President Nicușor Dan will lead Romania’s delegation to the high-level segment of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, which will take place in New York next month, according to an announcement from the Presidential Administration.

The central theme of the next UN session is 'Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.'

The head of state will deliver the national statement in the plenary session of the UN General Assembly on September 23. He will highlight Romania’s efforts to support the organization’s reform process and the country’s contribution to ensuring peace, security and an international order based on rules and norms, according to the same source.

This is the first time president Nicușor Dan will attend the UN General Assembly. Last year, Romania was represented by foreign minister Oana Țoiu. Dan explained at the time that he did not go to New York because he considered it “more useful” to be present in the country.

At the next UN assembly, the president will also participate in New York in events organized on the sidelines of the high-level segment. He will hold bilateral meetings with other heads of state or government, including to support Romania’s candidacy for the leadership of the International Organisation of La Francophonie.

Former European Commissioner Dacian Cioloș is supported by Romania for the position of Secretary General of the OIF.

World.title: Environment Ministry says Romania exceeded PNRR target with over 5,000 recycling islands completed
World.content:
Romania has completed 5,091 digitized recycling islands nationwide, exceeding its target of 5,000 under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), the Environment Ministry announced. The investment’s total budget is EUR 72.75 million.

The waste collection systems have been installed across 36 counties, with Bacău, Bihor, Arad, Cluj, and Constanța among those hosting the largest numbers.

“The commissioning of these thousands of islands contributes to modernizing Romania’s waste management infrastructure,” interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said. “Through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, we managed to exceed the target of 5,000 islands and help Romanians make the transition to a circular economy more easily.”

The systems allow waste to be separated into five categories: paper and cardboard, plastic and metal, glass, biodegradable waste, and residual waste.

“Beyond projects and financing, the circular economy is built through cooperation between authorities, the private sector, and citizens,” minister Buzoianu also said. “These islands will contribute to a cleaner environment in the communities where they operate.”

Three types of collection systems were financed through the program: enclosed above-ground islands, above-ground islands with individual containers, and underground islands with individual containers. According to the ministry, the underground systems are intended in part for urban and tourist areas where available space is limited.

The investment also includes the development of a software platform for operating the recycling islands and managing the data they generate. It further covers measures to promote the “pay-as-you-throw” principle.

World.title: Animation film festival Animest returns to Bucharest in October with nature-themed edition
World.content:
The Animest International Animation Film Festival will hold its 21st edition in Bucharest from October 2 to 11, with a program exploring the relationship between people and the natural environment. Screenings and events will take place at Cinema Muzeul Țăranului, Cinemateca Eforie, Instituto Cervantes, and CINETic.

The thematic section will comprise three short-film programs titled Living with Nature, Human Nature, and Nature, curated by Animest artistic director Mihai Mitrică and French film journalist and historian Alexis Hunot.

“We propose three directions for observing how animated film approaches vital topics: questioning our relationship with the environment, reflecting on human nature, and imagining nature in our absence,” Hunot said.

The selection includes Karni Arieli and Saul Freed’s Wild Summon, which presents the life cycle of wild salmon through human figures, and Mark Baker’s The Village, a black comedy about the inhabitants of an isolated community. Other titles include Chris Landreth’s Ryan, which explores the life of Canadian animator Ryan Larkin, and Vergine Keaton’s Je criais contre la vie. Ou pour elle, in which a herd of deer begins hunting the dogs that pursued it.

The festival’s 2026 visual identity was created by Brazilian-Welsh illustrator and animation director Luiz Stockler. It depicts nature entering an urban apartment and transforming the interior into a plant-filled space.

Animest is also accepting applications for two programs aimed at Romanian animation creators. TOON SCRIPTS is a competition for animated series concepts and scripts, while PITCH, PLEASE! is a development workshop for animated short-film projects. Applications for both programs remain open until September 7 through the festival’s official website.

Limited Ten Stops and Full Trip passes for Animest.21 are available through Eventbook. Further details can be found here.

World.title: Romanian startup launches tool to assess websites’ visibility in AI search
World.content:
Romanian company Human AI Labs has launched Blind Spot, a platform that assesses whether websites can be understood, cited, and recommended by generative AI systems. The tool evaluates sites against 70 technical and content-related criteria and generates an AI visibility score.

Blind Spot analyzes factors including access for AI crawlers, structured data, semantic clarity, quotable content, digital authority, and trust signals. It then identifies issues that could make a website difficult for generative systems to interpret or cite and provides recommendations for addressing them.

The platform is designed for services such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews, which can extract and synthesize information rather than only display lists of links.

“For years, companies optimized for Google: keywords, backlinks, titles, and meta tags. All of these remain important, but AI search works differently,” said Human AI Labs founder Andrei Mihnea Răileanu. “It needs structure, clarity, coherent data, easily quotable content, and authority signals that it can verify. A website can be excellent for people and still be difficult for AI to read.”

Unlike tools that monitor how brands appear in AI-generated answers, Blind Spot focuses on a website’s underlying infrastructure. Its score is calculated using deterministic criteria without AI participating in the evaluation, according to the company. For some technical issues, the generated report can also include code examples or implementation guidance.

During its beta stage, Blind Spot audited several Romanian websites and recorded an average AI visibility score of 48 out of 100. The most common issues included incomplete structured data, content that was difficult to cite, unclear authority signals, and an inconsistent presence in sources that AI systems could treat as references.

Human AI Labs filed a patent application with Romania’s State Office for Inventions and Trademarks (OSIM) in June 2026 covering elements of the platform’s architecture, including its normalized extraction methodology, deterministic scoring, and semantic gap analysis.

Blind Spot is available online, with a free audit covering the first pages of a website. The platform also offers six months of free access to eligible nongovernmental organizations and a free diagnostic audit for startups.

World.title: Western Romania: Thick smoke covers city of Timişoara for second day as wildfires rage in Serbia
World.content:
A thick layer of smoke covered Timişoara on Friday, August 21, for the second consecutive day, following recent out-of-control wildfires in Serbia. In response, authorities recommended that residents stay indoors.

Thousands of hectares of forests and grassland have burned in the neighboring country in recent days, and smoke easily crossed into Romania. A day earlier, on Thursday, August 20, dozens of calls to the 112 emergency number from Timişoara and the county reported a strong smell of smoke, according to News.ro.

Sent to verify the surroundings, Romanian firefighters said that no fires were identified. “Based on the information available, the smoke observed in Timiş County could most likely originate from the large-scale dry vegetation fires in the Dubovac area, Serbia. Depending on weather conditions and wind direction, the smoke may also be felt in our county,” ISU Timiş said.

In recent days, no fewer than 45 vegetation fires have been recorded, with the most intense one in the sandy Deliblato area of Serbia, a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, where flames have burned approximately 3,500 hectares of vegetation.

Two other major active fires are in the Stolovi mountain area (Serbia), where approximately 200 hectares of forest and low vegetation have burned, and further south of it, where around 60 hectares of forest have burned.

Serbia has appealed to Russia for help in fighting forest fires due to the lack of aircraft available from the European Union, the country’s Interior Ministry announced. Serbia is not an EU member, but has access to EU emergency assistance through the European bloc’s Civil Protection Mechanism. This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and an emergency response team to help Spain fight forest fires under this mechanism, but forest fires across Europe have depleted EU resources.

Until the fires are extinguished, the Timiş Public Health Directorate recommended that the population close their windows and refrain from outdoor activities. “This situation may lead to an aggravation of respiratory symptoms, especially among vulnerable people with chronic respiratory conditions (bronchial asthma, etc.) and cardiovascular conditions,” DSP Timiş said.

Lead consultant in pulmonology in Timişoara, Cristian Oancea, provided further recommendations, noting that smoke from vegetation fires contains a mixture of fine particles and toxic gases that can affect the respiratory system, including in healthy people.

“One of the main dangers is represented by fine PM2.5 particles. Due to their very small size, they can penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and reach the level of the pulmonary alveoli. Even short-term exposure to high concentrations of smoke can irritate the eyes, nose and throat, cause coughing, runny nose, wheezing, a feeling of pressure in the chest or shortness of breath,” he said on Facebook.

Moreover, according to the doctor, smoke produced by fires can also contain carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that, at high concentrations, prevents the normal transport of oxygen in the body. “For people diagnosed with asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis or other chronic respiratory diseases, exposure to smoke can lead to worsening symptoms or the occurrence of an exacerbation. In severe cases, going to the emergency room or even hospitalization may be necessary,” he added.

Timiş County Council vice-president Alexandru Iovescu commented on the situation and said that Serbia has not yet requested the help of firefighters from Timiş County to extinguish the vegetation fires.

The official noted that the Environmental Guard has activated the sensors for monitoring air quality. “There is no reason to panic, but it is good to be careful and follow the recommendations of specialists. We are in contact with the responsible institutions and will communicate any important information,” Iovescu said.

World.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
World.content:
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia.

Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.

“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.

The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.

Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.

For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.

“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.

Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.

Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.

“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.

Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.

He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.

After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.

In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.

In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.

His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

In recent years, multiple instances of Bulgaria denying asylum or deporting people under questionable conditions have come to light, as well as cases of police brutality, such as recent allegations of widespread violence against migrants being held in a detention centre in Pastrogor.

World.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
World.content:
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.

While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.

World.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
World.content:
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.

“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.

There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.

Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.

However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.

“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.

“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.

However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.

“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.

On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.

“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.

“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.

Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Hungary’s Public Media News Back on Air as Magyar Marks 100 days
World.content:
Budget talks underway; location of Prague’s ‘mega-hospital’ confirmed; norovirus outbreak suspected at Czech spa

The Czech government held its first post-summer recess cabinet meeting on Monday, with the 2027 budget top of the agenda. Throughout the week, ministers have been holding one-on-one talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerova, with many of them emerging from the closed talks with promises of budget increases for their individual portfolios. Talks are still in the preliminary stages, and the draft budget should be submitted by the government by the end of September, with the ruling ANO party flagging healthcare and transport infrastructure as its two top priorities. Looking at some of the key announcements, Defence Minister Jaromir Zuna of the far-right SPD party said he expects defence spending to increase to 191 billion Czech crowns (about 7.9 billion euros) next year, thus reaching 2 per cent of GDP in contrast to this and the previous year. On the culture front, Minister Oto Klempir said he was striving to increase his department’s budget to 20 billion crowns (around 825 million euros) in 2027. And while the Culture Ministry has long been expected to start funding directly Czech public media from January next year as the government prepares to scrap licence fees, recent statements from officials close to finance chief Schillerova suggest a new model might be chosen: specifically, that the cancellation of licence fees might first be postponed, and that the nearly 8 billion crowns intended for Czech TV and Czech Radio would come not from the Culture Ministry, but from the General Treasury Administration – a separate chapter for public expenses that are not assigned to specific ministries in advance that includes, for instance, emergency funding to deal with natural disasters.

A key campaign promise of the current government, the Czech capital’s future “mega-hospital” will be built on the grounds of the current Kralovske Vinohrady University Hospital (FNKV) in Prague, the government announced this week. “It’s not like the entire campus will be demolished, we will only use part of the campus where there’s currently unused land,” vowed Health Minister Adam Vojtech as he unveiled the wide-ranging plans for the new hospital, where some of the current FNKV departments along with those of other Prague hospitals are set to be relocated. Just weeks ago, the government commissioned the ministries of health and defence to transfer the land to the Defence Ministry by the end of August. Plans to designate the new facility as a military hospital to include the costs in reported defence expenditures – and meet NATO requirements – have been met with scepticism by some who point out that mostly civilians will be treated there, and that Prague already has the Central Military Hospital (UVN).

The Regional Hygiene Station of the Olomouc region, in eastern Czechia, confirmed four new cases of people falling ill with what initial findings suggest could be noroviruses, bringing the total number of cases to 115 patients since the start of the outbreak at the Priessnitz spa in Jesenik earlier this month. “The regional hygiene station is recording a decrease in the number of newly reported cases,” a spokeswoman said, pointing to the effectiveness of the anti-epidemic measures taken by regional authorities and the spa’s management since the first cases began emerging, and highlighting that the risk of transmission to the wider population remained low. “Within a few days we managed to prevent the spread of the infection”, meanwhile assured the spa’s director Roman Provaznik, who also criticised the spread of fake news and alarmist statements on social media about the situation at his establishment. The cause of the outbreak remains unclear to date, however, and lab examinations are still ongoing to determine how more than 100 people fell ill with intestinal flu-like symptoms.

World.title: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property?
World.content:
As the issue of the ownership of state and defence property goes to the very core of sovereignty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it has evaded a neat and lasting solution. For years, international interest has wavered, leaving the question to be answered at a later and hopefully more favourable date.

Today, however, with Washington increasingly driven by business motives in energy, mining and other critical infrastructure, there is mounting concern that the US could seek to drive through a settlement that is ultimately detrimental to the country’s fundamental interests.

World.title: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators
World.content:
Garbage trucks pull up every day at the landfill that serves the Albanian capital, next to Sharra cemetery in the Erzen Valley. The pile of waste grows ever higher, sometimes catching fire and emitting clouds of pungent smoke.

It wasn’t supposed to be like this.

The promotional videos depicted a futuristic complex of two glass pyramids supported by a metal structure, where the waste would be incinerated.

Instead, nine years after the contract for the incinerator was signed, the people who said they’d build it went on trial in mid-July, accused of pocketing tens of millions of euros in public funds that should have been spent on finally solving the problem of Tirana’s waste.

Of the 12 accused, alleged masterminds Mirel Mertiri and Klodian Zoto are on the run.

World.title: ‘Return Hubs’ for Migrants Anticipated in Balkans for ‘Era of Deportations’
World.content:
The infrastructure is already there. With generous help from the EU, Balkan countries have built a network of detention and reception centres to hold migrants over the last decade. Some, including Bosnia and Serbia, already have agreements with EU members to accommodate their migrants.

“There are quite a lot of camps that are fully equipped with beds and everything needed. So, they [the currently inactive detention centres] can very easily be put in use again within 24 or 48 hours, very quickly,” said Milica Svabic, a lawyer at the Belgrade-based KlikAktiv, an NGO providing legal support to migrants and asylum seekers.

The new EU return regulations are yet to come into force. After European Council and European Parliament negotiators reached a deal on the regulations on June 1, MEPs officially adopted them on June 16. But the new rules still must be signed off by the Council of the European Union before they come into force.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and a number of human rights organisations have strongly condemned the regulations, warning that outsourcing detention to ‘third countries’ outside the European bloc bypasses fundamental human rights protections.

However, some EU member states, such as the Netherlands, Greece, Austria, Germany and Denmark, have already started exploring arrangements with third countries. As yet, there is no official confirmation on which countries these may be.

Western European governments are under domestic political pressure, exacerbated by the surge in popularity of far-right parties, to exert much stronger control over migration and deport migrants if they have no legal basis to remain.

The European Commission told BIRN that “a few member states launched an initiative looking into return hubs earlier this year”.

“The Commission has been invited as an observer, and we are following discussions closely … The Commission is not negotiating any such agreement or arrangement,” it said in a written response.

Nicholas Ioannides, deputy minister for migration in Cyprus, which currently holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union, said in June that the plan is to set up these hubs “maybe in Africa or Asia”, but “not close to European borders”.

Some Western Balkan leaders have previously rejected the idea of hosting return hubs, most notably when Britain explored the same option with unnamed countries in the region, as the BBC reported last year.

While Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti expressed openness towards the idea, Albania has heavily criticised the concept of return hubs, even though it has set up migrant holding camps for use by Italy. Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said in October 2025 that his country will not be hosting rejected asylum seekers from Britain.

Nikola Kovacevic, a Serbian lawyer who has represented refugees for more than a decade, told BIRN that if return hubs are located in the Western Balkans, the EU will “send people who have a terrible situation, but don’t meet requirements for asylum”, while “simultaneously testing” whether the state to which they are to be returned is a safe enough.

Kovacevic argued, however, that “Serbia, as a country which cannot effectively protect the human rights of refugees and asylum seekers, is not a safe third country”.

Balkan migration centres

World.title: Orange weather warning issued as heavy rain and storm winds forecast for Saturday
World.content:
Environment Agency forecasts heavy rain, thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 20 meters per second over the weekend. Difficult weather conditions may lead to trees and branches breaking and cause power outages, grid operator Elektrilevi warns.

On Saturday afternoon and evening, heavy rainfall will spread across Estonia, with thunderstorms in places and wind strengthening in many areas with gusts of 15–20 meters per second. On Sunday, the risk of heavy rain and thunderstorms remains in many places, and rainy weather will continue at the beginning of next week.

Heavy rain and wind gusts may break trees and branches and cause power outages in some areas. Over a 24-hour period, rainfall totals of 50-70 millimeters are expected, with up to 90 millimeters in some areas.

"Elektrilevi is closely monitoring the weekend weather conditions, and our control center and volunteer crisis reserve are ready to respond to possible faults with increased capacity. We recommend people stay indoors when the weather worsens, charge phones and power banks in advance, and stock up on necessary drinking water and food at home," said Elektrilevi board chairman Mihkel Härm.

Power line repairs. Source: Jaanus Tanilsoo/Elektrilevi

More detailed guidance can be found in the power outage instructions on Olevalmis.ee.

Elektrilevi asks that all power outages be reported through the MARU app. This allows fast information exchange between the customer and Elektrilevi during electrical faults.

Current information on the number and locations of outages can be followed on Elektrilevi's outage map.

The Rescue Board has issued a dangerous storm warning. During heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong winds, stay indoors if possible and keep pets inside as well. Avoid unnecessary driving. If driving is unavoidable, choose a speed suitable for the weather conditions and be aware of trees, branches and other obstacles that may fall onto the road. Stay away from fallen power lines and report them to Elektrilevi's fault line at 1343. During thunderstorms, avoid open areas and stay away from bodies of water and isolated tall trees. In a power outage, use a battery‑powered flashlight as a light source, not candles.

Orange level or dangerous weather warning issued for Saturday, August 22. Source: Screenshot/Environment Agency

World.title: Photos: Tallinn unveils redesigned Iceland Square
World.content:
Iceland Square, located in front of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs building in Tallinn, was formally opened on Friday with a new Iceland‑inspired appearance.

Among those attending the opening were Iceland's president Halla Tómasdóttir, Estonia's president Alar Karis, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna and Tallinn mayor Peeter Raudsepp.

For the 35th anniversary of Estonia's restoration of independence, Iceland Square was refurbished and received a new landscape design.

The new design is inspired by Iceland's nature and architecture and helps make the symbolic meaning of the place more visible. The solution, created through cooperation between the Tallinn Urban Planning Department and the Central District Administration, gives the square a new look and creates opportunities to use the urban space more than before.

The project authors are architect Markus Puidak from the chief architect's office of the Tallinn Urban Planning Department and landscape architect Maire Suimets from the Environment and Communal Services Department. The concept authors are Artur Raik, Riina Parve, Katariina Kangro and Madis Keerd.

The landscape construction work on Iceland Square was carried out by Ardens OÜ. The cost of the work was 59,192 euros, of which 12,400 euros was co‑financed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Iceland was the first country in the world to recognize Estonia's restored independence on 22 August 1991. To commemorate this historic event, the area between Rävala Street and Theatre Square was named Iceland Square in 1998.

During the Soviet period, a statue of Vladimir Lenin stood in the same area.

World.title: Minister: Estonian tax rules prevent disclosure of firms trading with Russia
World.content:
The law currently prevents the state from publishing a list of companies that conduct business with Russia and Belarus, said Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo (Reform Party). He also could not say whether the law should be amended for that purpose.

"Regarding the publication of such a list, the law as it stands today does not allow the state to publish these companies. To do that, the law would have to be changed," Keldo said.

According to Keldo, the Taxation Act prevents the disclosure of such companies because the information concerns company data.

"We do have annual reports that are public. If someone wishes, they can look up who provides which services, to which countries goods are exported, or with whom cooperation is carried out. But the state cannot publish such information itself — the current law does not allow it," he added.

Keldo could not say whether compiling and publishing such a database by a private individual would be lawful. "Data protection experts would have to answer that," he said.

He added that the government has not discussed whether the law should be amended to allow such lists to be published.

"We need to discuss this. At the moment, it has not been under discussion in the ministry or the government. Since the issue has now surfaced, we will look into it and talk, for example, with the Chamber of Commerce, employers, and entrepreneurs to understand their view — whether and to what extent unequal behavior among Estonian companies can be seen," Keldo said.

"Today I certainly won't say that we will do it, but I also cannot say that we won't. We need to look into what the pros and cons of such a list would be," he said.

"First, we need to understand what exactly we would make public, because there is definitely a data protection issue. If we simply publish company names, I suspect that many of those names will mean nothing to the public. In that case, do we add beneficial owners, ownership structure, shareholders, and so on? Publishing this information is not simple. The question immediately arises: what information and how much do we publish — only companies, or also the physical persons who are owners? All of this needs careful consideration. There are personal data and data protection issues, and we must consider whether this method is effective and what we aim to achieve. All of this needs to be discussed with stakeholders," Keldo said.

Keldo said he would support, as a first step, a complete ban on importing goods from Russia or Belarus at the EU level. "Publishing and public shame or condemnation would certainly put those companies under greater pressure, but I believe most entrepreneurs want equal market conditions and fair competition," he said.

The Latvian Central Statistical Bureau (CSB) will begin publishing a list (link in Estonian) of companies that export goods to Russia and Belarus or import goods from those countries every month, according to amendments to the law on supporting Ukrainian civilians adopted by the Latvian parliament, noted Latvian public broadcaster LSM.lv. The published Excel file lists 170 entities in alphabetical order.

This is not a list of companies violating international sanctions. It includes companies that continue business activities in sectors not covered by sanctions.

World.title: Estonian intel: Russia's military losses outpacing recruitment
World.content:
Russia is still attacking Ukrainian civilian infrastructure and pressuring the front but losing more troops than it recruits, Estonian military intelligence said Friday.

Russia lost an average of 1,400 troops a day last week, Col. Ants Kiviselg, director of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) Military Intelligence Center, said at Friday's weekly briefing.

"This trend is continuing, with Russian military losses exceeding the number of newly recruited soldiers by several thousand a month," he noted.

Front-line fighting remained intense, averaging 231 combat engagements a day, with the heaviest fighting around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka in Donetsk region, followed by areas near Sloviansk, Hulyaipole and southern Slobozhanske. Ukrainian forces also mounted counterattacks in several areas.

Russian long-range strikes hit infrastructure, homes and other civilian targets in at least 10 Ukrainian regions, while airstrikes caused power outages in at least six. Attacks on Ukrainian ports and nearby shipping also continued.

Most civilian casualties since May 2022

Long-range Russian weapons continue to account for most civilian casualties. July saw Ukraine's highest monthly civilian toll since May 2022, with 437 people killed and 2,610 injured — 70 percent more than in July 2025.

Jet-powered drones, Kiviselg noted, now account for between one-fifth and two-thirds of Russian attacks, with their share continuing to grow.

Russian air attacks also affected neighboring Moldova. An S8000 Banderol loitering munition entered Moldovan airspace and crashed less than 20 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.

Kiviselg said Moldovan President Maia Sandu has said some Russian drones enter the country's airspace accidentally, while other flight paths suggest deliberate incursions.

Ukraine steps up its own strikes

Ukraine, meanwhile, stepped up strikes on Russian and Russian-held energy and military targets. Ukrainian forces carried out two major attacks on Crimea's energy infrastructure last week, with drone units also targeting Bastion-M missile systems, airfields, radars and drone-control equipment on the peninsula.

According to Kiviselg, Ukrainian troops have struck nearly 240 energy facilities in Crimea since July 1.

Recent Ukrainian strikes also hit a Russian rocket-fuel plant in Rostov Oblast, oil refineries in Leningrad Oblast and Bashkortostan, Wildberries warehouses in Moscow and Tver Oblasts, a chemical plant in Moscow Oblast as well as Savasleyka Air Base in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast.

Kiviselg added that a recent strike on Roscosmos' Progress facility in Samara Oblast, which assembles Soyuz-2 rockets used to put satellites into orbit, could hobble Russian military capabilities by delaying launches for Rassvet, Russia's planned alternative to Starlink.

Russia's online retail, public events being affected

Attacks on Russia's fuel industry have also caused fuel shortages, with reduced availability reported in 10 regions and among Russian units fighting in Ukraine, while strikes on seven of Wildberries' ten largest warehouses have cut the Russian online retail giant's turnover by as much as 25 percent.

Ukrainian strikes are also impacting public events in Russia. Kiviselg said Russian authorities canceled a military music festival along with other military-patriotic events, noting that organizers' cited circumstances beyond their control is likely a reference to the threat of Ukrainian drone attacks.

World.title: Hendrik Johannes Terras: Where will agriculture's €546 million go?
World.content:
Estonia's lower level of agricultural support was taken into account when calculating funding for the next EU budget period. This increased Estonia's allocation by roughly €546 million. The European Commission left it to Estonia to decide how to use this opportunity, writes Hendrik Johannes Terras.

At the Ministry of Finance, a working group of 17 specialists assessed ministries' requests and drafted the first allocation proposal. According to the sector, only €295 million of this would actually go toward developing agriculture and food production: €245 million for food security and €50 million for the food industry.

Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi has said he fought to keep the money within the agricultural field. Looking at the budget lines, that is true. But within those lines, the money is intended for very different purposes.

The Ministry of Climate is slated to receive €117 million from agricultural funding. This would go toward biodiversity in private forests in Natura 2000 areas, maintaining heritage meadows, protecting water and soil, and forestry investments. To find this money, agricultural measures had to be reduced.

These expenses serve environmental goals. Agriculture needs fertile soil and clean water, and heritage meadows can combine nature conservation with livestock grazing. But biodiversity support in Natura 2000 private forests does not build pig farms or increase egg production, and forestry investments do not improve Estonia's food self‑sufficiency.

If agricultural money is used for forest‑related environmental obligations, a choice has been made in favor of environmental goals at the expense of agriculture and food production. This cannot later be counted as investment in production capacity.

Of the €245 million planned for food security, €85 million would go toward increasing self‑sufficiency and critical production capacity — pig farming, poultry meat and eggs, horticulture, potatoes, greenhouses, irrigation, storage, and breeding.

€110 million is intended for productivity and competitiveness: technology, resource efficiency, biogas, renewable energy, and value‑adding.

€50 million goes toward crisis resilience. This includes biosecurity and land improvement, but also reserves, logistics, food safety, and the capabilities of the Agriculture and Food Board (PTA) and the state's laboratory and risk assessment center (LABRIS). Not all of this money goes to agricultural enterprise investments.

The food industry would receive €50 million over seven years — down from €78.1 million in the current budget period.

This is how the sector arrives at €295 million. Even that figure includes activities that do not result in new farms, greenhouses, production lines, or processing capacity.

"Biodiversity support in Natura 2000 private forests does not build pig farms or increase egg production."

Farmers view the funding plan differently than budget planners. A pig farmer wants to know whether he can build or modernize a farm. A horticulture producer needs greenhouses, irrigation, and storage. A dairy producer needs processing capacity. The food industry needs new lines and technology. More value must be created from grain in Estonia.

Our starting point is not good. In 2024, the value of buildings, machinery, and equipment in Estonian agricultural enterprises was €1,567 per hectare, compared with the EU average of €2,456. Output value was €1,350 per hectare in Estonia and €3,025 in the EU.

Last year, Estonia imported €539 million more in agricultural and food products than it exported. These numbers will not improve through environmental obligations, crisis reserves, or agency capabilities — only through increased production and processing capacity in Estonia.

Since February, I have said that the €546 million opportunity must be used to develop agriculture and food production. Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the €546 million must go to agriculture and food production.

That promise must be visible in the funding plan. Environmental money must be called environmental money, crisis reserves must be called crisis reserves, and production investment must be called investment.

Seventeen specialists made the first allocation proposal based on the entire country's financial needs. The sector looks at the same proposal through the lens of whether Estonia will have more capacity to produce food domestically in 2034. The government must now decide which need carries more weight when allocating the €546 million.

World.title: Estonia pushes 112 accessibility deadline to 2027 as service falls short
World.content:
Many still face barriers using Estonia's 112 emergency line, including deaf people and those unable to speak safely in an emergency, as full accessibility is pushed to 2027.

While Estonia was supposed to meet accessibility requirements by June 2025, the necessary systems still aren't fully in place. Currently, people can contact the Emergency Response Center by voice call or SMS, but neither option works equally for everyone.

For example, deaf or hard of hearing people, as well as those who have had a stroke, whose speech is impaired or who cannot safely speak in an emergency may need alternatives such as video calls or real-time text (RTT).

Mari Tuulik, an accessibility advocate with the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People (EPIKoda), said SMS service doesn't ensure access for everyone, including those with difficulty reading or writing.

"This also affects deaf people who use Estonian Sign Language (EVK) but for whom Estonian is essentially a foreign language," Tuulik said, noting that sign languages have their own grammar and vocabulary.

"In time-critical situations, the most accessible option for deaf people would be for at least some emergency dispatchers to know EVK well enough to communicate," she added. "That would be the best option."

'They had three years to get this done'

Accessibility requirements for emergency lines took effect June 28, 2025. Because Estonia's emergency line does not yet meet them, however, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications plans to invoke an exception allowed under EU rules and move the deadline to June 28, 2027.

Accessibility expert Jakob Rosin said the work should have started sooner.

Emergency dispatchers at an Emergency Response Center in Estonia. Source: ERR

"I've actually seen no good reason why this is taking so long," Rosin said, adding that state agencies didn't only learn about the need for accessibility improvements last year.

Estonia's accessibility legislation took effect in 2022 already, he added, "so there were at least three years to get this done."

The Emergency Response Center is testing new technology, including RTT. Unlike with SMS, or regular text messages, real-time text would allow the emergency dispatcher to see the caller's text as it is being typed.

A video solution is also still in the works, as options offered by phone manufacturers do not meet all users' needs.

SMS still best option for now

Sirli Seegar, the center's social affairs expert, said the goal is to combine multiple forms of communication in a single 112 call.

"Our long-term goal is to offer a complete conversation during a 112 call," Seegar said. "This would mean that the caller and emergency dispatcher could speak, type in real time and share video all during the same call."

She said RTT should be ready to roll out by next June, with officials continuing to work on a video solution. In the meantime, despite follow-up questions and responses taking longer by text, SMS still remains the main option for callers who cannot communicate by voice.

World.title: After five years in office, President Alar Karis has chores waiting at home
World.content:
After five years in Kadriorg, Estonian President Alar and First Lady Sirje Karis are looking ahead to what's next, with plenty of chores to catch up on at home.

"Life has been quite interesting, and I've learned a lot over these five years," said Sirje Karis, speaking at the couple's final Restoration of Independence Day Rose Garden reception as hosts. "I've met many wonderful people, both in Estonia and around the world."

While her husband's term as president is coming to an end, Sirje Karis expects to retain some of her public duties as First Lady after leaving the presidential residence.

"Unfortunately, I can't simply leave all of my responsibilities behind, so some things will remain," she added.

Even so, Sirje Karis said she is looking forward to spending more time around the house in Tartu again.

"I have my own garden and greenhouse," she added. "I love gardening."

DIY or don't

After leaving Kadriorg, the couple will also have to work out how to divide their time between Tallinn and Tartu. "We'll probably spend more of our time in Southern Estonia," Alar Karis said.

The president said he has a growing list of chores and projects waiting to be tackled once he leaves office.

"Our home has become a summer home," he admitted. "You head there and notice the spiderwebs are back again."

"I won't paint ceilings or floors, but I still do a lot of things myself when I can be at home," said Sirje Karis.

Not everything will be a DIY project, however. Karis joked that just a trip to a hardware store can leave even the president overwhelmed by the huge selection.

"You may want to do it yourself, but you simply don't know how," he said. "We've reached the point where if you don't know how to do something yourself, you should leave it to the pros."

Still busy for now

For now, Karis still has little time for home projects. Over the next five weeks, before his presidential term draws to a close, his time in Estonia will be limited by a string of visits abroad.

"In two or three days, I'm off to Ukraine, then Latvia and Italy, and after that it's trips to the Nordic countries, Germany and New York," he said.

The Riigikogu convenes to elect the next president of Estonia on September 2.
