World.title: Saudel now a typhoon, LPA becomes tropical depression outside PAR
World.content:
FORECAST. PAGASA Weather Specialist Veronica Torres explains the bureau's 4 am forecast for Typhoon Saudel and the tropical depression, both outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, on August 22, 2026.

PAGASA is not ruling out the possibility of the tropical depression entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility ahead of Typhoon Saudel

MANILA, Philippines – Saudel strengthened from a severe tropical storm into a typhoon at 8 pm on Friday, August 21, while the low pressure area (LPA) also being monitored developed into a tropical depression at 2 am on Saturday, August 22. Both are located outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Saudel was located 2,710 kilometers east of Northern Luzon as of 3 am on Saturday, moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

Its maximum sustained winds are now at 130 km/h, with gustiness of up to 160 km/h.

The typhoon is still projected to enter PAR by Monday, August 24. It might stay far from Philippine landmass, but it is likely to enhance the southwest monsoon or habagat.

The expected enhancement of the southwest monsoon would mean significant rainfall, especially in Luzon, during the last week of August.

For now, the southwest monsoon is bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to the Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Batanes, Cagayan, Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, and Pampanga, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Central Luzon, Metro Manila, and Calabarzon on Saturday.

Flash floods and landslides remain possible during periods of moderate to heavy rain or severe thunderstorms.

Meanwhile, the tropical depression was located 1,195 kilometers east of northeastern Mindanao as of 3 am on Saturday — right outside PAR. It is moving west at just 10 km/h, with maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Veronica Torres said the weather bureau is not ruling out the possibility of the tropical depression entering PAR ahead of Saudel, since it is “momentarily” heading west. But afterwards, she explained, it could move northeast or away from the Philippines.

PAGASA also continues to monitor the LPA or remnant low that used to be Tropical Depression Neneng. It was last spotted 735 kilometers north northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, at 3 am on Saturday.

The remnant low has a medium chance of redeveloping into a tropical cyclone within 24 hours, but it continues to move away from PAR.

PAGASA previously estimated that up to four tropical cyclones may develop within or enter PAR in August. So far, there have been three during the month: Tropical Depression Luis, Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira), and Neneng.

The next two local tropical cyclone names are Obet and Pilandok. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev: Kurultai Elections Could Be ‘Most Interesting’ in Kazakhstan’s History
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called Kazakhstan’s first elections to the new unicameral Kurultai a historic event and urged citizens, notably young people, to take part in the Aug. 23 vote.

In an address to the nation on Aug. 21, Tokayev described the campaign as substantive, open and competitive, highlighting televised debates, meetings with voters, media coverage and discussions on social networks as platforms for parties to present their programs, reported Akorda.

“Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in the history of our country,” Tokayev said.

New faces and ideas

President Tokayev noted the emergence of new political figures and ideas during the campaign, as well as the active participation of young people, professionals and entrepreneurs.

He linked this engagement to Kazakhstan’s ongoing reforms to strengthen political culture and expand citizens’ participation in public administration.

Tokayev also said the campaign demonstrated a shift in the public agenda toward ideas of development and progress.

New stage of reforms

According to Tokayev, the Kurultai elections will mark a new stage of reforms following the entry into force of the new Constitution.

Tokayev said the new legislative body would play an important role in the country’s future development.

“The new legislative body should become a common platform for constructive views and aspirations. The Kurultai will set a high pace for the further modernization of the country,” he said.

President Tokayev also expressed confidence that the new legislature would include professionals and patriots committed to the country’s development.

Focus on participation

Tokayev said domestic and international observers monitored the election campaign and will also work at polling stations on election day.

Against the backdrop of geopolitical tensions and growing global challenges, Tokayev said Kazakhstan faces complex tasks in its efforts to become a developed state.

He described participation in the election as an important expression of civic responsibility and called on citizens, especially young people, to vote on Aug. 23.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Campaign Puts Competing Policy Priorities in Focus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first campaign for the new Kurultai has brought all seven registered political parties into a national political debate, with televised discussions and public meetings highlighting their policy priorities ahead of the Aug. 23 vote.

A campaign built around debate

The campaign has emphasized televised debates. Over four weeks, representatives of all seven parties took part in discussions broadcast by Qazaqstan TV, Channel 7, Jibek Joly and 24KZ. Different formats covered topics ranging from education and human capital to economic growth, social policy and regional development.

The final debate on Aug. 19 brought the leaders of all seven parties together to discuss how economic growth could translate into better living standards. The format gave party leaders an opportunity to present their programs, challenge opponents and respond to questions.

The debates also created a common public space in which parties had to explain their positions in direct exchanges with political opponents.

This aspect of the campaign was highlighted at a meeting of the Kazakhstan Institute for Public Development’s SARAP Expert Club, which brought together political, academic and civil society representatives on Aug. 20.

Kazakhstan Institute for Public Development Deputy Chairperson Zhanar Bukanova described televised debates as an important feature of the campaign because they provide opportunities for open discussion of party programs and political positions, expand voters’ access to information and contribute to substantive political competition.

“At the same time, elections are not the final point of the socio-political process. After voting is completed, responsibility to society only increases. It is important that the initiatives voiced during the campaign and the demands of citizens find their continuation in concrete decisions. Therefore, after the elections, it is also important to maintain dialogue between the state, political parties, civil society and experts,” Bukanova said.

From broad priorities to policy solutions

Economic and social matters occupied much of the campaign. Employment, household incomes, education, healthcare, social protection, entrepreneurship and regional development repeatedly featured in party programs and televised discussions.

The parties nevertheless placed different emphasis on these topics. Auyl Party focused on agriculture and regional development, while Ak Zhol highlighted entrepreneurship and business interests. Baytaq Green Party centered its campaign on environmental subjects, while the People’s Party of Kazakhstan and Nationwide Social Democratic Party gave greater emphasis to social policy. Adilet presented a program covering law and order, regional development, economic competitiveness, digitalization and social policy.

Taken together, the campaign showed that parties often identified similar concerns but differed in what they emphasized and the approaches they proposed.

Beyond party programs, the campaign also provided a broader forum for discussing topics raised by voters and communities. Public meetings and regional campaigning allowed parties to present their positions outside the televised debates and engage directly with citizens.

Key election details

The Aug. 23 election will be the first nationwide vote under Kazakhstan’s new parliamentary model. Citizens will elect 145 members of the Kurultai, the new unicameral Parliament, through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency. Seven parties are contesting the election, with a 5% threshold for entering the legislature.

Campaigning ended at midnight on Aug. 21, followed by a campaign silence day on Aug. 22. More than 12.6 million people are eligible to vote.

A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor the Kurultai election.

According to data from territorial election commissions, all polling stations across the country are ready for election day as of Aug. 21. The necessary conditions have also been created to ensure that people with limited abilities can exercise their voting rights.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Volunteer Portal Proposal Could Turn Global Initiative Into Practical Tool
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s proposed international volunteer portal could be more than an image project, giving the country an opportunity to turn its global volunteer agenda into a practical mechanism for international cooperation, said an expert with the National Volunteer Network.

“If the initiative is implemented, for our country this will be much more than an image project. It is an opportunity to establish the role of a country that not only supports volunteering domestically, but also proposes concrete mechanisms for its development at the global level,” Aiman Nakispekova, coordinator of the International Volunteer Center at the National Volunteer Network, told The Astana Times.

From initiative to practical mechanism

Kazakhstan proposed creating a unified international portal to register volunteers, determine their status and systematize areas of activity during a meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information Aida Balayeva and UN Volunteers Executive Coordinator Toily Kurbanov on Aug. 19.

The proposal follows Kazakhstan’s initiative to proclaim 2026 the International Year of Volunteers for Sustainable Development, endorsed by the UN General Assembly.

On Aug. 20, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Kurbanov to discuss Kazakhstan’s role in advancing the global volunteer agenda. Tokayev said more than 1,000 events are being held in Kazakhstan during the year, while the number of volunteers has approached 300,000. Kazakhstan is also developing a volunteer movement concept through 2030 and introducing a digital volunteer passport.

Nakispekova sees the portal as a logical continuation of these efforts, moving Kazakhstan from a political initiative toward a practical international tool. She stressed that it should not necessarily be viewed as a new institution created by Kazakhstan, but as international volunteering infrastructure developed with its support and participation.

What could make it different?

International volunteering already has digital infrastructure. UN Volunteers operates a Unified Volunteering Platform where candidates create profiles and apply for assignments within the UN system.

Kazakhstan’s proposal could add value by going beyond UN recruitment and connecting national volunteer organizations, volunteers and projects across countries.

Kazakhstan already has relevant domestic experience. Its Qazvolunteer platform connects volunteers, organizations and projects and includes opportunities for volunteering abroad. An international model could build on this experience while accommodating different national systems and local priorities.

The system behind the platform

The portal’s value would ultimately depend on the infrastructure supporting it.

Tatyana-Tinkay Koreshkova, an expert with the National Volunteer Network, said the priority should be coordination and verification.

“For this to work well, what is needed is not so much a website or portal as a powerful back office,” she told The Astana Times.

Such a system would need to verify volunteers and opportunities, connect organizations, support safety and coordinate logistics. This would require sustained cooperation among participating countries and organizations.

What Kazakhstan could gain

For Kazakhstan, the initiative could strengthen its international profile while giving practical substance to its leadership in the

global volunteer agenda. A functioning system could also facilitate the exchange of experience, increase the visibility of volunteer contributions and strengthen cross-border civil-society cooperation.

The main test will be implementation, including common approaches to verification, coordination, safety, financing and measuring results.

During Kurbanov’s meeting with Kazakh Minister of Foreign Affairs Yermek Kosherbayev on Aug. 19, the officials discussed expanding Kazakh volunteers’ participation in UN activities and promoting Kazakhstan’s experience in volunteering internationally. They also discussed developing the volunteer agenda beyond 2026 at the national, regional and international levels.

If these mechanisms are developed, Kazakhstan could move from promoting volunteering as a global priority to helping build practical infrastructure for cross-border volunteer cooperation.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Reforms, Investment and Regional Role
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles on Kazakhstan featured in international media worldwide this week. Today’s foreign media digest covers Kazakhstan’s AI education initiatives, political reforms and upcoming Kurultai election, investment prospects, and growing role in Central Asian and Eurasian cooperation.

Kazakhstan rolls out AI education from school to university

In the 2026-27 academic year, Kazakhstan’s first artificial intelligence university plans to enroll 600 students and trainees. AI use is also being expanded in schools, with a separate pilot planned for ten small rural schools. Kazakhstan is therefore trying to build its AI talent pipeline from both ends of the education system, reported The Times of Central Asia on Aug. 18.

Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek announced the first intake at Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU) during a government meeting.

Nurbek said 400 students would be admitted to bachelor’s programs, including 308 on state grants, while another 100 would join master’s programs.

“In addition, the Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund will send 100 of its employees to study under the MBA AI+X program,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s next chapter: Reform, resilience, and partnership with Europe

EU Reporter published an article on Aug. 18 by Roman Vassilenko, Kazakhstan’s ambassador to Belgium, highlighting Kazakhstan’s political reforms, economic resilience, strategic importance in energy and transport, and growing partnership with the European Union.

“On 23 August, Kazakhstan will hold its first elections to the Kurultai, the new highest representative body established under our new Constitution. The elections represent an important stage in the political modernization and the building of a Just Kazakhstan initiated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The new Kurultai and the elections to it are part of a broader effort to strengthen representative institutions, widen political participation and build a more resilient political system. A total of seven political parties compete in the elections, seeking to clear the 5% threshold.

As a Kazakh saying goes, ‘Where there is unity, there is strength.’ For us, the strength of a modern state rests not only on economic performance, but also on effective institutions, public participation and confidence in the future.

As we approach this critical milestone, it is important to put it in a broader geopolitical context, including our cooperation with the world and with the European Union,” reads the article.

Investment outlook for Kazakhstan equities: Strategic allocation to Eurasia’s hidden blue-chip market

EU Reporter published an article by Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner & Portfolio Strategist at Das Family Office in Singapore on Aug. 18, highlighting Kazakhstan as an under-owned but increasingly attractive investment market, citing its strong economic growth, competitive valuations, robust banking sector, strategic position in uranium, energy and the Middle Corridor, and ongoing economic reforms while acknowledging risks such as commodity-price volatility, geopolitical uncertainty and market liquidity.

The article argues that Kazakhstan offers global investors and family offices a compelling long-term diversification opportunity beyond traditional developed and emerging markets. It highlights the country’s expected GDP growth of around 4-4.5%, strong performance of the tenge and domestic equities, leadership in uranium production, growing logistics and financial sectors, and improving institutional and corporate governance. While recognizing risks linked to commodities, geopolitics, currency movements and market liquidity, the author concludes that Kazakhstan’s attractive valuations, strong financial institutions, strategic resources and economic reforms support a BUY recommendation for Kazakhstan equities as a strategic long-term allocation.

Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyz Republic’s multidimensional foreign policy and the future of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization

The article by Ahmet Sağlam, a Turkish international relations and business development specialist, in EU Reporter on Aug. 17 examines the evolving role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) amid the Russia–Ukraine and Iran–US conflicts, highlighting Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic as key Central Asian actors whose multidimensional foreign policies and balanced relations with China, Russia, the EU, the US and the Turkic World can help keep the SCO focused on regional stability, economic cooperation and connectivity rather than becoming an anti-Western military bloc.

The article particularly emphasizes Kazakhstan’s role within Central Asia and the SCO, portraying it alongside Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic as an important balancing actor that maintains diversified partnerships across major geopolitical centers. Kazakhstan’s cooperation with China through the Belt and Road Initiative, security and economic ties with Russia, growing energy and investment cooperation with the European Union, and strategic engagement with the United States and the Organization of Turkic States are presented as part of a broader multi-layered balancing approach. The author argues that this multidimensional diplomacy strengthens Central Asia’s ability to maintain open communication between competing powers and could contribute to the SCO remaining an inclusive platform for dialogue, connectivity and economic cooperation rather than becoming a confrontational geopolitical or military bloc.

EU backs Middle Corridor expansion through South Caucasus

In August 2026, the European Union launched a new transport connectivity platform aimed at linking Europe with Central Asia through the Black Sea and the South Caucasus, reported Azernews on Aug. 18.

“According to the Europe-Caucasus-Asia Transport Corridor (TRACECA), EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that cargo volumes along the Trans-Caspian route could increase fivefold over the next 15 years.

Together with international financial institutions, the EU plans to mobilize approximately €2 billion for infrastructure development in the Black Sea region and the South Caucasus.

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are highlighted as the key participants in the development of the corridor.

Kazakhstan has invested $35 billion in transport infrastructure over the past seven years and has indicated that it plans to continue investing in the sector to strengthen its position as one of the key links between China and Europe,” reads the article.

World.title: Mid-August Weekend Full of Art, Music and Adrenaline
World.content:
ASTANA – From gallery openings and live music to high-octane drift shows, Astana and Almaty are heading into the weekend with a packed cultural and entertainment calendar. The Astana Times has rounded up some of the most interesting events worth stepping out for, whether you are looking for art, music, adrenaline or simply something different to do.

Astana

Leonardo da Vinci’s work exhibition, Aug. 21- Sept. 30

An exhibition dedicated to Leonardo da Vinci invites visitors to discover the artistic and scientific legacy of one of history’s most influential minds. Through reproductions, multimedia elements and interactive displays, the exhibition explores the inventor’s creative vision, engineering ideas and masterpieces, offering a closer look at the Renaissance era.

Venue: Palace of Peace and Reconciliation; 57 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Arctic Monkey, Maneskin Tribute concert, Aug. 23

Enjoy an evening of alternative rock favourites and sing along to some of Arctic Monkeys’ most recognisable hits in a lively tribute concert.

Venue: Harat’s Irish Pub; 2T Zheltoksan Street. Tickets are available here.

“From Athens to Astana” exhibition, Aug. 21-Sept. 30

Explore the history of the Olympic Games through Olympic Relics from Vladimir Potanin’s collection, featuring rare artifacts, memorabilia and stories that celebrate the legacy and spirit of international sport.

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; 54 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Living Paintings” exhibition, Aug. 21-31

Discover the famous seascapes of Ivan Aivazovsky through a multimedia exhibition that combines classic art with immersive visual technology.

Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Act Festival, Aug. 22

Experience a vibrant festival filled with live music, creative energy and performances bringing together artists and audiences for an unforgettable weekend.

Venue: Park Koktobe; 35 A Omarova Street. Tickets are available here.

Erzhan Tajimbetov’s live concert, Aug. 23

Spend an evening with soulful live music and expressive performances as talented artists come together for a memorable concert.

Venue: Muzcafe; 117 Abai Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Red Bull Car Park Drift, Aug. 21-22

Feel the adrenaline as professional drivers take on a high-speed drift competition, showcasing precision, control and spectacular car performances.

Venue: ASP Arena; Tickets are available here.

World.title: Kanye West Concert Brings $11 Million to Kazakhstan, Boosting Almaty’s Event Tourism
World.content:
ASTANA – Kanye West’s first solo concert in Central Asia generated an estimated 5 billion tenge (US$11 million) in tourism-related economic impact for Almaty, highlighting the growing role of major international concerts in attracting tourists and generating economic activity in Kazakhstan.

The concert, held on Aug. 15 at Almaty’s Central Stadium, attracted 31,000 spectators, including approximately 7,700 international visitors from more than 50 countries. Foreign guests came from Australia, China, Germany, the Kyrgyz Republic, Russia, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States, Uzbekistan, among others. Around 2,000 international visitors were fans following the artist’s global tour.

According to Almaty’s Tourism Department, accommodation demand rose sharply between Aug. 13 and 16, with the average occupancy rate reaching around 98%. Kazinform reported on Aug. 20 that the concert was identified as one of the year’s major events for the city’s event tourism.

The show was initially scheduled for Aug. 14 but was postponed by one day due to deteriorating weather conditions. Despite the delay, organizers completed preparations for the large-scale production, assembling the main spherical structure within five days and bringing equipment to Almaty by one cargo aircraft and seven trucks. More than 4,400 people worked at the venue on the day of the concert, including security personnel, police, municipal services, technical and production teams, medical staff and stadium employees.

Previous major concerts in Kazakhstan

The economic impact of the Kanye West concert follows a series of major international performances that have strengthened Kazakhstan’s position as an emerging destination for global entertainment and event tourism.

In August 2025, Jennifer Lopez’s first concert in Kazakhstan generated nearly 10 billion tenge (US$21 million) in overall economic turnover in Almaty, while its multiplier effect in Astana was estimated at around 6.5 billion tenge (US$12 million).

The Backstreet Boys concerts were held in both Almaty and Astana in September 2025, with the Astana performance alone generating an estimated 7.8 billion tenge (US$17.1 million) in broader economic impact, according to Tengri News.

Kazakhstan’s concert calendar has continued to expand in 2026. Earlier this year, Deep Purple performed in Almaty, followed by Megadeth in June and Ricky Martin in July. The country also hosted major international festivals featuring artists such as Flo Rida, Busta Rhymes, Tyga, Nicole Scherzinger, Timbaland and Keri Hilson. Further major performances are scheduled, including Enrique Iglesias in September and artists participating in Park Live Almaty on Aug. 21-23.

The growing number of global performers and international visitors highlights Kazakhstan’s efforts to use major cultural events to increase inbound tourism, generate economic activity and strengthen the country’s visibility as a regional entertainment hub.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan’s AI Challenge Might Not Be Adoption, but Capability
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is moving rapidly to position artificial intelligence at the center of its economic modernization strategy, investing in computing infrastructure, skills, startups and Kazakh-language technologies as governments worldwide compete for a place in the emerging AI economy.

Kazakhstan has an increasingly ambitious AI agenda. The government has made AI part of its broader economic modernization strategy, betting that it can improve public services, attract investment and help the country generate more value beyond its traditional reliance on raw materials.

It has been investing heavily in computing infrastructure, training, startup ecosystems, and Kazakh-language models. At the 38th plenary session of the Foreign Investors’ Council in July, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev explicitly called the integration of AI into state investment policy a “critically important priority.”

The government has adopted a Digital Code and a law on artificial intelligence, launched the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, and designated 2026 as the Year of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development.

This push comes at a time as AI is becoming both a major global industry and an increasingly important source of economic and strategic power. UN Trade and Development estimates the global AI market will rise from $189 billion in 2023 to $4.8 trillion by 2033. This is a 25-fold increase in just a decade.

Globally, AI push is concentrated among a handful of countries. U.S. private AI investment alone reached nearly $286 billion in 2025, more than 23 times the level in China, according to Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index.

Global corporate AI investment more than doubled in 2025, while private companies produced more than 90% of the year’s notable AI models.

For emerging economies, the concentration of AI infrastructure in a small number of countries can make this race appear expensive, not to mention that training large language models requires massive quantities of computing power, electricity, connectivity and capital.

Kazakhstan is unlikely to compete with the United States or China at the most capital-intensive layer of the AI industry nor does it need to. Experts say its opportunity lies in combining global AI technologies with domestic expertise, while building its own capabilities in areas where dependence creates economic or strategic vulnerabilities.

Strong foundation

The country’s AI push builds on years of its experience of deploying digital technologies at a scale. Advanced technologies are increasingly embedded in government services and banking.

“Right now, especially in the artificial intelligence applications in fintech, Kazakhstan is one of the most progressive countries in the world,” Huseyin Atakan Varol, dean of the School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence and director of the Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence at Nazarbayev University, told The Astana Times.

He pointed to technologies including palm-recognition authentication and AI-powered banking assistants as examples of how quickly digital tools have entered everyday life.

International indicators tell a similar story but also expose an important weakness. Kazakhstan ranks 10th globally for online government services, according to figures from the World Intellectual Property Organization. Yet it ranks 115th for university-industry collaboration and 112th for venture-capital deal activity relative to the size of its economy.

Dr. Varol said Kazakhstan still allocates a relatively small share of its economy to research and development, with the government providing most of that funding. While spending on science has increased in recent years, spending on research and development does not reach 1%.

“Nearly all of this allocation comes from the state, very little from the private companies,” he said. “So basically, industry, academia, government interaction, the triple helix structure is not yet fully working in Kazakhstan.”

That may prove to be one of the important constraints on Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions. While the government can establish institutions, purchase computing infrastructure and train specialistics, building a durable innovation economy requires more.

Alem.AI center in Astana is intended to help close that gap by connecting education, research, startups and companies.

“We have some real and simple goals. The first one is to build a community of professionals, who not just use but understand what AI actually is. It means that we train different categories,” Alyona Slavkina, head of the Alem.AI Development Office, told The Astana Times.

The community is supposed to include schoolchildren, students, working professionals, researchers and entrepreneurs. The idea is to create a pathway from first exposure to AI to education, research and eventually the development of commercial products.

The challenge, however, is that AI is evolving faster than conventional education systems. Olzhas Urazalin, head of Tomorrow School, said technologies and development tools can change within months, while formal academic programs often require years to adapt.

“Many graduates have strong theoretical knowledge, but very limited experience working with modern AI tools, real data sets, and product development. This indeed creates a gap between learning and creation. Young specialists often learn how to use existing AI solutions, but they rarely get the opportunity to understand how these systems are built, or how to develop new ones,” Urazalin said.

Tomorrow School is built around an alternative model. Students learn primarily through projects rather than conventional lectures and work on real problems brought into the curriculum by businesses. The program is free, runs for 18 months and is open to applicants without traditional technology backgrounds.

“In my opinion, Kazakhstan must focus on developing, first of all, creators, not only consumers of AI technology,” he said, highlighting talent, infrastructure, and international collaboration as priorities.

Development pathways

Dr. Varol describes two broad pathways for technological development. One is indigenous development, which requires substantial investment, time and a long-term commitment. The other is what he calls “technological piggybacking,” adopting technologies already developed elsewhere.

For Kazakhstan, Varol said that generative AI requires elements of both approaches.

“We have been also debating and discussing a lot about what is the best strategy for Kazakhstan, especially in the development of generative AI technologies. Our internal deliberations always pointed out that we must develop these technologies indigenously as well,” he said.

Varol also stressed that developing domestic capabilities is not only about owning a model, but also about creating a pool of specialists with expertise who can later move into startups, established companies and new commercial products.

Recent events also demonstrated that access to foreign technologies can become subject to government restrictions. In June, the U.S. government temporarily imposed export controls barring foreign nationals from accessing Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, including foreign-national employees of Anthropic itself.

“Creators of these technologies can stop your access to these technologies and this creates a very big dependence risk,” said Dr. Varol.

Technological sovereignty, however, should not be confused with technological self-sufficiency. Mohamed Eissa, chief investment officer at the International Finance Corporation, emphasized that this explains why emerging markets are unlikely to compete directly at that layer of the industry.

“You are not seeing LLMs [large language models] being developed in emerging markets because you need compute, connectivity, power,” Eissa said. “Those things are big infrastructure gaps in emerging markets.”

But he draws an important distinction between building AI infrastructure and using AI. He pointed to a rapidly growing AI company in content creation that originated from Kazakhstan as an example.

“But using AI in emerging markets, you don’t need to build that to be able to use it. That is an opportunity in emerging markets: finding innovative people who have really good ICT skills, have focused on a business problem and now have the tools to compete with Silicon Valley,” he said during The Development Podcast on the World Bank Group YouTube channel.

That may be one of the most important opportunities for Kazakhstan. According to him, in emerging markets, the much larger opportunity may be the application of AI to businesses that already exist. Likewise, in Kazakhstan, potential economic impact of AI should not be measured only by how many programmers, AI startups or research laboratories the nation generates, but rather by whether this technology raises productivity gains across the wider economy.

Existing strengths

Dr. Varol said some of the applications of AI lie in sectors where the country already has an expertise. Mining, energy and logistics are among them.

“Kazakhstan is one of the richest countries with respect to mining and natural resources, but most of these natural resources are exported with a small amount of added value to other countries,” he said.

Using AI and digital technologies in those industries, he noted, could allow Kazakhstan to generate more value from resources before they leave the country.

Where dependence matters

There are areas, however, where Kazakhstan has stronger reasons to maintain domestic capabilities. Dr. Varol said questions about where information is processed and stored become significantly more consequential when AI systems are used by companies or public institutions.

“In general, I believe this is also very important with respect to the sovereignty aspects of a country,” he added.

Language presents a different form of dependence. Global AI systems are trained on enormous quantities of data, but languages are represented very unevenly in those datasets.

Dr. Varol said approximately half of publicly accessible internet content is in English, compared with only around 0.03% in Kazakh. That means developing Kazakh-language AI starts long before a model is trained.

ISSAI, which was founded in 2019, has developed the country’s first LLM in 2024. Drawing on the institute’s experience, Dr. Varol explained that researchers first need to collect texts and other data, remove poor-quality material, organize the information and convert it into formats suitable for machine learning.

Researchers faced another problem once a model has been trained on how to determine whether it actually understands the language.

“Because the internationally accepted method for doing this is called model benchmarking and all model benchmarks are in English language or Chinese language, but none were in Kazakh language. Basically, we also have created a suite of benchmarking data sets,” he said.

The development of Kazakhstan’s LLM illustrates another benefit of indigenous AI development. The process itself creates capabilities. The team had to recruit and train specialists while learning to operate multi-node AI computing infrastructure, expertise that had not previously been used at that scale. The significance of the project therefore extends beyond the model it produced. It helped build a domestic pool of engineers with experience in the infrastructure and workflows required for advanced AI development.

Kazakhstan’s AI strategy therefore does not require choosing between complete technological independence and reliance on global platforms. The more realistic task is to determine which capabilities the country needs to control, which technologies it can efficiently import and where AI can create the greatest economic value.

World.title: Cathay Pacific to Launch Direct Flights From Almaty to Hong Kong  in January 2027
World.content:
ALMATY – Hong Kong-based airline Cathay Pacific will launch direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong on Jan. 9, 2027, establishing the first direct air link between Kazakhstan and Hong Kong and expanding connections between Central Asia and the carrier’s global network.

The airline will operate the route three times a week using wide-body Airbus A330-300 aircraft. The launch is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Hong Kong and countries participating in the Belt and Road Initiative, according to the airline.

“Cathay Pacific is committed to strengthening connectivity between Hong Kong, the Chinese mainland and the rest of the world,” said Rakesh Raicar, the airline’s regional general manager for South Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

He said the carrier’s network would provide travelers from Kazakhstan with convenient onward connections while also improving access to Kazakhstan for international travelers.

The new route will also provide additional cargo capacity in the belly holds of passenger aircraft. Through the Cathay Cargo network, this could support trade flows between Kazakhstan, Hong Kong and other international markets by expanding access to key trade routes and cargo connections.

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Armenia-Azerbaijan exports could begin ‘soon’: Pledges, figures and remaining barriers
World.content:
Exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists that “exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan could begin in the near future”. He also said that bilateral trade was already on the agenda. According to Pashinyan, Azerbaijani specialists visited Armenia in September 2025 and January 2026 to discuss infrastructure issues, including power lines, railways and pipelines.

The statement comes against the backdrop of tangible but still highly asymmetrical trade relations between the two countries, which began to take shape following the signing of the declaration in Washington in August 2025.

Official data and figures

According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported around $17.4m worth of goods to Armenia between January and July 2026. The shipments consisted mainly of petroleum products, particularly diesel and petrol. Over the same period, Azerbaijan’s indirect imports from Armenia amounted to just $960. This figure was recorded in March, with imports falling to zero in subsequent months.

Following the lifting of transit restrictions in October 2025 and the start of the first fuel deliveries in December, Azerbaijan has facilitated both direct exports to Armenia and the transit of goods from Russia and Kazakhstan, including grain, fertilisers and other products. Volumes remain small, but the direction of travel has changed: borders that had been closed for decades have effectively begun to open.

There has yet to be any official commercial export from Armenia. In January 2026, Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said the two sides had exchanged lists of potential goods for bilateral trade. These included aluminium foil and raw materials for its production, ferromolybdenum, textiles, flowers, greenhouse produce including tomatoes and peppers, raw materials for brandy production, and other goods.

The specific contents of the lists and the expected volumes of shipments have not yet been officially published. Further development of trade will depend on agreements between companies.

What could be traded, and why?

Azerbaijani experts note that, at the initial stage, developing trade in industrial goods and raw materials appears more realistic than focusing primarily on food products. Vugar Bayramov, an MP and member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, citing preliminary estimates, puts the potential annual trade turnover for 38 categories of goods at up to $300m. These include food and industrial products as well as raw materials. In his view, mutual supplies of goods other than fuel could begin between the two countries in the near future.

Economist Natig Jafarli says the process is developing gradually. According to him, Azerbaijan has an advantage in energy resources, while potential Armenian exports could include agricultural products, fish, fruit and iron ore. However, Azerbaijan is not yet importing goods from Armenia, while the necessary infrastructure, including bank transfers, insurance and contractual mechanisms, has yet to be fully established.

Akif Nasirli, chairman of the Centre for Liberal Economists, believes food products could also be viable export candidates, including fruit and vegetables such as apricots, peaches, cherries, tomatoes and peppers, as well as fish, mineral water and wine. In his view, restrictions on the Russian market are forcing Yerevan to seek alternative export markets.

Former Finance Minister Fikret Yusifov has previously argued that, if trade relations are restored, a trade deficit for Armenia would be inevitable, but that these economic ties should nevertheless be developed for the sake of peace.

There is also a widespread view among experts that food and beverages are psychologically more sensitive categories of goods. Construction materials, cable and electrical products, industrial raw materials, chemicals and light-industry goods, by contrast, may be perceived considerably more favourably.

Psychological barrier

This is one of the deepest and most sensitive aspects of the issue. Expert assessments published by Caliber note that memories of the 44-day war remain fresh. The appearance of products labelled Made in Armenia on shop shelves could initially provoke mixed reactions, ranging from curiosity to social media campaigns. Trust in food and beverages, including wine and brandy, is particularly important, as some consumers may have irrational concerns about their safety. With industrial goods and construction materials, by contrast, the country of origin is less visible to consumers and purchasing decisions tend to be more pragmatic.

During a transitional period, neutral packaging in English or Russian, or rebranding, could potentially be used. The appearance of Azerbaijani fuel on the Armenian market has already created a precedent for a kind of “economic truce”. A similarly pragmatic approach could work in the opposite direction, although this will not happen automatically.

In both societies, support for peace does not yet necessarily translate into an equally positive attitude towards goods from the neighbouring country. Traders from border areas who wished to remain anonymous, as well as entrepreneurs with experience of informal “re-exports” through Georgia using channels that have existed since the 1990s, say that price and quality could eventually become the decisive factors. However, this process could take years.

Practical obstacles and possible timeframes

Issues surrounding certification, phytosanitary controls, customs procedures, bank transfers and insurance have yet to be fully resolved.

Logistics currently operate mainly through Georgia. Direct rail links and the TRIPP corridor are still at the infrastructure development stage. Competition also remains high, with suppliers from Turkey, Russia and Iran already present in the market alongside domestic producers. The competitiveness of Armenian goods will therefore depend on their price, quality and logistics costs.

Under an optimistic scenario, small-scale shipments of industrial goods and raw materials could begin within several months to a year. A more realistic scenario would see trade gradually expand over one to three years, while under a pessimistic scenario, political fluctuations and public reaction could delay the process considerably.

What to watch next

Key indicators could include the first genuine commercial shipments from Armenia appearing in customs statistics, the introduction of banking mechanisms for cross-border payments, official approval of a list of potential goods for trade, and changes in the procurement policies of retailers such as Bravo, Araz and others.

Independent polling and sociological research in both countries will also be needed to assess public attitudes towards goods labelled “Made in …”. Without such data, statements about future trade will remain largely expressions of intent.

World.title: ‘From crisis management to stability’: Pashinyan unveils new government programme
World.content:
Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

The Armenian government has approved its programme for 2026-2031. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said it marked a shift from crisis management to stability. Looking back on his eight years as prime minister, he said the coronavirus pandemic, followed by the war and the post-war situation, had forced the government to operate in crisis-management mode. Now that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established peace, the government can “return to the unfinished part of the agenda of the 2018 Velvet Revolution”.

The new programme focuses on stability, he said. Pashinyan stressed that it rests entirely on the concept of “Real Armenia” and the principles underpinning the establishment of the Fourth Republic.

In 2025, the ruling Civil Contract party announced a new strategic goal: establishing the Fourth Republic of Armenia. The party congress unanimously adopted a declaration to this effect. According to the document, the Fourth Republic “will be based on the concept of preserving the internationally recognised sovereign territory of the Republic of Armenia, covering 29,743 sq km, in accordance with the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration”. The declaration says the party reached this decision after analysing the history of the Third Republic. The Third Republic refers to the present-day Republic of Armenia, which declared independence following a nationwide referendum in 1991. The First Republic refers to the republic proclaimed on 28 May 1918. Accordingly, Soviet Armenia is considered the Second Republic.

“Following the 7 June 2026 election, the ideology of ‘Real Armenia’ won. This means it has become the official ideology. Armenia is therefore entering the stage of its history that we call the Fourth Republic. We must continue and give new momentum to democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms,” the prime minister stressed.

Government plans for the next five years

According to the new programme, the Armenian government will pursue the following goals in 2026-2031:

strengthening and further institutionalising the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan;

maintaining and further developing a favourable security environment around Armenia, in particular by normalising and developing relations with countries in the region and deepening existing partnerships beyond it;

unblocking Armenia through the Crossroads of Peace project and the “Trump Route” (TRIPP) transit programme;

liberalising the visa regime with the EU for Armenian citizens;

deepening democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms.

With whom does Yerevan plan to deepen partnerships under its “balanced foreign policy”?

In 2026-2031, the Armenian government will pursue a “balanced and proportionate” foreign policy.

“It has proved effective in stabilising Armenia’s external environment. Regionalisation plays a key role in foreign policy, whose goal is to ensure conditions in which Armenia can not only live without external support, but do so comfortably,” the document says.

Based on this approach, the government places particular importance on further developing relations with Georgia, Iran, Turkey and Azerbaijan. The government has outlined the following steps for each neighbouring country:

Georgia

Yerevan will continue implementing the measures set out in the Declaration on Establishing a Strategic Partnership between Armenia and Georgia. This will create new mutually beneficial opportunities for political, trade, economic, energy and transport cooperation, as well as regional and joint infrastructure projects.

Iran

Armenia will continue energy cooperation with Iran, develop cross-border infrastructure and expand transport routes through Iran, including North-South and Persian Gulf-Black Sea corridors.

Turkey

The Armenian government will continue efforts to establish diplomatic relations with Turkey, open the Armenian-Turkish border and put at least two modern border crossing points into operation. It also plans to restore and expand transport, energy and digital infrastructure, as well as bilateral and multilateral trade.

Azerbaijan

The government plans to continue efforts to sign and ratify a peace agreement and carry out work on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. Contacts between civil society and business communities in the two countries will continue, helping to establish bilateral trade.

The foreign policy priorities specifically include deepening strategic partnerships with the European Union, the US, France and China. With Russia, Armenia plans to “transform and deepen its partnership”.

Against the backdrop of tensions over the ban on Armenian food and other exports to Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which Russia leads, the programme says:

“Work will continue to ensure the full and uninterrupted exercise of the EAEU’s fundamental freedoms — the free movement of labour, services, goods and capital — as well as to develop relations with member and observer states.”

Regarding relations with the European Union, the programme stresses that Armenia will continue working to meet standards in democracy and the rule of law, as well as in the economic, financial and other spheres.

Armenia intends to deepen its partnership with the United States further. Cooperation will continue based on the principles set out in the Strategic Partnership Charter and bilateral memorandums of understanding.

“The TRIPP project, the ‘Trump Route’, will be implemented, at least in terms of operating energy and railway infrastructure, while integrating Armenia into major regional infrastructure projects,” the programme says.

Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze
