World.title: Presentation of the book “Her Yönüyle Iğdır” held at the Azerbaijan House in Igdir
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. A presentation ceremony for the book “Her Yönüyle Iğdır” was held at the Azerbaijan House in Igdir.

Authored by Ziya Zakir Acar, head of the Azerbaijan House in Igdir, the publication contains information about Igdir’s history, cultural heritage, customs and traditions, as well as various aspects of the city’s social and cultural life. The book was produced with the support of the State Committee of the Republic of Azerbaijan on Work with the Diaspora.

The presentation ceremony was attended by Igdir Governor Mustafa Fırat Taşolar, Head of the Iğdır Provincial Police Department Niyazi Turgay, Professor Uğur Şimşək, Adviser to the Rector of Igdir University, Hüseyin Ateş, Chairman of the Iğdır Provincial Organization of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), Mücahit Tanık, Head of the Melekli town of Iğdır, as well as representatives of the public and cultural spheres and art enthusiasts.

Speaking at the event, Ziya Zakir Acar provided information about the purpose behind the publication of the book, the preparation process and the topics covered in the publication. He noted that the main purpose of the work is to research and preserve Igdir’s historical and cultural heritage and bring it to a wider audience.

The speakers emphasized the importance of studying Igdir’s ancient history and rich cultural heritage and passing them on to future generations. It was noted that the book “Her Yönüyle Iğdır” is one of the important sources for promoting the city’s historical and cultural values.

At the end of the event, a book signing ceremony was held for the participants.

The presentation ceremony was remembered as an important event contributing to the further strengthening of relations between Azerbaijan and Türkiye based on shared spiritual values.

World.title: Sodden Mundi Mundi offers complimentary day as sun shines on Broken Hill festival
World.content:
Thousands had to be turned away from the Mundi Mundi Bash outback music festival in Broken Hill after record rainfall turned its campground into a field of mud this week.

But two relatively dry days — and welcome sunshine for the final day — has seen organisers open the gates for hangers-on to come into the festival free of charge.

"The sun came out yesterday, it's out again today [and] any of those people who were turned away who are still hanging around Broken Hill, we're going to let them come in today," the event's founder and organiser Greg Donovan told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

Mr Donovan said the event's full program had been fulfilled, including performances from Jessica Mauboy, Troy Cassar Daly and the Teskey Brothers. The final day is set to feature The Whitlams, Baby Animals, John Butler and Jon Stevens.

Cars queue up to enter the flooded Mundi Mundi Bash campsite. (ABC News)

Safety first as region sees a third of its annual rainfall

The Mundi Mundi site saw around 75mm of rainfall over an 11-day period, according to Mr Donovan.

"To put that into context, the rain we've had just over this little period amounts to one-third of the annual rainfall for Broken Hill," he said.

The decision to restrict entry to the campsite was made after many vehicles became bogged in the mud as arrivals were checked in on Monday night.

"We had another 2,000 coming the following day, there was just no way the campsite had the ability to take that many more people … 25 to 30 per cent of the campsite became unusable," said Mr Donovan.

He said around 10,000 were still able to see the festival. Around 15,000 people were originally ticketed to enter.

World.title: Family worried for man missing since Melbourne shooting
World.content:
The loved ones of a Melbourne father who went missing after a shooting in the city's north-west say they hold grave fears for his welfare.

Police have been conducting a large-scale search for a 37-year-old man whom the ABC understands to be Khaled Malas.

Mr Malas, of Meadow Heights, has not been seen since August 19.

Investigators said he was allegedly shot in the chest that evening about 7:20pm after a dispute at a home in Wildwood.

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, has been charged with intentionally causing serious injury.

He appeared in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court on Friday night and is due to return in November.

The ABC understands the dispute allegedly has to do with a $500,000 debt.

Investigators said they held significant concerns for Mr Malas's welfare and that it was likely he had succumbed to his injuries.

A long-time friend of Mr Malas told the ABC he was a successful auto truck electrician.

He said family and friends feared the worst.

"It's such horrible news," the friend said.

"Khaled was a humble hard-working man that loved his young family, it's absolutely devastating."

Police are urging anyone with information to come forward.

World.title: Inside the libertarian city on a Caribbean island backed by Silicon Valley
World.content:
Alice Chen opens a glass door and leads the way past a wall of stickers bearing slogans such as "Make Death Optional" and "Live on Bitcoin". The room we've entered is part messy science lab, part share-house kitchen.

"Welcome to the Maker Space," Chen says. Sunlight peeks through palms swaying in the afternoon breeze outside, but what we've come to see lives in the windowless black tent sitting in the corner.

Chen unzips the door and retrieves a beaker from a small fridge inside.

"You can't find this anywhere else in the world," she says, holding up a vivid green liquid. This is what she came all the way from Canada to Próspera, a libertarian enclave on the Honduran island of Roatán, to develop — a live algae drink she says could add 20 years to your life.

"It's only possible here in Próspera because of their meta-regulatory framework," Chen says.

Alice Chen holding the live algae drink she's developing in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Artworks on the walls in Próspera's shared working space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

"Make death optional" is one of the slogans on display in the Maker Space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

In Canada, where Chen was studying for her PhD, it would have taken months, if not years, to get approval to test the product.

"I would have been kicked out of any university even for just consuming it myself," she says.

So when she heard about the libertarian utopia in the Caribbean where she could bring it to life without those regulatory constraints, she dropped out and flew south.

In Próspera, businesses get to choose their own regulations from a menu of over 30 countries — or even propose new ones.

"We couldn't find any, so we created our own," says Alice, who's already assembled a small group of willing volunteers to test the product.

"The fact is, nowhere else in the world would regulators allow us to experiment, like, is this safe for human consumption, right?"

Chen's experiment is nothing out of the ordinary among the tight-knit group of biohackers, tech entrepreneurs and crypto bros who inhabit Próspera, a private city run by an American company. Próspera itself is a radical experiment, billed as "the future of human governance, privately run and for profit".

Roatán is a tourist island 60km off the coast of mainland Honduras. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

The Beta District was the first 58-acre parcel of land incorporated into the zone. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

So-called "startup cities" with light regulations, ultra-low taxes and minimal government oversight have long been a dream in online libertarian circles in the US. In Honduras, one of Latin America's poorest nations, it's become a reality. Próspera might be the most advanced test case for those libertarian ideas, which some hope to take global.

The project has the backing of America's tech elite. The Delaware-based company that runs the zone says it's raised almost $200 million in investment, including from venture capital firms linked to Silicon Valley billionaires Peter Thiel, Sam Altman and Marc Andreesen. Supporters say private cities like Próspera can help alleviate poverty in nations plagued by corruption and crime.

But in Honduras, where more than half the country lives in poverty, those claims have been the subject of fierce debate. The former government tried to shut Próspera down, claiming it was an affront to national sovereignty, offering little benefit to the nation. To its critics, it's an experiment gone dangerously wrong.

Duna Residences and the guard station along Próspera's main road. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Making its own laws

A boom gate halfway along the main road, manned by a smiling security guard with a handgun at his side, is the first real sign we're crossing into a parallel reality. Honduran law mostly ceases at the barrier gate. Beyond it, Próspera can make its own laws.

The guard checks that visitors have filled out the "agreement of co-existence", an online form binding them to the zone's system of private arbitration. Apart from criminal matters, cases are heard online by an Arizona-based panel of retired judges.

The Beta District, Próspera's main campus, is a sloping 58-acre plot fringed by palm trees and overlooking the Caribbean Sea. Calling it a "city" is generous, but there are plans to change that. For now, there's a a handful of buildings: a hostel, a robotic woodworking factory, and a futuristic-looking white dome giving off Fyre Festival vibes. There's a small shop where everything's bought with Bitcoin, the zone's preferred currency. Towering over all is Duna Residences, a gleaming 14-storey residential tower.

A robotic woodworking factory is staffed mostly by locals, Próspera says. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Duna Residences is home to about 45 permanent residents. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A small hostel is among a handful of buildings in Próspera's main campus. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A white dome is used to host events. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Closer to the beach, there's a restaurant and office complex, where we meet Erick Brimen, the Venezuelan-born former banker who founded Próspera in 2017.

"Really the whole thing started here, in this particular building," he says, sitting in a boardroom taking in views of the coral reef just offshore. "This was jungle before."

Próspera was created with the blessing of the Honduran government, after it legalised special jurisdictions known as ZEDEs — a Spanish acronym for Zones for Employment and Economic Development. Political instability and government corruption have long made Honduras toxic for foreign investment. The ZEDEs were meant to be the antidote.

A view from the restaurant over the coral reef. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Loading...

Brimen describes them as "pockets of stability" designed to lure foreign investors. Próspera's low tax rates are one of the big drawcards, with businesses paying as little as 1 per cent.

It's a formula he claims has already attracted 500 companies to the zone and created thousands of jobs.

"It's a poverty alleviation tool and an economic accelerant," Brimen says. "What we're doing here, I think, can lift people up from around the world by the billions."

Honduras first got the idea for the zones from a TED Talk. In a 2009 YouTube video, Paul Romer, who went on to become Chief Economist of the World Bank, argued "charter cities" run by stable foreign governments — think Canada or Norway — could help lift developing nations out of poverty.

But the model Honduras went on to adopt bore little resemblance to Romer's vision, allowing foreign companies to run the zones with an extraordinary degree of autonomy.

Próspera has the power to create its own legal system, courts, police force, tax code and regulations — even set its own building code. Duna tower would have been illegal to build anywhere else on the island.

"The zoning outside caps you at 12 stories," says Brimen, as we scale the steps at the base of the tower. "And indeed, those extra stories were authorised through the internal approval process."

The fight to shut it down

Some critics have denounced Próspera as a "state within a state". Fernando Garcia, a former minister for the economy in the left-wing Libre party, says it undermines Honduras's national sovereignty.

"It's totally affected," he says. "A state has three components: government, population and territory. All three are affected by Próspera. The libertarians want the states of the world in their current form to disappear."

He also disputes the idea Próspera is generating wealth for Hondurans. Even by Próspera's own reckoning, only about 30 companies are physically present in the zone, a fact Garcia seizes on.

"What [the companies] do is turn Próspera into a tax haven for tax evasion in their countries of origin," he says. "They don't live there or generate any activity there. They generate it in their countries of origin."

Fernando Garcia was given a special presidential commission under the previous government to shut down Honduras's ZEDEs. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Garcia believes Próspera undermines Hondras's national sovereignty. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Erick Brimen dismisses the suggestion the city is doing anything wrong.

"In Próspera, there are taxes and people must pay them, and there are regulations and people must follow them," he says.

Próspera pays 12 per cent of the taxes and fees it collects to the Honduran government, and Brimen says there's evidence it's already bringing in new investment.

The libertarian experiment on a Caribbean island backed by Silicon Valley Watch Foreign Correspondent's Paraside Inc. on ABC iview.

In 2022, Fernando Garcia was brought in by the leftist government of Xiomara Castro to shut Próspera down. The government set about repealing the laws that made the ZEDEs legal.

In response, Próspera launched legal action against the state of Honduras for $US10.7 billion — roughly a third of GDP — in a move Garcia says was akin to "blackmail". Ultimately, his effort to rid the country of its ZEDEs was a lost cause.

Libre was turfed out of office in national elections last December, which saw the right-wing Nationals returned to power — the party that ushered Próspera into existence in the first place.

That election, decided on a margin of just 1 per cent, remains a source of much contention in Honduras. Garcia claims it was "stolen" by a man with a renewed interest in the Western hemisphere, and a desire to "consolidate the position of libertarians in Honduras" — Donald Trump.

The US president made an extraordinary intervention in the fiercely contested poll, publicly backing the National Party and pardoning its jailed former leader, Juan Orlando Hernandez, days before Hondurans cast their ballots. Those actions are widely seen as having tipped the scales for his preferred party to win.

An outer suburb of Tegucigalpa, the capital of Honduras. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Gang crime and lack of opportunity have driven many from the Honduran capital. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Some say safeguarding the future of Próspera might have had something to do with it. Trump had been publicly and privately lobbied by his long-time advisor Roger Stone, who penned a blog post urging the president to pardon Hernandez in order to "crush socialism" and "save" the "freedom city".

One of the world's foremost experts on Central America, Chris Sabatini, believes Stone was doing the bidding of a group of libertarian tech bros.

"They're an emerging, very powerful bloc of political activists that are basically funded to the teeth and are willing to step out and start to push their own agenda," he says.

Brimen is coy about the president's intervention, merely saying that Trump was trying to make the region more "stable and prosperous" and that the development deserved the support it received.

Regardless of the president's knowledge of or support for Próspera, Sabitini says his actions have "basically guaranteed that Próspera will remain … as long as Donald Trump is in the White House".

The view from the pool deck on Duna Tower. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A city of the future

Expansion is now the goal. From the pool deck on Duna tower, Brimen points over a nearby hill towards Pristine Bay, a sprawling resort and golf course that's been incorporated into the zone.

ZEDEs can add territories and they don't even need to be connected, and according to Brimen Próspera is a patchwork of some 1,000 acres, including a port on the Honduran mainland at La Ceiba, with a total area larger than Monaco.

In time, he believes the population could reach 100,000.

"If you think, in 20, 30 years' time, it's very feasible," Brimen says.

For now though, it's eerily quiet. Próspera claims 1,700 people have filled out an online residency form, but only about 200 people actually live here permanently. One of them is Rich Lee, who's among the 45 or so permanent residents in Duna tower.

He moved here from the US about two years ago, after a death in the family caused him to reconsider things.

"There were a lot of people here and it was really happening," Lee says. "There was a lot of really awesome projects, bleeding-edge stuff.

"I thought, 'This is what I need' — you know, 'I'm kind of starved for this right now.' So I moved out here."

The golf course and resort at Pristine Bay has been incorporated into the zone. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

An old restaurant is now a Bitcoin education centre. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Even the swimwear is Bitcoin-themed in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Lee came to turn his biohacking hobby into a startup business. Standing in the Maker Space, he shows off his implants, of which there are seven in total, including a chunky tap-to-pay credit card chip under the skin in the back of his right hand.

He has Bluetooth headphones permanently implanted and magnets in his fingertips to "touch an otherwise invisible world of electro-magnetic fields."

It's also a handy pub trick. "Honestly, this has got me so much free beer," Lee says, dangling a bottle cap from the tip of his finger.

In the US, body modification tech is a legal grey area, Lee says, and unlikely to attract the hefty financial backing needed to pass FDA approvals. He believes the US system of regulation is broken.

"The idea that regulation in the US is making things safer, I think, is kind of a fallacy. Currently it takes about a billion dollars to bring a pharmaceutical or, like, a gene therapy, to market, and about 10 years," Lee says.

"So we're at this weird place where we've painted ourselves into the corner with regulations in a lot of cases."

Loading...

A "taser knife", an invention used for sport in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A biohacking-themed artwork in the Maker Space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Lee isn't the only biohacker to find his way to Próspera. This is where the ultra-wealthy longevity guru Bryan Johnson came to receive an unregulated gene therapy for the 2025 Netflix documentary Don't Die.

Medical experimentation has become one of the zone's hallmarks. But billionaire celebrities are a rarity, according to Lee.

"I think there's this fantasy that it's this inaccessible place for elites that are, you know, doing crazy experiments on this anarchist island. But we're just people out here and we're definitely not billionaires," he says.

Later that evening, a handful of residents gather in the Maker Space for a weekly games night. Many believe Próspera's doing good for the island.

"Most people don't come here to do anything except laze around and build a nice house and buy a boat," says Jason, another resident biohacker.

"But when you start to talk to people about, we're pushing forward science, we're going to put in regenerative medicine, ears start perking up."

An island of opposition

Not all the locals agree. Just along the beach from Próspera is the old fishing village of Crawfish Rock, which gets its name from the spiny lobster that once flourished here. It's an English-speaking community of about 600, tracing its roots back to British colonial days. People here are split over the private city next door.

Vanessa Cardenas, a community leader whose family has lived here for five generations, is one of its most vocal critics.

"No-one ever expected this kind of situation to ever occur," she says.

"For them to come and say they want to build a country in my country, where they have their own laws, regulations, their everything — they don't pay the taxes I pay and I'm from here. It's preposterous. I mean, it makes no sense."

The village of Crawfish Rock is Próspera's nearest neighbour. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Vanessa Cardenas is one of the most vocal critics. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Residents of Crawfish Rock in church. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Cardenas acknowledges that Próspera has provided jobs for the community, but says that has deepened divisions.

"There's a lack of trust now," she says."Because if you're working with them, you're getting a salary, so they're good to you. But then there's us, we're seeing the danger. I can't trust you or talk with you about certain things, so it has caused some division."

Cardenas worries about a return to the village's colonial past.

"Our country has ever been explored and our riches taken for somewhere else. It has never stayed for the Honduran people," she says.

That's a charge Erick Brimen rejects.

"It's the opposite," he says.

"It's a government choosing to liberate its people from the shackles of poor regulatory and legal environments by partnering voluntarily with partners that are capable to provide better conditions. So colonialism is exactly the opposite of what we're doing."

Exporting the movement

Back in Próspera, there's a broad gash in the green hillside behind Duna tower where the next big residential development is taking shape. The tangled jungle has been hacked back to make way for five squat, European-style apartment buildings.

"I've been looking into building a similar thing in Portugal," says Ivan Syrtsov, the young Ukrainian who's developing the site.

"Permit-wise, it would take me approximately four years. Over here, it's two weeks."

Young Ukrainian property developer Ivan Syrtzov is building a residential complex, pictured on the screen behind him. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Construction of five new apartment buildings is moving forward at a rapid pace. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

He didn't even need to consult the council before breaking ground — just a private insurance company.

"It's interested in making money, right? And if that's the case, then they try to make a rapid review of the project and work as efficiently as possible," Syrtsov says.

But he is here with more than just a quick-hit real estate project in mind. He got interested in Próspera at a "Network State" conference, where speakers discussed building new cities around alternative models of governance. If it succeeds here in Honduras, he plans to take the idea global.

"I would really love to build a city of my own," Syrtsov says. "So, become competition of Próspera."

It's a vision shared by Brimen, who believes "countries all around the world are going to want to emulate" his model city.

"Anything that works to lift people up can and should be replicated," he says.

For Fernando Garcia, it's all the more reason to keep fighting to put an end to Próspera.

"In Honduras, the battle against the libertarians of the world is being waged," he says.

"This is the spearhead."

Watch Foreign Correspondent's journey through Próspera on YouTube or ABC iview now.

World.title: US mum was 'begging for help' before killing children, family testifies
World.content:
In October 2022, Lindsay Clancy messaged her mother:

"Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I'm really sick. Something is wrong."

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

Ms Clancy was a former labour and delivery nurse known as a dedicated and loving mother to three children aged five and under.

But her mental health had begun to decline after the birth of her third son, Callan.

Despite repeatedly seeking help from medical professionals, she continued to report a poor mental state.

By December, she had confessed to her mother and then-husband that she had thoughts of harming her children.

A few weeks later, Ms Clancy had killed all three children and attempted to end her own life.

Clancy was 'begging for help', family says

On January 24, 2023, Ms Clancy took her daughter, Cora, to a doctor's appointment and sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, photos of their children throughout the day.

When Mr Clancy returned home later that day after running errands, he discovered Ms Clancy lying paralysed in their backyard.

Lindsay Clancy jumped from the bedroom window of the family home after killing her children. (Reuters: CJ Gunther/Pool)

He found their two eldest children dead from strangulation in the family basement. Callan, who was eight months old at the time, died in hospital a few days later.

Whether Ms Clancy killed her children is not in dispute at her triple-murder trial currently underway in the US state of Massachusetts.

US mum on trial for murder says voice told her to 'kill the children' A mother who says she was suffering postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children and attempted to take her own life is now on trial for their murder.

Her defence lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argues she was a loving mother who was overcome by postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.

He says Ms Clancy repeatedly sought help from medical professionals and was prescribed several psychiatric medications that made her spiral "out of control".

When her family testified for the defence this week, they described a woman who was anxious, paranoid and suicidal.

Ms Clancy's mother, Paula Musgrove, said on Monday she often stayed with her daughter between October and December 2022.

She said Ms Clancy was afraid of sleeping alone and believed the medications she was taking "were destroying her mind".

The jury was shown a text message Lindsay Clancy sent her mother about her declining mental health. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

Her former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, testified on Tuesday that Ms Clancy had been "begging for help" in the months leading up the killings.

"Lindsay was struggling; we were all concerned," she said.

The jury was shown texts between the two in which Ms Clancy spoke about fears she had developed a dependence on benzodiazepines and could not sleep without taking them.

"I'm not okay and I'm terrified of taking meds tonight," Lindsay texted her mother-in-law on November 30, 2022.

Disputed picture of mental health

Earlier in the trial, the jury heard Ms Clancy had sought treatment for severe mental health problems, including admitting herself to a psychiatric hospital.

But witnesses also noted Ms Clancy would not always take the medications prescribed to help with her insomnia, anxiety and depression, and that she expressed fears she was addicted to some of them.

'His little face turned into a dragon': One mother's experience of postnatal psychosis Ariane Beeston worked as a child protection officer, the vicarious trauma of that work impacted her when she had a child of her own.

The defence has argued that Ms Clancy was over-medicated and that her care was disjointed, with doctors not speaking to one another or sharing notes.

The defence also showed she was discharged from one facility after just one day and denied a higher level of care at another when she could not show she had a suicide plan.

Prosecutors questioned the seriousness of Ms Clancy's suicide attempt and showed through texts and photos that she performed many normal activities the day of the killings, including taking her children to the doctor and playing with them in the snow.

Her doctors have testified they never saw Ms Clancy exhibit signs of mania or psychosis, though she did repeatedly talk of feeling suicidal.

Psychologist Paul Zeizel testified that he found no evidence Lindsay Clancy was faking psychiatric symptoms. (AP: Amanda Sabga/The Boston Herald/Pool)

Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist who spent more than 35 hours with Ms Clancy over dozens of visits and reviewed her medical records, said he found no evidence she was faking or exaggerating psychiatric symptoms.

He testified that psychotic symptoms could come and go, and that a person experiencing psychosis can still perform ordinary activities such as making a phone call or driving a car.

On cross-examination, prosecutors pointed out mistakes Dr Zeizel made in his report about Ms Clancy and questioned whether he could be objective about her diagnosis when he was seeing her as a patient and working with the defence, including by appearing at a news conference with Mr Reddington.

Clancy faces life without parole

Ms Clancy has not testified and is not required to do so, but jurors have seen her break down in sobs at several points, including when prosecutors showed the jury autopsy photos of the children.

If convicted of murder, Ms Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty because of a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

ABC/AP

World.title: Parents thrilled as 'bike gang' gets young boys off the couch
World.content:
The term "bike gang" is usually associated with Harley-Davidson motorcycles, tattoos and rule-breakers, but some young boys in South Australia's Riverland are offering a different take.

Whether it be after school or on the weekend, the boys can be found on their pushbikes in their hometown of Renmark.

Eleven-year-old Jude Clark and his best mate Christos Babaniotis are part of one of the groups that are impossible to miss, all of whom are affectionately known as the "bike boys".

"Sometimes there's one group, and then on the other side of town there's another group," Christos said.

"We'll just find each other and just start riding all together."

Jude Clark and Christos Babaniotis and their friends ride to school together. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"You meet new people you haven't seen really and that's pretty cool," Jude said.

The boys said the groups included children aged between 10 and 16, but insisted there was little competition about which "bike gang" was the best.

"Some people say 'I'm better at wheelies', but that's it," Christos said with a big smile on his face.

Winning trust of parents

In an age where parents are desperate to get their kids off their screens, what has been the secret in this regional South Australian town?

Jude's parents Daniel and Nicole Clark said it was all about trust, community and friendship.

Daniel and Nicole Clark say trusting Jude to be responsible and think for himself was a good decision. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"I was very hesitant, and there was a lot of pestering from Jude," Ms Clark said.

" He would ask, 'Can I go riding? My mates go riding. Why can't I go riding?' "

Eventually, Ms Clark was worn down and Jude and his mates were hitting the streets for hours at a time.

"Now I walk outside, and there are seven or eight kids playing basketball in the driveway, bikes everywhere," she said.

Christos Babaniotis says he is better at tricks. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

The Riverland couple said the bike boys had allowed their son Jude to grow in confidence and develop social skills.

"Jude was a kid who wouldn't go into the shops by himself," Ms Clark said.

"Now he goes out, and he's got $10 for the day, or he's got less than that, and he has to figure out if he's got enough; he has to make decisions for himself."

Off screens and in real world

Mr Clark said the decision to give Jude more freedom was partly based on getting him away from screens.

"We wanted him to build resilience and leadership," he said.

Christos Babaniotis (left) is one of many boys frequently at the Clarks' house before and after school. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"That's something we wanted for our kids because we really had an awesome childhood, getting into a bit of trouble, getting out of trouble.

" Jude's a pretty responsible kid. He built both our trusts, which allowed us to give him a bit more freedom. "

Cyber psychology researcher Jocelyn Brewer said a lot of young children were still dealing with the effects of social isolation from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ms Brewer said she continued to advocate for a balanced approach from parents when figuring out how long was too long to be looking at a screen.

"Young boys really benefit from being embodied, being able to kind of take mediated risks and kind of explore their environment," she said.

Jocelyn Brewer says she would like to see more publicly available spaces for teenage boys. (Supplied: Jocelyn Brewer)

"A lot of it is just about being around one another and building skills in conversation and communication."

Regional communities creating lifelong bonds

It will come as no surprise to anyone who has ever lived regionally that the communities are tight-knit.

Daniel believes it has contributed to a renaissance of kids playing outside, at least in the Riverland town.

"You probably wouldn't have this level of trust if you were in a city," he said.

"Jude knows if he does the right thing, then the freedoms will continue.

"But if he does the wrong thing, we'll probably find out before he gets home."

Bike races between Christos Babaniotis and Jude Clark are often too close to call. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Ms Clark echoed her husband's thoughts and said having trusted people within the community made her feel comfortable that the boys were safe at all times.

"There's grandparents that see them out and about, or friends of friends," she said.

"The boys are great; they'll go up and say hello to people they know."

Christos and Jude said they appreciated the freedom and trust they had received from their parents.

That appreciation, however, did not extend to an invitation for the older generation to tag along.

"Nup, no parents allowed," Christos said with a smile.

World.title: Third woman engages lawyer over 'incredibly traumatic' Sydney Swans scandal
World.content:
A lawyer representing a third woman involved in the Sydney Swans sexual assault scandal says a potential civil lawsuit is being looked at.

Slater and Gordon senior lawyer, Jackson Pannam, has been engaged to represent a woman who he said contacted police immediately following the alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne in the early hours of Monday, August 17.

"Our client has had her entire world turned upside down and is now trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience," he said.

He said the firm's lawyers "see the profound and long-lasting impact that serious injury, loss and abuse can have on people's lives".

Jackson Pannam says the woman's world has been "turned upside down" by the incident. (ABC News)

On Friday, Carbone Lawyers announced separately that it was representing two women, believed to be adult entertainers involved in the incident, and looking into launching a civil claim.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the Pullman Hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' victory against Essendon last Sunday night.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Mr Pannam said following her initial contact with police, his client was continuing to speak to them as part of their investigation into the incident.

"Everyone deserves to be safe going about their life, at home, at work, and in public spaces without risk of being assaulted or harmed," Mr Pannam said.

"We're standing with our client to give her support at this difficult time, and to help her get the justice she deserves."

Mr Pannam described the woman as "extremely distressed" by what had occurred, and asked for her privacy, and that of the other women involved, to be respected.

He said his client had not spoken to the media.

A police investigation is still underway, but they have not made any arrests or laid charges.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

World.title: A father’s will left $100,000 to charity. His daughters fought for a share
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWInheritance A father’s will left $100,000 to charity. His daughters fought for a share Michaela Whitbourn August 22, 2026 — 1:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A father of three died with almost $100,000 in unspent superannuation. His three daughters, two of whom had been cut out of his will, wanted it split equally between them. His middle daughter was ultimately paid the entire sum – even though his will suggested the cash should go to charity. It can be difficult for a will-maker to know where their unspent superannuation will end up. Matt Willis The case highlights difficulties faced by will-makers in ensuring that their unspent superannuation goes to their intended beneficiary. It also displays particular obstacles to leaving money to charity. The decision to give the money to the middle daughter was made by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which handles complaints for most superannuation funds.



New research by University of Sydney Law School Associate Professors Natalie Silver and Ben Chen reveals that the authority often departs from the wishes expressed by a will-maker when resolving complaints about the distribution of a deceased’s superannuation. The authors analysed 269 decisions by the authority and found that it distributed the super according to the will in 13 or 11.2 per cent of the 116 cases that discussed the will. The authority gives primacy to the interests of dependants, the authors say. Super among Australians’ chief assets Silver and Chen argue that the law on distributing a deceased’s superannuation is unduly complex, and say that changes would make it easier for the money to be left to charity. “Together with the family home, superannuation is now the principal source of wealth for most working Australians,” they write in a forthcoming Melbourne University Law Review paper.



Most Australians now die with the majority of wealth they had when they retired, including most of their super balance, according to a Treasury report cited by the authors. Australia’s compulsory superannuation system provides “a rich source of potential charitable bequests” that could unlock billions, they say, helping the government to reach its aim of doubling philanthropic giving by 2030. Super may not be covered by a will Under the existing law, it is difficult for a will-maker to ensure who gets their superannuation when they die. This is because the pool of money is managed separately by a super fund trustee and does not automatically form part of a deceased’s estate. Chen said that the current situation was “unnecessarily complex”. Many of the problems would be resolved, he said, if there was a default rule that super funds should pay unspent superannuation to a deceased’s “legal personal representative”, which is typically their executor.



The executor would then distribute the funds according to the will, including to any nominated charities. AFCA’s role But super fund trustees are responsible for distributing the funds. They are not bound by the will and can only distribute the funds to a narrow group of people. AFCA handles complaints about how the funds are distributed, and in limited cases the Federal Court may hear an appeal. The main way for a person to ensure that their intended beneficiary gets their unspent super is to sign a document called a binding death-benefit nomination, which must be followed by most super fund trustees. The binding nominations have significant limitations. Unlike a will, they expire after three years, though there may be a way to set up a “non-lapsing” nomination in some cases.



How charities are disadvantaged In addition, only a small class of dependants, such as a spouse or child, or a deceased’s executor or administrator, can be named as beneficiaries in binding nominations. Charities cannot be included, nor can many individuals. “The definition of dependant is quite narrow,” Silver said. It typically did not include parents, siblings or close friends. The only way to direct the money to a charity is for a super fund member to name their executor or administrator in a binding nomination, and to include the charity separately in their will. This two-stage process results in “unnecessary cost and complexity ... in making a charitable superannuation bequest”, Silver and Chen say, and it disadvantages charities.



A tax applies when a charity receives superannuation through a deceased estate, which also acts as a disincentive. By contrast, when the money is paid to some dependants it is tax-free. ‘Not unique to charities’ “The obstacles that we identify in the paper in relation to charities are not unique to charities,” Chen said. Restrictions on who can be named in a binding death-benefit nomination make it harder to leave the money to other beneficiaries, including many extended family members. The same two-step process would need to be followed. The authors say that two changes would help ensure more people left their unspent super to charity: super fund members should be able to name a charity directly in binding death-benefit nominations, and bequests to charities from unspent super should not be taxed.



They argue the changes would be cost-effective to the government and could accommodate the interests of dependants and other family members. The daughters’ fight In the case of the three daughters, the wishes of the father were far from clear. He had lodged a nomination in April 2019, saying his middle daughter should be paid his unspent super in full. But that document was non-binding. His will in October that year made more complex arrangements for this daughter that would have resulted in the super ultimately being paid to charity. He died months later, in 2020.



Related Article Exclusive

Inheritance She cared for her ailing husband for years. There was a sting waiting in his will AFCA, resolving a complaint, found it was unfair and unreasonable not to pay the sum in full to the middle daughter. The authority gave primacy to the father’s wishes in his non-binding nomination. “Although his wishes as expressed in his will are not to be ignored, they are not to be taken as determinative,” it said. Silver said current rules for distributing a deceased’s unspent super were unworkable chiefly because the compulsory superannuation system had not been designed with inheritance in mind. “It was designed to provide savings to be used as income during retirement,” she said. “But the problem is that now a lot of Australians are dying with the majority of their superannuation still intact.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: North shore share house sells for $200,000 below its reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions North shore share house sells for $200,000 below its reserve Robyn Willis August 22, 2026 — 1:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A group of seven vendors sold a property they jointly owned in Naremburn for $2.7 million, $200,000 less than its reserve, on Saturday. Five of the vendors have been living in the five-bedroom property at 22 Park Road, with two others living in Dubbo and Japan, respectively. All were present, in person or on the phone, for the auction. Three parties registered to bid for the two-storey, five-bedroom home, with two taking part. Bidding opened at $2.5 million and rose in increments of $50,000 and $25,000 before a series of $10,000 bids. The property had a guide of $2.75 million and a reserve of $2.9 million.



Related Article Exclusive

Sydney house prices The property premium Sydney families are paying for the right state school There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Both the successful bidders and the underbidders were families planning to renovate to make the place suitable for their multi-generational needs. Forsyth Real Estate sales agent Joe Campisi said that it was challenging to manage so many vendors, especially when the bidding stalled. “I was surprised they all agreed to the same price,” he said. “I told them during the week that this would happen [with the lower bid] and then it actually happened, which helped them accept the decision.”



The period home in Naremburn sits on a 607-square-metre corner block. The new owners plan to renovate to accommodate three generations of their family. Domain Campisi said that, in general, vendors are now more aligned with buyer expectations. “Owners are becoming more aware of what the market is doing,” he said, “and they are more open to accepting the bid on the day rather than waiting to see what will happen afterwards.” The property was one of 479 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Kensington, a young family were the only bidders to register for a three-bedroom apartment, paying $30,000 less than the reserve.



Cooley auctioneer Briannan Davis knocked back their bid of $1.1 million to buy 7/22 Villiers Street before entering a bid of $1.25 million on behalf of the vendor. After 40 minutes of negotiating, the bidders raised their offer to $1.29 million and the property sold under auction conditions. It had a guide of $1.2 million and a reserve of $1.32 million. The vendors are moving out of the area and want to upsize. Belle Property Bondi Junction sales agent Edward Brown described market conditions at present as “normal”. “We don’t have that manic flow of people with FOMO. They are a lot more considered in their buying, but they are still looking for good quality,” he said.

World.title: Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss Michael Koziol Updated August 22, 2026 — 12:52pm ,first published August 22, 2026 — 2:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Personal letters from Natalie Harp to her boss Donald Trump have been revealed in full for the first time, shedding light on a relationship between the US president and one of his closest aides that has become the subject of intense scrutiny. Two letters, written by Harp during or immediately after a trip to the United Kingdom in 2023 – when Trump was out of office – reveal an aide deeply concerned about having upset or offended Trump in some way, and desperate to foster an intimate relationship with him. Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s executive assistant, wrote letters to him that have been described as “lovesick” and “weird”. Getty Images The lengthy letters were published by author Michael Wolff and US news site The Daily Beast, to which Wolff is a regular contributor. Wolff said on a podcast he released the letters now because they showed a relationship “that should not exist in a professional setting”. In one, Harp asks for Trump’s forgiveness after apparently upsetting him during a golfing holiday to Scotland. “I was alone in the van outside Customs without my passport, I panicked, and I should have just called Secret Service instead of you,” she wrote.



“I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland … If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me. “I want things to always be right between us … I never want to bring you anything but joy. I’m sorry I lost my focus. You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life.” That letter was signed: “With all my heart, Natalie.” In a subsequent letter to Trump, Harp said the UK trip gave her a chance to learn about herself and unplug. “I didn’t have to be ‘Human Printer’,” she said, a reference to her job of printing off news and complimentary articles for Trump to read.



“With so much thinking time, I confess it did have a slightly negative effect at times, that I know you picked up on, but the end result, I believe, will be worth it. “I had no idea how rapidly I was approaching burnout, and starting to envy those whose only ‘job’ seems to be to talk with you, and look pretty. I want that job!!! “So many times, I’m just trying to stay afloat with all that’s coming in for you, I look like a hunchback who didn’t have time to freshen up (at least you know what I should look like)! “I miss the days when you used to call, during my Talkshow days, and we’d talk about everything and nothing. I want to get back to that synergy. We shouldn’t have to talk about work all the time!!”



Harp went on to tell Trump she needed to reunite her “past self” with her current person to become the best version of herself and “make you proud”. “Please, when I fail, will you tell me?” she wrote. “You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more. Loading “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ - And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” That letter was signed: “Always, Natalie.” Excerpts of the letters had previously been published by The New York Times. Wolff described the content as “lovesick”, “submissive” and “weird”, and said while he did not believe Harp was Trump’s girlfriend, they were evidence of an inappropriate relationship between the president and a workplace subordinate.



“The relationship here is not a relationship that should exist in a professional setting,” he said on The Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast. “This ain’t normal.” Related Article Trump's White House Innuendo and rumour: Who is Natalie Harp, the ‘human printer’ who follows Trump everywhere? Harp, 35, joined Trump’s staff while he was out of office and worked on his 2024 election campaign. Since his return to the Oval Office, she has served as executive assistant to the president, including drafting and posting his remarks on Truth Social – his preferred method of communication. Contacted for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told this masthead Harp was one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on the president’s team. “The Fake News’s continued attacks on President Trump and his Administration prove exactly why trust in media is at historic lows,” he said. “The media should focus on reporting real news and stop trying to smear dedicated public servants.”



Harp was thrust into the spotlight last weekend after Democratic senator and potential presidential candidate Jon Ossoff told a rally that Trump would rather travel on his plane “with Natalie” than do his job. That was a reference to Harp being one of a handful of aides selected by Trump to take a secret flight out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, rather than travel on “Air Force One”, which had been deemed a security risk amid threats from Iran. Trump and Harp appear together at a 2023 golf tournament at Trump’s Bedminster Golf Club, where Harp allegedly spent a summer sleeping in a locker room. NYT Natalie Harp this week disembarking Marine One with President Donald Trump following a weekend in New Jersey at his golf club. Getty Images Multiple senior aides and cabinet secretaries were left to travel on the Boeing 747 – as well as the travelling press pack, who were not told of the security risk or that Trump was not on board.



On Wednesday, MS-NOW revealed Harp had worked in the White House and Trump’s inner circle for more than a year without receiving a security clearance. MS-NOW reported that Trump intervened amid rising concerns from security officials and White House lawyers, and that she now has a clearance. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist who was chief-of-staff to Barack Obama as president, said if it was true that “the person closest to [Trump] and his thinking on a daily basis has no security clearance and refuses to submit to the process of getting it, it’s a deadly serious issue”. Axelrod was previously critical of Ossoff’s decision to raise Harp at his rally, saying it “seemed gratuitous and unnecessary”. Trump’s allies accused Ossoff of trafficking in innuendo and smearing a public servant with the implication she was having a sexual relationship with her boss. Trump, when asked during the week for a response to Ossoff’s remarks, said that Ossoff looked like Pee-wee Herman, the childish comedy character created by Paul Reubens.



Natalie Harp in the Oval Office during a meeting to sign an executive order about vaccines. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission Nick Wright August 22, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a picture that lives on Taylor Smith’s laptop of a time when her parents were the happiest she had seen them. She had just tasted premiership success with the Brisbane Lions – a maiden AFLW title for a club that had reached two grand finals before but failed to go the distance. Only six months later, her father, Shaun, was gone – a sudden heart attack when he was 52 leaving a heartbreaking void in the family. “Grief is a crazy process for everyone. It’s up and down all the time. There are little moments where you reflect on it, or might look at a picture, and the reality of it might just hit you in the face,” Smith tells this masthead five years on from her dad’s death. Taylor Smith pictured during her Brisbane Lions days. Getty Images “My mum lost her soulmate at a time when my brother and I were at an age where we were building our own lives, and they were getting their life together back.



“They were spending their weekends on jet skis and wine tours and all these sorts of things, and to see that taken away from mum, and then my grandparents lost their son, and no parent wants their kid’s time to be up before theirs. Related Article AFLW Among the league’s pioneers, Shannon says her mum’s memory pushes her forward “Watching all that unfold, those effects continue for so long.” After 76 games in Brisbane colours, Smith began charting a new journey at the Sydney Swans – kicking a game-high three goals on club debut to inspire an eight-point triumph of the Crows. That clash in Adelaide was attended by her mother, Smith chuckling at how she loved “sharing all the content that comes out – she’s so funny”.



As for Shaun, he was a Brisbane supporter whom Smith always wanted to impress, such was the respect he garnered. So how would he feel about her donning the red-and-white guernsey? Loading “I think he’d be a Swans supporter now as well. I think he’d appreciate the chance I took and the steps I took to grow as a person and challenge myself,” Smith says. “I think he would appreciate that more; I don’t think it would matter too much about the colours.”



Smith hints that it was the loss of Shaun that inspired her to take on a new adventure. Related Article AFL 2026 As Fagan surpasses Matthews, he has a mission. But it’s not another title “When my dad passed, I had this real clarity of ‘life is so short – if you have a dream, you have to chase it’. Even just with holidays, he really wanted to travel to Japan and go skiing, and he kept saying for three or four years ‘we’ll go on a family holiday’,” Smith says. “Now he’ll never get to have that experience, and it was just one of those things that made me realise we don’t always have tomorrow. It made me feel like I wanted to live my life to the absolute fullest, to challenge myself and grow and never be comfortable.” Perhaps what Smith adored most about her relationship with Shaun was how whenever she decided to pursue something, she discovered her father had done the same. She recalls coming home in grade 4 after setting a school high jump record, only to be told by her dad that he did the same in his younger years.



When she opted to pursue Aussie rules, he told her he used to be the captain of his club. Smith is now determined to use the harrowing family chapter to inspire change, featuring in a Heart Foundation fundraising campaign, We’re All In, for research initiatives. Taylor Smith will be booting goals for the Swans in 2026. AFL Photos While survival rates have improved, heart disease remains one of Australia’s biggest killers, claiming about 115 lives daily, while the foundation’s State of the Heart Survey 2025 revealed 70 per cent of people did not consider heart disease to be a relevant concern at their stage of life. As Smith reveals, the most frustrating part of the loss was that her mum had regularly insisted he “go get your heart checked”, with the response often being “I’m healthy”.



The 26-year-old recalls filming the campaign, and throughout the day feeling strong and excited by the message she was sharing. The next day, she broke down. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Trying to be a superstar’: The mindset shift behind Ashcroft’s latest exploits “I just crashed and burned because the reality of saying ‘I lost my dad to a heart attack’ multiple times to get the right shot really hit me. I was emotional, but it was also quite empowering to know what was going to come from my vulnerability,” Smith says. “Hopefully, it will save a few lives. If it saves two lives it means all those family members related to that person don’t have to go through what my family went through.” Smith and the Swans will seek to remain unbeaten in the AFLW campaign when they clash with Essendon on Sunday. World.title: 43 minutes, 22 balls and five wickets: Starc wreaks havoc in second Test
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket 43 minutes, 22 balls and five wickets: Starc wreaks havoc in second Test Nick Wright Updated August 22, 2026 — 10:58am ,first published August 22, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: It took 43 minutes for Australia’s first Test capitulation in Darwin to feel like a distant memory, as Mitchell Starc tore the heart out of the Bangladesh’s top order with an opening spell masterclass to begin the second Test, and leave the visitors reeling a 6-35 at lunch. For the 28th time in his Test career, the 36-year-old claimed a wicket in his first over of an innings – catching Shadman Islam’s outside edge with a full, out-swinging delivery which flew to Cameron Green in the gully with his opening delivery. Mitch Starc has claimed a five-wicket haul in his first 22 balls in Mackay. Getty Images Skipper Pat Cummins’ decision to bowl after winning the toss looked better by the over, as Starc struck first ball of his second over as well – Tanzid Hasan (0) unable to dig out a full ball outside off, and instead guiding it off the edge to Beau Webster in the slips. Starc was on a tear. His next ball, he trapped Najmul Hossain Shanton lbw – with the Bangladesh captain’s challenge ultimately deemed to be clipping leg stump based on the umpire’s call.



The left-arm spearhead was in a mood to impress the Great Barrier Reef Arena crowd, drawing a low edge from Mominul Haque (nine) in his third over, with Green diving low to his left to claim an impressive catch. When a vicious Starc bouncer caught Litton Das high on the bat in his fourth over, only for Webster to drop a sitter in the slips, it appeared maybe Bangladesh had some fortune going their way. Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne in Mackay. Getty Images But that hope was eradicated next ball when Starc trapped him on the pads for a duck, and despite the appeal being turned down, replays confirmed the ball had pitched in line and was hitting to deliver Starc a five-wicket haul in 22 balls. It took nine overs from that point for another breakthrough, Cummins getting one to nip off the seam from off stump into middle to bowl Mushfiqur Rahim for five.



It means Australia’s under-siege batting line-up may not have to wait long to launch their redemption mission after their failings in Darwin, with Bangladesh reeling at 5-12 inside 10 overs. Trailing 1-0 in the series on the back of their shock nine-wicket defeat, the Australians stepped out in Mackay with the one change – Queensland’s Matt Renshaw replacing Jake Weatherald to open the batting alongside Travis Head. Aside from Steve Smith’s first innings 71 and Cameron Green’s drought-breaking century in the second dig, Australia were humbled across five days by the typical Test cricket minnows, and will be seeking redemption in north Queensland. Marnus Labuschagne in particular will need a big score, managing scores of one and 31 in the Northern Territory, which led coach Andrew McDonald to issue a warning that the 32-year-old “needs runs”. Bangladesh made one change to their triumphant line-up, with left-arm quick Shoriful Islam coming in for Ebadot Hossain. Second Test XIs Australia: Travis Head, Matthew Renshaw, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (capt), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood Bangladesh: Tanzid Hasan, Shadman Islam, Mominul Haque, Najmul Hossain Shanto (capt), Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das, Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Hasan Mahmud, Taskin Ahmed, Taijul Islam, Shoriful Islam

The decision to give the money to the middle daughter was made by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which handles complaints for most superannuation funds.



New research by University of Sydney Law School Associate Professors Natalie Silver and Ben Chen reveals that the authority often departs from the wishes expressed by a will-maker when resolving complaints about the distribution of a deceased’s superannuation. The authors analysed 269 decisions by the authority and found that it distributed the super according to the will in 13 or 11.2 per cent of the 116 cases that discussed the will. The authority gives primacy to the interests of dependants, the authors say. Super among Australians’ chief assets Silver and Chen argue that the law on distributing a deceased’s superannuation is unduly complex, and say that changes would make it easier for the money to be left to charity. “Together with the family home, superannuation is now the principal source of wealth for most working Australians,” they write in a forthcoming Melbourne University Law Review paper.



Most Australians now die with the majority of wealth they had when they retired, including most of their super balance, according to a Treasury report cited by the authors. Australia’s compulsory superannuation system provides “a rich source of potential charitable bequests” that could unlock billions, they say, helping the government to reach its aim of doubling philanthropic giving by 2030. Super may not be covered by a will Under the existing law, it is difficult for a will-maker to ensure who gets their superannuation when they die. This is because the pool of money is managed separately by a super fund trustee and does not automatically form part of a deceased’s estate. Chen said that the current situation was “unnecessarily complex”. Many of the problems would be resolved, he said, if there was a default rule that super funds should pay unspent superannuation to a deceased’s “legal personal representative”, which is typically their executor.



The executor would then distribute the funds according to the will, including to any nominated charities. AFCA’s role But super fund trustees are responsible for distributing the funds. They are not bound by the will and can only distribute the funds to a narrow group of people. AFCA handles complaints about how the funds are distributed, and in limited cases the Federal Court may hear an appeal. The main way for a person to ensure that their intended beneficiary gets their unspent super is to sign a document called a binding death-benefit nomination, which must be followed by most super fund trustees. The binding nominations have significant limitations. Unlike a will, they expire after three years, though there may be a way to set up a “non-lapsing” nomination in some cases.



How charities are disadvantaged In addition, only a small class of dependants, such as a spouse or child, or a deceased’s executor or administrator, can be named as beneficiaries in binding nominations. Charities cannot be included, nor can many individuals. “The definition of dependant is quite narrow,” Silver said. It typically did not include parents, siblings or close friends. The only way to direct the money to a charity is for a super fund member to name their executor or administrator in a binding nomination, and to include the charity separately in their will. This two-stage process results in “unnecessary cost and complexity ... in making a charitable superannuation bequest”, Silver and Chen say, and it disadvantages charities.



A tax applies when a charity receives superannuation through a deceased estate, which also acts as a disincentive. By contrast, when the money is paid to some dependants it is tax-free. ‘Not unique to charities’ “The obstacles that we identify in the paper in relation to charities are not unique to charities,” Chen said. Restrictions on who can be named in a binding death-benefit nomination make it harder to leave the money to other beneficiaries, including many extended family members. The same two-step process would need to be followed. The authors say that two changes would help ensure more people left their unspent super to charity: super fund members should be able to name a charity directly in binding death-benefit nominations, and bequests to charities from unspent super should not be taxed.



They argue the changes would be cost-effective to the government and could accommodate the interests of dependants and other family members. The daughters’ fight In the case of the three daughters, the wishes of the father were far from clear. He had lodged a nomination in April 2019, saying his middle daughter should be paid his unspent super in full. But that document was non-binding. His will in October that year made more complex arrangements for this daughter that would have resulted in the super ultimately being paid to charity. He died months later, in 2020.



Related Article Exclusive

Inheritance She cared for her ailing husband for years. There was a sting waiting in his will AFCA, resolving a complaint, found it was unfair and unreasonable not to pay the sum in full to the middle daughter. The authority gave primacy to the father’s wishes in his non-binding nomination. “Although his wishes as expressed in his will are not to be ignored, they are not to be taken as determinative,” it said. Silver said current rules for distributing a deceased’s unspent super were unworkable chiefly because the compulsory superannuation system had not been designed with inheritance in mind. “It was designed to provide savings to be used as income during retirement,” she said. “But the problem is that now a lot of Australians are dying with the majority of their superannuation still intact.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: North shore share house sells for $200,000 below its reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions North shore share house sells for $200,000 below its reserve Robyn Willis August 22, 2026 — 1:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A group of seven vendors sold a property they jointly owned in Naremburn for $2.7 million, $200,000 less than its reserve, on Saturday. Five of the vendors have been living in the five-bedroom property at 22 Park Road, with two others living in Dubbo and Japan, respectively. All were present, in person or on the phone, for the auction. Three parties registered to bid for the two-storey, five-bedroom home, with two taking part. Bidding opened at $2.5 million and rose in increments of $50,000 and $25,000 before a series of $10,000 bids. The property had a guide of $2.75 million and a reserve of $2.9 million.



Related Article Exclusive

Sydney house prices The property premium Sydney families are paying for the right state school There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Both the successful bidders and the underbidders were families planning to renovate to make the place suitable for their multi-generational needs. Forsyth Real Estate sales agent Joe Campisi said that it was challenging to manage so many vendors, especially when the bidding stalled. “I was surprised they all agreed to the same price,” he said. “I told them during the week that this would happen [with the lower bid] and then it actually happened, which helped them accept the decision.”



The period home in Naremburn sits on a 607-square-metre corner block. The new owners plan to renovate to accommodate three generations of their family. Domain Campisi said that, in general, vendors are now more aligned with buyer expectations. “Owners are becoming more aware of what the market is doing,” he said, “and they are more open to accepting the bid on the day rather than waiting to see what will happen afterwards.” The property was one of 479 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Kensington, a young family were the only bidders to register for a three-bedroom apartment, paying $30,000 less than the reserve.



Cooley auctioneer Briannan Davis knocked back their bid of $1.1 million to buy 7/22 Villiers Street before entering a bid of $1.25 million on behalf of the vendor. After 40 minutes of negotiating, the bidders raised their offer to $1.29 million and the property sold under auction conditions. It had a guide of $1.2 million and a reserve of $1.32 million. The vendors are moving out of the area and want to upsize. Belle Property Bondi Junction sales agent Edward Brown described market conditions at present as “normal”. “We don’t have that manic flow of people with FOMO. They are a lot more considered in their buying, but they are still looking for good quality,” he said.
