World.title: Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss Michael Koziol Updated August 22, 2026 — 12:52pm ,first published August 22, 2026 — 2:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Personal letters from Natalie Harp to her boss Donald Trump have been revealed in full for the first time, shedding light on a relationship between the US president and one of his closest aides that has become the subject of intense scrutiny. Two letters, written by Harp during or immediately after a trip to the United Kingdom in 2023 – when Trump was out of office – reveal an aide deeply concerned about having upset or offended Trump in some way, and desperate to foster an intimate relationship with him. Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s executive assistant, wrote letters to him that have been described as “lovesick” and “weird”. Getty Images The lengthy letters were published by author Michael Wolff and US news site The Daily Beast, to which Wolff is a regular contributor. Wolff said on a podcast he released the letters now because they showed a relationship “that should not exist in a professional setting”. In one, Harp asks for Trump’s forgiveness after apparently upsetting him during a golfing holiday to Scotland. “I was alone in the van outside Customs without my passport, I panicked, and I should have just called Secret Service instead of you,” she wrote.



“I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland … If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me. “I want things to always be right between us … I never want to bring you anything but joy. I’m sorry I lost my focus. You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life.” That letter was signed: “With all my heart, Natalie.” In a subsequent letter to Trump, Harp said the UK trip gave her a chance to learn about herself and unplug. “I didn’t have to be ‘Human Printer’,” she said, a reference to her job of printing off news and complimentary articles for Trump to read.



“With so much thinking time, I confess it did have a slightly negative effect at times, that I know you picked up on, but the end result, I believe, will be worth it. “I had no idea how rapidly I was approaching burnout, and starting to envy those whose only ‘job’ seems to be to talk with you, and look pretty. I want that job!!! “So many times, I’m just trying to stay afloat with all that’s coming in for you, I look like a hunchback who didn’t have time to freshen up (at least you know what I should look like)! “I miss the days when you used to call, during my Talkshow days, and we’d talk about everything and nothing. I want to get back to that synergy. We shouldn’t have to talk about work all the time!!”



Harp went on to tell Trump she needed to reunite her “past self” with her current person to become the best version of herself and “make you proud”. “Please, when I fail, will you tell me?” she wrote. “You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more. Loading “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ - And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” That letter was signed: “Always, Natalie.” Excerpts of the letters had previously been published by The New York Times. Wolff described the content as “lovesick”, “submissive” and “weird”, and said while he did not believe Harp was Trump’s girlfriend, they were evidence of an inappropriate relationship between the president and a workplace subordinate.



“The relationship here is not a relationship that should exist in a professional setting,” he said on The Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast. “This ain’t normal.” Related Article Trump's White House Innuendo and rumour: Who is Natalie Harp, the ‘human printer’ who follows Trump everywhere? Harp, 35, joined Trump’s staff while he was out of office and worked on his 2024 election campaign. Since his return to the Oval Office, she has served as executive assistant to the president, including drafting and posting his remarks on Truth Social – his preferred method of communication. Contacted for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told this masthead Harp was one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on the president’s team. “The Fake News’s continued attacks on President Trump and his Administration prove exactly why trust in media is at historic lows,” he said. “The media should focus on reporting real news and stop trying to smear dedicated public servants.”



Harp was thrust into the spotlight last weekend after Democratic senator and potential presidential candidate Jon Ossoff told a rally that Trump would rather travel on his plane “with Natalie” than do his job. That was a reference to Harp being one of a handful of aides selected by Trump to take a secret flight out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, rather than travel on “Air Force One”, which had been deemed a security risk amid threats from Iran. Trump and Harp appear together at a 2023 golf tournament at Trump’s Bedminster Golf Club, where Harp allegedly spent a summer sleeping in a locker room. NYT Natalie Harp this week disembarking Marine One with President Donald Trump following a weekend in New Jersey at his golf club. Getty Images Multiple senior aides and cabinet secretaries were left to travel on the Boeing 747 – as well as the travelling press pack, who were not told of the security risk or that Trump was not on board.



On Wednesday, MS-NOW revealed Harp had worked in the White House and Trump’s inner circle for more than a year without receiving a security clearance. MS-NOW reported that Trump intervened amid rising concerns from security officials and White House lawyers, and that she now has a clearance. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist who was chief-of-staff to Barack Obama as president, said if it was true that “the person closest to [Trump] and his thinking on a daily basis has no security clearance and refuses to submit to the process of getting it, it’s a deadly serious issue”. Axelrod was previously critical of Ossoff’s decision to raise Harp at his rally, saying it “seemed gratuitous and unnecessary”. Trump’s allies accused Ossoff of trafficking in innuendo and smearing a public servant with the implication she was having a sexual relationship with her boss. Trump, when asked during the week for a response to Ossoff’s remarks, said that Ossoff looked like Pee-wee Herman, the childish comedy character created by Paul Reubens.



Natalie Harp in the Oval Office during a meeting to sign an executive order about vaccines. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission Nick Wright August 22, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a picture that lives on Taylor Smith’s laptop of a time when her parents were the happiest she had seen them. She had just tasted premiership success with the Brisbane Lions – a maiden AFLW title for a club that had reached two grand finals before but failed to go the distance. Only six months later, her father, Shaun, was gone – a sudden heart attack when he was 52 leaving a heartbreaking void in the family. “Grief is a crazy process for everyone. It’s up and down all the time. There are little moments where you reflect on it, or might look at a picture, and the reality of it might just hit you in the face,” Smith tells this masthead five years on from her dad’s death. Taylor Smith pictured during her Brisbane Lions days. Getty Images “My mum lost her soulmate at a time when my brother and I were at an age where we were building our own lives, and they were getting their life together back.



“They were spending their weekends on jet skis and wine tours and all these sorts of things, and to see that taken away from mum, and then my grandparents lost their son, and no parent wants their kid’s time to be up before theirs. Related Article AFLW Among the league’s pioneers, Shannon says her mum’s memory pushes her forward “Watching all that unfold, those effects continue for so long.” After 76 games in Brisbane colours, Smith began charting a new journey at the Sydney Swans – kicking a game-high three goals on club debut to inspire an eight-point triumph of the Crows. That clash in Adelaide was attended by her mother, Smith chuckling at how she loved “sharing all the content that comes out – she’s so funny”.



As for Shaun, he was a Brisbane supporter whom Smith always wanted to impress, such was the respect he garnered. So how would he feel about her donning the red-and-white guernsey? Loading “I think he’d be a Swans supporter now as well. I think he’d appreciate the chance I took and the steps I took to grow as a person and challenge myself,” Smith says. “I think he would appreciate that more; I don’t think it would matter too much about the colours.”



Smith hints that it was the loss of Shaun that inspired her to take on a new adventure. Related Article AFL 2026 As Fagan surpasses Matthews, he has a mission. But it’s not another title “When my dad passed, I had this real clarity of ‘life is so short – if you have a dream, you have to chase it’. Even just with holidays, he really wanted to travel to Japan and go skiing, and he kept saying for three or four years ‘we’ll go on a family holiday’,” Smith says. “Now he’ll never get to have that experience, and it was just one of those things that made me realise we don’t always have tomorrow. It made me feel like I wanted to live my life to the absolute fullest, to challenge myself and grow and never be comfortable.” Perhaps what Smith adored most about her relationship with Shaun was how whenever she decided to pursue something, she discovered her father had done the same. She recalls coming home in grade 4 after setting a school high jump record, only to be told by her dad that he did the same in his younger years.



When she opted to pursue Aussie rules, he told her he used to be the captain of his club. Smith is now determined to use the harrowing family chapter to inspire change, featuring in a Heart Foundation fundraising campaign, We’re All In, for research initiatives. Taylor Smith will be booting goals for the Swans in 2026. AFL Photos While survival rates have improved, heart disease remains one of Australia’s biggest killers, claiming about 115 lives daily, while the foundation’s State of the Heart Survey 2025 revealed 70 per cent of people did not consider heart disease to be a relevant concern at their stage of life. As Smith reveals, the most frustrating part of the loss was that her mum had regularly insisted he “go get your heart checked”, with the response often being “I’m healthy”.



The 26-year-old recalls filming the campaign, and throughout the day feeling strong and excited by the message she was sharing. The next day, she broke down. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Trying to be a superstar’: The mindset shift behind Ashcroft’s latest exploits “I just crashed and burned because the reality of saying ‘I lost my dad to a heart attack’ multiple times to get the right shot really hit me. I was emotional, but it was also quite empowering to know what was going to come from my vulnerability,” Smith says. “Hopefully, it will save a few lives. If it saves two lives it means all those family members related to that person don’t have to go through what my family went through.” Smith and the Swans will seek to remain unbeaten in the AFLW campaign when they clash with Essendon on Sunday. World.title: Luke Sayers and new girlfriend step out among powerbrokers at Million Dollar Lunch
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Luke Sayers and new girlfriend step out among powerbrokers at Million Dollar Lunch Fiona Byrne August 22, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Embattled business identity Luke Sayers has been flying under the social scene radar since his lewd photo scandal, divorce and the high-stakes defamation action launched against him by his ex-wife Cate erupted into the public sphere. So it was a surprise when the former Carlton president turned up at the Million Dollar Lunch on Friday. The lunch is one of Melbourne’s most enduring power networking events, is flooded with bold-type names and is awash with media. So Sayers and his striking blonde marketing manager girlfriend, Alexandra Elms, were hardly going to escape notice. Luke Sayers and girlfriend Alexandra Elms leave the Million Dollar Lunch at Crown on Friday. Handily, Sayers arrived late to the event at the Crown Palladium, which meant he avoided the pesky media wall and photographers, and he and Elms were seated with property development company Bonleaf rather than on the table of Tenet, the advisory company that he founded. CBD popped over for a bit of a chat with the former PwC Australia chief executive and his alluring partner, but after a quick handshake Sayers dropped his head and ducked off without uttering a word, while Elms took off in the opposite direction like an Olympic sprinter. Very odd.



Sayers was later spotted in conversation with Australian Grand Prix chair Martin Pakula, wrapping an arm around Pakula’s shoulders and laughing loudly. Sayers speaks with a guest at the lunch. Sayers was one of 762 guests who made their way past giant Alice in Wonderland-type flowers, a ballerina and two human Grecian statues before walking through an emerald velvet-draped entrance to the garden party-themed fundraiser for the Children’s Cancer Foundation. The event was busting with Melbourne decision-makers and powerbrokers and, for good measure, a couple of billionaires – hello, Dennis Bastas and Rick Smith. As CBD predicted, plenty of guests made a beeline to Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo, who is just two weeks into his new role. Abdo was spotted chatting with Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss Sally Curtain and was later in conversation with Lord Mayor Nick Reece.



Tennis Australia boss Andrew Abdo (left) and Todd Woodbridge at the lunch. Sam D’Agostino The political class was well represented, with Major Events and Racing Minister Anthony Carbines, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, Liberal MPs Georgie Crozier and Brad Rosewell, and One Nation’s Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell all in attendance. Seated next to Victoria Racing Club chief executive Kylie Rogers was Lexus Australia’s new chief executive, Jack Hobbs, who moved into the top job in January and will be a fixture at Flemington during Melbourne Cup week in November at the car brand’s famous marquee. Jayco boss Gerry Ryan dug deep, pledging $50,000 to the Children’s Cancer Foundation, a gift that was matched by Bastas and then Smith’s Highland Foundation. Liberal MPs Georgie Crozier (left) and Jess Wilson at the lunch. Sam D’Agostino



Also among the guests were VRC chair Neil Wilson, Australian Grand Prix chief executive Travis Auld, Crown Resorts executives David Tsai and Ed Domingo, Racing Victoria chief executive Aaron Morrison, Mitchelton Group chief Andy Ryan and Melbourne Storm chief executive Justin Rodski. Also there were Logie winner Todd Woodbridge, property developer Renato Pellicano, Zagame Group’s Bobby Zagame, Gigi and Ed Myer, Decjuba boss Tania Austin, Australian Fashion Festival deputy chair Kallie Blauhorn, former Channel Nine presenter Livinia Nixon, ex-Crown executive Peter Crinis, InsureBuild boss Stuart Patterson, and James Roche from Roche Holdings. Cricket great Ricky Ponting, whose wife Rianna is chair of the Million Dollar Lunch committee, had to scoot as the day pushed on, for a late afternoon flight to catch. Before he departed, the Pontings pledged $25,000 from their family foundation, which contributed to the more than $2.3 million raised on the day. Rianna and Ricky Ponting pledged $25,000 from their family foundation. Sam D’Agostino Meanwhile, as the big money flowed and networking went into overdrive, one person quietly went about selling raffle tickets for the Children’s Cancer Foundation – Fiona Carroll. The wife of Premier Ben Carroll was at the lunch helping out the foundation as a volunteer. Now that is impressive.

World.title: Fleeing driver in Palmerston North leaves officer in critical condition
World.content:
A police officer remains in a critical condition after being hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North overnight.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the officer was a young father and known to be a "good bloke".

He said the officer was still in critical condition and on a ventilator.

Bennett said the driver had been signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue but allegedly fled.

"Minutes later, the vehicle, which was not being pursued, hit a police officer laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road. The officer suffered critical injuries and was airlifted to Wellington Hospital, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

"The circumstances of what occurred remain under investigation. From our initial enquiries, the vehicle appeared to be stolen."

Bennett said the two young people who were arrested were 14 and 15 years old.

"After fleeing, the vehicle was monitored as it travelled out of the city. The officer was positioned behind his patrol car preparing to deploy spikes at a driveway between Rongotea Road and Gillespies Line," Superintendent Bennett said.

"The suspect vehicle was travelling eastbound on the wrong side of Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when it struck the police vehicle, and then the two officers. The seriously injured officer was thrown into the side of a car that was parked in the drive."

The two youths were taken into custody at the scene.

Police are due to speak to the alleged offenders and charges are being considered, Bennett said.

The Police officer had been laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when they were hit and injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers visited the injured officer in Wellington Hospital this afternoon and commended the police response.

"No amount of training can prepare you for a situation where you are trying to save the life of a colleague and friend, and they acted with exceptional professionalism.

"This incident highlights the risk my staff face while doing their jobs to keep their communities safe and I would like to acknowledge the efforts of everyone involved last night."

Chambers said he would be travelling to Palmerston North on Saturday evening to speak with the staff there and meet some of those involved in this incident

"We are humbled by the support from members of the community and people across the country, and on behalf of my staff, I thank everyone who has sent kind messages of support."

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The police critical incident investigation is ongoing, and the Independent Police Conduct Authority has been notified.

"We are extremely grateful the outcome was not worse and that is thanks to the efforts of those who responded. The officers' colleagues were faced with an appalling situation and I'm incredibly proud of them," Bennett said.

A scene examination was carried out by the Serious Crash Unit and a section of the road remains closed.

"This work will take time, and we will share information when we are in a position to do so," Bennett said.

"In the meantime, we are wrapping support around the staff members involved and their whānau, as well as their colleagues."

'Waiting and hoping for the best outcome'

Police Minister Mark Mitchell told RNZ he was travelling to Wellington to support the injured officer.

"The Commissioner and I will be providing any support that the family require," he said.

"Policing by its sheer nature does carry risk, there's no doubt about that, but of course that doesn't lessen or reduce the impact that is felt when one of our police officers is injured in the line of duty.

"They are out there protecting their community, they are representative of us, they do carry that risk, but it doesn't make it any easier when a police officer is seriously hurt, injured or killed."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The president of the Police Association, Steve Watt, said family of the officer were by his bedside in hospital.

He said incidents like this were felt by all members.

"Ultimately, the police is a big family and when these sorts of things happen it really cuts deep and it affects us all," he said.

"Much like the rest of our members, we're waiting and hoping for the best outcome."

Watt said they were working with police's welfare network and organising wrap around support not only for the officer but for his family.

"There's a reasonably large contingent of family that have headed to Wellington, so we'll look to continue to support them and make sure that they're well looked after," he said.

The Police officer had been laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when they were hit and injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Echoes of previous case

The injuring of the Palmerston North officer comes 18 years after Sergeant Derek Wootton was killed while laying road spikes in Porirua, north of Wellington.

The 52-year-old was working the night shift when a report was received of a serious assault and carjacking.

Police patrols saw the reported stolen Honda near Porirua and followed it to Titahi Bay. The Honda had reached speeds of 160km/h as it drove through residential streets. Wootton was struck by the car as he deployed the spikes at around 3am on Dimock Street in Titahi Bay. The impact propelled him nearly 30m down the road.

Wootton had previously worked as a builder and milkman before joining the police, and was first posted to Porirua as a constable when he graduated in 1994. Then-Wellington Police District Commander Pieri Munroe described him as an experienced frontline supervisor.

Andrew Popo, a 32-year-old Mongrel Mob member, was charged with dangerous driving, dangerous driving causing death and failing to stop after a motor accident. He was also charged with aggravated robbery, the theft of a Honda Prelude and kidnapping a 16-year-old. He was sentenced to eight years and nine months in jail for manslaughter.

Justice McKenzie says he took into account Popo's genuine remorse and his guilty plea to the manslaughter charge, but also noted a previous history of offending and gang connections.

World.title: Southland student's curiosity earns science honours and a ticket to the US
World.content:
Sophie Ineson admits she never quite outgrew her childhood habit of asking "why, why, why?"

The Year 13 Southland Girls' High School student has instead channelled her relentless curiosity into complex after-school problem-solving, like inventing medical products that work in space and simulating the effect of microplastics on seabirds' digestive enzymes.

Ineson has become a local science fair phenom, with her projects earning $50,000 towards her tertiary education and a trip to the International Science and Engineering Fair in the United States in May.

"I just like doing things that haven't been done before, looking at something that's new and can actually make a big impact on the world," she said.

Ineson's latest project, an investigation into the psychology of conservation messaging, has just won her a clutch of awards at the Southland Science Fair and caught the interest of the Department of Conservation (DOC).

The idea germinated from a visit to her grandparent's house by the beach in Dunedin.

"They actually had a sea lion that was right outside their door, pregnant with a pup, and it gave birth to the pup outside on their property and was raising it there. It's now my grandparents pup, per se," she said.

Ineson said her grandparents kept a careful watch over the sea lion but she could not help wondering what would have happened if their house was owned by someone who did not want sea lions on their property.

She set to work surveying 60 local senior high school students to see how they reacted to different conservation messages.

Somewhat surprisingly, guilt-based messages like "getting too close hurts more than you think" were less effective than empowerment-based messages like "smaller actions from you: a better life for wildlife", she said.

Ineson said she was in contact with DOC staff who seemed interested in translating her findings to the real world.

Sophie Ineson's award-winning project comparing guilt-based and empowerment-based conservation messages. Supplied

She also worked on a space science project last year, designing a product called "Hydro Heal" for wounds in microgravity.

She said minor skin injuries healed differently in space than on Earth and waste had to be managed carefully, meaning it was less than ideal to have "stinky old bandages lying around".

Using hemp seed oil and other natural materials, Ineson created a biodegradable, gelatinous formula to replace plasters.

To test it, Ineson applied her prototype to cuts on apple skins, measuring the browning of the fruit to see if the gel sealed and protected the surface.

Her project was awarded the Prime Minister's Space Prize for Student Endeavour, which included $50,000 to use towards her tertiary studies in New Zealand.

Earlier, on a trip on the Spirit of Adventure ship, Ineson saw plastic floating in the water and was inspired to study the effects of microplastics on seabirds.

Again, Ineson said she was curious to understand "the why", that being the biological effects it had on the birds.

Working with her school science department, Ineson simulated a penguin's digestive tract in a lab using test tubes, water baths and incubators and learnt that the microplastics disrupted vital digestive enzymes.

"I was looking at how the plastic is actually absorbing the enzymes which are in their food, giving them less energy to survive," she said.

As a possible solution, Ineson also researched hydrophobic coatings used to stop barnacles from sticking to ship hulls and whether a similar concept could be applied to plastics to stop enzymes from binding to them.

The research earned her an endorsement through the Southland Science Fair to represent New Zealand at the International Science and Engineering Fair in Phoenix, Arizona.

"To be able to represent my country doing something I love was really awesome," she said.

The event featured "rows and rows and rows" of science fair projects from around the world, interviews with news reporters and an Olympics-style opening ceremomy, she said.

As she approaches the end of high school, Ineson said she was already looking ahead to a future in scientific inquiry.

She has applied to study Biomedical Science at the University of Otago, where she hoped to combine her interests in biology and psychology.

Ineson said letting her curiosity run free had been deeply gratifying, as was "seeing how my small little bit of research from Southland can get all the way to Phoenix, Arizona and actually make some sort of difference in the world".

World.title: Motor industry calls for bipartisan approach to clean car standard
World.content:
Motor industry groups are calling for a bipartisan approach to import charges on high-emission vehicles, after the government confirmed it would retain Labour's Clean Vehicle Standard.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop confirmed the policy would not be scrapped on Friday. However, it has not yet decided on the new penalties it will enforce, saying it will work with the motor industry to develop settings that are "realistic and achievable".

Introduced by the previous government, the Clean Vehicle Standard charges importers a penalty for cars that exceed the target emissions level, but that can be offset by also importing cars with lower emissions.

Drive Electric chair Kirsten Corson said the industry was struggling to keep up with the "flip-flop jandal politics" surrounding the rules.

"What we're really calling for is a bipartisan approach so we can have strategic, long-term, consistent policies that send a really strong signal to the industry but also support [electric vehicle] uptake."

"At the moment, we've got flip-flop jandal politics where we're changing it every two or three years, which makes it super hard for the industry.

"An automotive importer is ordering their stock usually 12 months in advance. They need clear settings so that they can order the right stock."

But she said retaining a Clean Vehicle Standard was "the right call".

"If we were to abolish it ... that would be pretty embarrassing. Russia is the only other country [without it]."

However, she said some importers felt the penalties were "too weak".

Australia charges importers between $50 and $100 per gram of tailpipe emissions over the limit for new vehicles, compared to $15 in New Zealand since Bishop slashed the penalty by nearly 80 percent in November 2025.

On Friday, Transport Minister Chris Bishop confirmed the Clean Vehicle Standard would not be scrapped. RNZ / Mark Papalii

At the time, Bishop said importers could not source enough low-emissions vehicles to avoid being penalised.

Corson hoped the government would consult with the whole industry, not just importers, on both new and used vehicle targets transparently.

Motor Trade Association chief executive Lee Marshall said they wanted the country to have the highest quality and most environmentally friendly vehicles possible.

"Before the 80 percent discount came into effect, there's no doubt the standard was too aggressive, too punitive.

"Even by this year's standards, the most fuel efficient, smallest hybrid vehicles in the market were not too far away from qualifying for a penalty. So we took the view it was unrealistic.

"I think [the Clean Vehicle Standard] is the right tool to use. What we'll be keen to see is that the standard applied is something that is aspirational but achievable rather than being idealistic."

Marshall said they were "mildly concerned" that the government had planned to conclude public consultation on the new targets in 2027, ahead of them taking effect from 1 January, 2028.

"Of course, there is an election in November and depending upon who ends up in power, they might have quite different attitudes to what the right number looks like.

World.title: Are currency conversion charges a rip-off? Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast,'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter,'Money with Susan Edmunds.

I was wondering about the currency conversion charges that banks and credit card companies add when you make a non-NZ dollar transaction. Is there a real cost to banks, or is it just another way of clipping the ticket? My feeling is it's the latter and, as it already seems to me that banks offer a lower exchange rate than, for example, the rates we hear broadcast on RNZ each day, maybe they're clipping the ticket twice. I can't imagine currency conversion involves a bank teller banging away at an adding machine, but perhaps my cynicism is misplaced. Disabuse me, if you can. But if there is no real cost here, I do wonder what these practices add to bank profits each year.

I wasn't sure myself, so I went to ask the banks. Westpac told me that the currency conversion fee on its consumer credit cards was designed to cover the costs it was charged to make the transactions, and was cost-neutral.

Claire Matthews, a banking expert at Massey University, said there was a real cost to the transactions but it was about profits as well.

"The banks need to maintain foreign exchange holdings to back these transactions, plus there are the costs of the transactions - as with all transactions. There is also an exchange rate risk associated with transactions in another currency, because the exchange rate may change between the time the transaction occurs and it is finally settled.

"The difference noted between the rates reported by RNZ and charged for transactions, is simply because the former is the wholesale rate that applies for large - millions of dollars - transactions which has lower transaction costs and the latter is the retail rate."

She said there were an increasing number of alternatives for international transactions that could offer better exchange rates or lower fees, so if you were worried about incurring them regularly, you could look at other options.

A banking expert says there are real costs to non-NZ dollar transactions - but currency conversion charges are about profits as well. 123RF

How much money can be put into your KiwiSaver? Is there a limit?

No, there's no limit.

When you're making contributions from your pay, you can set the amount at anything up to 10 percent. But you can make any additional voluntary payments you want to on top of that.

You might hear other countries talking about limits on what can go into super savings, but that is generally because there is a tax incentive associated with that. In New Zealand, we don't have those perks so there is no limit.

Whether it's appropriate to put your extra investment in there will depend on your wider circumstances, though.

My wife and I are recently retired with a mortgage-free property with a value of approximately $2.6m. We have $900,000 cash and are interested in your thoughts on how best to utilise these funds. The funds are currently sitting in a bank term deposit due to become available.

We are well travelled and will not go far moving forward, maybe one more European trip and annual Gold Coast holidays. We have a reasonable appetite for risk. We have never been involved in the share market but retain an open mind around various opportunities.

Ana-Marie Lockyer, chief executive at Pie Funds, said it's probably worth taking some more risk with at least some of your money.

"Holding $900,000 entirely in cash protects you from share market volatility but exposes you to inflation and the risk that your money doesn't grow sufficiently over a long retirement."

She said she might suggest you put some of your money into a diversified portfolio including some shares.

"Given the amount involved and the fact they are entering a new stage of life and new to investing, now would be a good time to sit down with a financial adviser. An adviser can help them think through what they want their retirement to look like, how much income and access to capital they are likely to need, and what their longer-term goals are.

"From there, they can work out an appropriate mix of cash, income and growth assets that reflects both those needs and their appetite for risk. The aim shouldn't simply be to take more risk for the sake of higher returns, but to make sure their $900,000 is invested in a way that gives them the right balance of security, flexibility and long-term growth."

World.title: Rollers Bakery, made famous by golfer Ryan Fox, reports attempted break-in
World.content:
Kiwi golfer Ryan Fox's favourite bakery is cleaning up after an apparent break-in attempt.

Rollers Bakery on Auckland North Shore had queues out the door last month after Fox gave it a shoutout following his British Open win.

On Saturday the bakery said on social media "someone attempted to break in by kicking in our front doors and smashing a window".

"We can't physically open our doors due to damage," a post on its Facebook page said.

"They didn't steal anything or damage inside the shop.

"We appreciate all the messages but we don't need help cleaning up or anything. Just going to go through insurance steps and/organising glass/door repair."

New Zealand's Ryan Fox speaks as he holds a press conference beside the Claret Jug after winning the Open Golf championship at Royal Birkdale, England, July 19, 2026. AFP

One fan of the bakery said on the post the "urge for foxy pies is too great for some people it seems".

The 'Foxy', named after the golfer, is a steak, bacon jam and cheese pie.

Fox had been a regular customer for just over a year, co-owner Tamara Tait told RNZ's Morning Report in July.

Rollers Bakery was cleaned out of pies, after the Ryan Fox shout out. Supplied

"He's just super humble and comes in and grabs his pie usually like, when he's landed from the airport."

World.title: Christchurch city councillor calls for bed register to crack down on unapproved Airbnbs
World.content:
A Christchurch city councillor is calling for a bed register to crack down on units being used for short-stay accommodation without permission.

His comments come after the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment backed a ruling that multi-unit or apartment owners must ask permission before using residential properties as a holiday or short-term rental.

The council had sought a determination from the ministry because it felt the owners of a unit had changed its consented use as a household unit by making it available for short-term accommodation.

Councillor Nathaniel Hertz Jardine said the move added more weight to the council's argument that more regulation of short-stay accommodation was needed.

"The underlying issue is that we decide democratically as a city which areas of our city should be used for long-term residents, which are the residentially-zoned areas, and which ones should be used for tourist accommodation, which is commercial zones.

"What Airbnb operators do is they use areas that should be for long-term residents, and they basically convert them into motels and hotels, and this ruling just highlights that you shouldn't be doing that," he told RNZ.

It reinforced the need for a national bed register, he said.

"Even with this ruling, councils are still going to find it very hard to locate and identify those properties that are being incorrectly used with short-stay accommodation. So we still really need central government to help us with a register so we can get that information directly from platforms like Airbnb."

Hotel and motel operators had raised concerns about short-stay accommodation not adhering to rules around accessibility and fire safety. A bed register would make tracking properties and whether they were following the rules easier too, Hertz Jardine said.

Christchurch has seen a boom in townhouses in the central city. Frank Films

The council would wait for appeals over the ruling to be heard before moving forward, he said, so they would have certainty it reflected the new status quo.

"Then we're going to have to look really seriously about how that affects our responsibilities as a council about enforcing these safety standards across all of the Airbnb units in the city.

"Regardless of which way that ruling goes, we still need help from central government for a bed register, for a bed tax, and for better zoning rules so we can have real control over how our city is growing."

Short-stay accommodation operators were taking on a lot of risk, he added.

"If you haven't gotten a resource consent from your council, you're in a grey area and you're taking on a lot of financial risk. And we, as a council, we're not responsible for that risk.

"It could be that in a couple of years from now, it's going to be very hard for you to be operating that Airbnb unit.

World.title: Protesters interrupt ACT's South Island campaign launch
World.content:
Protesters received short shrift from ACT party faithful at its South Island campaign launch on Friday night.

There had been tight security at the Christchurch Town Hall, with bag searches for the hundreds of attendees and several people pre-emptively removed before the speeches began.

Three women calling for sanctions on Israel disrupted party leader David Seymour's speech, but were drowned out by jeers from the crowd.

The event comes days after a National Party public meeting in the city was disrupted around half a dozen times by people protesting Israel's wars in the Middle East, mining on the West Coast and southern data centres.

The ACT party had been announcing its proposal for of a national cancer centre, receiving a positive response at the event.

ACT party supporters argue with pro-Palestine supporters outside Christchurch’s Town Hall. RNZ/Keiller MacDuff

ACT list candidate Paul Henry publicly raised the idea as an off-the-cuff remark and said he expected to be chastised.

But he told the crowd at the launch the party has now adopted the policy, and will build the $2 billion centre if re-elected in November.

World.title: Live: Australia into the tail after Starc's five-wicket new ball spell
World.content:
Mackay's Harrup Park becomes the 12th Australian venue to host a Test match, with Australia desperate for an improved performance in the second and final Test against Bangladesh.

And they surely got it, Mitch Starc taking a wicket with the very first ball of the match and completing a five-wicket haul inside the opening hour to leave the tourists floundering on 5-13.

World.title: Lions coach 'feels sorry' for Swans as likely finals clash looms
World.content:
Embattled Sydney will brace for further fallout from the scandal that has rocked the AFL club, while finalising preparations for a dead rubber against North Melbourne on Sunday.

On Thursday, five players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon — were suspended for the rest of the season for "breaching club standards".

Separately, a police investigation continues into the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

On Friday, coach Dean Cox distanced himself from any blame for the events at the hotel, while captain Callum Mills said "we believe that the five players have let us down".

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham on Wednesday said the club-imposed sanctions would "torpedo" the second-placed Swans' premiership hopes.

Swans coach Dean Cox (left) and captain Callum Mills spoke to reporters on Friday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

In their SCG qualifying final, Sydney will most likely face reigning premiers Brisbane, who all but locked in third place with Friday night's 63-point win over Collingwood, unless Hawthorn leapfrog them on percentage with a big win over West Coast.

The team that finishes fourth plays runaway minor premiers Fremantle while third faces a decimated and embattled Sydney.

"I don't mind either or, to be honest with you," Lions coach Chris Fagan said after Friday night's match.

"It's just good to get the double chance.

"And I'm sort of thinking that Sydney have lost some players obviously due to the unfortunate thing that happened last week. But in some ways that can galvanise a club too.

"The guys that do get to play just might go that much harder and be that much more difficult to beat.

"So either way I'm just happy we finished top four. We travel well. Either way we're going to have to travel, so we'll take whatever comes our way."

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

Fagan hasn't spoken to his players specifically about the Sydney situation.

"There's been so much publicity around it — it almost goes without saying," Fagan said.

"I don't feel like I need to have a conversation with my players because it's pretty obvious, the repercussions for not thinking through your actions too clearly. And yeah, it's really unfortunate.

"I do feel sorry for Sydney because they have been such a terrific club in that regard for a long, long time but these sorts of things happen. It's just a bit of a head-scratcher, isn't it?

"You just wonder what was going through people's heads to let that occur."

Sydney on Friday disputed assertions there were more than five players in the East Melbourne hotel room on Monday morning.

James Rowbottom, Harry Cunningham, Angus Sheldrick, Caiden Cleary and Tom Hanily will replace the banned five players for the North Melbourne clash.

That game takes place after Sydney's AFLW clash with Essendon as part of a double header.

World.title: Argentina star hit with one of the biggest bans in World Cup history
World.content:
FIFA banned three Argentina players overnight, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents after losing the World Cup final.

The ban for Paredes — who grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground — ranks with the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suárez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.

Argentina defender Nahuel Molina was handed a seven-game ban while Thiago Almada was given a one-game suspension. FIFA imposed fines of $US90,000 ($AU125,000) on Paredes and Molina, and $US30,000 for Almada.

The ban for Paredes is effectively a one-year expulsion from the Argentina team as the FIFA calendar for national team schedules includes 10 games through June 2027.

All of those games could be friendlies with no competitive games currently scheduled.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina is confronted by Spanish captain Rodri after the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Martin Rickett/PA Images)

Gavi also was banned for one game, which is a Nations League match for Spain against England at Wembley on September 26.

An Argentina coach, Roberto Ayala, was also handed a three-game ban and a $US30,000 fine.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) was fined $US110,000 for a range of incidents during the World Cup, including players carrying a political banner about the Falkland Islands after the semifinal win against England, and discriminatory chants by fans.

AFA was also ordered by FIFA to spend $US100,000 on anti-racism projects. Argentina received $US34 million in World Cup prize money from FIFA.

AFA can appeal the longer sanctions and fines to FIFA, and likely after at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

"The AFA legal department will, in a timely manner, request from FIFA the grounds for the reviewable rulings in order to file appeals with the governing body's appeal committee, while retaining the future option of appealing to the CAS as a final recourse," the federation said in a statement.

Luis Suárez holds his teeth after biting Italy's Giorgio Chiellini. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

In 2014, Suárez was banned from all soccer for four months, including for his new club Barcelona, and eight more competition games for Uruguay for biting Italian defender Giorgio Chiellini in a World Cup group stage game in Brazil.

Paredes' 10-game ban equals that in 2013 for Josip Simunic of Croatia after winning a World Cup qualifying play-off. Simunic used a megaphone to lead fans chanting a slogan used by the country's pro-Nazi regime during World War II.

The on-field clashes at last month's final in East Rutherford, New Jersey — which were charged by FIFA as assault cases — came after Argentina lost a testy final to Spain where the team was mostly outplayed and barely created a scoring chance.

Spain forward Ferran Torres scored the only goal in the second period of extra time, after Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off.

FIFA disciplinary judges also ordered Argentina to play its next home game in a stadium limited to 50 per cent of capacity. FIFA deferred a second stadium sanction and a $US100,000 fine for probationary periods.

World.title: Wildcard woes: Why the Crows are walking a tightrope
World.content:
The weight of expectation can be a relentless burden.

For a success starved fanbase it can fuel volatility and in a two-team town it's a pressure cooker.

On the eve of finals, the Adelaide Crows find themselves walking a wildcard tightrope.

If the Lions, Hawks, Demons or Cats fail to lose their final round match-ups, which they are heavily favoured to win, the Crows would have to face Carlton or the Western Bulldogs in a sudden death showdown that 12 months ago didn't even exist.

Since the AFL expanded to 18 sides, a 15-win season guaranteed you a Top 6 finish in 11 of the 13 full length seasons and only twice locked in an away elimination final.

Now even if Adelaide beats GWS on Saturday night, it could still face the precarious possibility of being both the first minor premier in the AFL to exit in straight sets and the first ever side to lose a wildcard final.

It's a situation that will only amplify an emotional fanbase that is losing faith in its game plan and direction; often questioning selection and coaching online after results.

Adelaide's success starved fanbase make their opinions known. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Adelaide Head of Football Adam Kelly addressed their behaviour a month ago on SA Grandstand stating their performances were being exaggerated.

"Our game certainly stacks up. We've had some terrific wins and some disappointing losses but there are very few teams who don't have that," he said.

" Adelaide is a very noisy place. We just need to make sure we stay focused on what's important and stay grounded and realistic about where our game is at. "

Some pundits, including 4x Showdown Medallist Josh Francou, feel anything less than a preliminary final appearance would be a failed season.

"Based on last year and the list they've got, if I'm an Adelaide supporter and I'm not playing in a preliminary final that's a fail to me. You can't win a premiership from a wildcard," he said.

"I still have a lot of question marks over Adelaide. I can't work out what's happening off field with selection and they're the number one pressure team but when sides apply pressure to them they can't handle it."

Adelaide's AFL finals drought is over With a cohesive and suffocating defence, the Adelaide Crows have the tools to put the ghosts of 2017 behind them and reach the top of the AFL mountain.

Meanwhile, others believe a strong season doesn't always lead into another. Premiership winning Crow Rod Jameson foreshadowed this after Adelaide's qualifying final loss to Collingwood last year.

"It doesn't guarantee you'll play finals again next year. If they get a couple of key injuries and drop the odd game, they'll be under enormous pressure," he predicted.

The reality is winning a minor premiership guarantees nothing but a coin flip. Only 54 per cent of winners in the AFL era have gone on to secure a premiership within three years.

Is Nicks the man?

Unfortunately Crows fans are conditioned to a ruthless pursuit of success with Matthew Nicks the first coach in their history to survive three seasons without finals.

In the past, the club has been swift in its desire to bring a fresh voice in when momentum dwindled. Now it's headstrong in its pursuit of culture and firm in its belief Nicks is their man, extending him until the end of 2027 in December.

Matthew Nicks (left) has been Adelaide's coach since 2019. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Crows president John Olsen told ABC Sport ahead of their Round 13 clash with Geelong that the club was close to breaking its near 30-year drought.

"We are united in the view that we are nearly there," he said.

"We accept we have to take it up another gear with consistency but we're not far off the pace."

"Over my six years at the club I've seen impatient fans … sustained success is what every club wants to achieve. That means you have to be deliberate, focused and disciplined in how you go about attracting talent to the club."

Selection on the ground

Adelaide's underwhelming campaign can be attributed to numerous factors.

Availability of star players was a huge problem in the first half of the season.

Izak Rankine's pre-season hamstring issue and suspension meant the man who is currently the highest ranked player in the league over the last five rounds took eight weeks to be unleashed into the midfield.

Their three-time winning best and fairest winner and skipper Jordan Dawson had to take personal leave after the tragic passing of his brother.

Crows captain Jordan Dawson had to miss several matches this year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

All-Australian forward Riley Thilthorpe's output has dropped after tweaking his back travelling to Perth whilst Darcy Fogarty's own back issue saw him miss several weeks and key defender Mark Keane's broken ankle left the side without their defensive talisman until Round 15.

Despite the adversities, honourable losses to league heavyweights created optimism that once the troops were back the Crows would rise again.

To a degree they have, winning 8 of 11 games after their bye; but questions remain over their game plan and its ability to take the club to the top of the mountain.

The introduction and reshaping of numerous rules in the off season were designed to encourage free-flowing brands of footy.

Forever a Crow, Taylor Walker remains the boy from Broken Hill Taylor Walker arrived at the Adelaide Football Club as a 75-kilogram prospect who had only ever wanted to be a footballer. More than 300 AFL games and 700 goals later, he will retire as a club great.

Most have adopted that mantra with the ladder leading Fremantle Dockers giving Adelaide a harsh lesson last Friday on ball movement ending with +248 handball metres gained and 64 per cent ball use rating to the Crows 40 per cent.

It's a common theme for Adelaide who are last in the league for handball metres gained and third last for D50 to F50 transition.

It's a style that can open you up to immense pressure leading to high turnover rates in dangerous areas with the Crows 18th for defensive half turnovers.

The positive is they've improved on last year's midfield weakness, rising from 18th in clearance differential in the final month of 2025 to 7th in 2026 and are 4th across the season for score from centre bounce differential.

The other issue facing the Crows is selection. Their use of the new fifth bench rotation is puzzling with Matthew Nicks often prioritising pinch hit ruckman Toby Murray with limited impact.

Murray is second last for time on ground percentage (54 per cent) for players who've featured over 10 times. This decision came to a head last round when Murray had just two touches in 66 minutes.

Fans will farewell Taylor Walker at the Crows v GWS match on Saturday. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Meanwhile the management of retiring veteran Taylor Walker is in the spotlight after being flown to Perth but not selected for the finals shaping clash as a result of the clubs third game in 12 days; when the team faced cellar dwellers Richmond the week prior and could've rested their 36-year-old then.

It was an issue back in May when he played against Brisbane at the Gabba and then tore his hamstring in the Showdown five days later.

The AFL has openly said wildcard wins will be treated as a finals victory; news that was music to the ears of Essendon supporters who haven't won a final in over 8,000 days.

If Adelaide wins a match-up against a 10th placed side next weekend it might be a relief inside the four walls at West Lakes but will it satisfy a rabid fanbase?

We'll find out in a week's time.

You can hear ABC Sport's call of Adelaide v GWS from 7pm CST on ABC Listen and 891 ABC Adelaide.

World.title: 'Sad and disappointed' Sinner to miss first Grand Slam in seven years
World.content:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning his Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian wrote Friday that he will not be ready when the main draw begins on August 30.

"Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year," Sinner wrote in a post on X.

"We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I'm obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there."

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year's final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between the two has dominated men's tennis in recent years, and they met in the past three Grand Slam finals in 2025. Alcaraz took the most recent one with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner's title reign after he beat Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo.

He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.
